items.title: Antibacterial, antibiofilm, modulatory effects, pharmacokinetic profile, toxicity and molecular docking of Monarda fistulosa essential oil against Multidrug-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing spread of multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii strains and their high biofilm-forming capacity represent a serious global public health challenge, limiting therapeutic options. Given this scenario, the aim of this study was to evaluate the chemical composition, antibacterial and antibiofilm activity, modulatory effect in combination with carbapenems and ciprofloxacin, and in silico interaction mechanisms of Monarda fistulosa essential oil (MFEO) against nosocomial isolates of MDR A. baumannii , as well as to predict pharmacokinetic and toxicity characteristics. Phytochemical characterization via Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS) identified the monoterpene geraniol (92.3%) as the major constituent. Broth microdilution assays demonstrated significant antibacterial activity of MFEO, with Minimum Inhibitory Concentrations (MIC) ranging from 312 to 625 µg/mL and a bactericidal profile against all tested strains. In the synergism evaluation using the checkerboard method, MFEO exhibited an additive effect with meropenem and imipenem, reducing the carbapenem dosage required to inhibit bacterial growth in the most resistant strains, although it showed an indifferent interaction with ciprofloxacin. Furthermore, MFEO demonstrated strong dose-dependent inhibition during the initial cell adhesion phase and promoted significant eradication of pre-formed mature biofilms, outperforming meropenem control treatments at MIC, 2xMIC, and 4xMIC concentrations. In silico analyses indicated favorable pharmacokinetic profiles and low toxicity for the MFEO compounds, while molecular docking revealed moderate binding affinity of the compounds to the catalytic residues of OXA-24 and to the outer membrane protein A (OmpA). Taken together, these results demonstrate the potential of MFEO as a phytotherapeutic agent and as a promising adjuvant in combating severe infections caused by MDR A. baumannii .

items.title: Perceptions of psychosis and pathways to care in rural Zimbabwe: A mixed-methods study from the Z Factor community and public engagement project.
items.abstract: Background: Psychosis is among the most stigmatised, poorly understood mental health conditions in low- and middle-income countries. In rural Africa, pathways to care are shaped by interactions between stigma, family decision-making, cultural explanatory models, and structural barriers, yet limited research has examined how community perceptions of psychosis are formed and enacted within social contexts. Methods This convergent mixed-methods study was nested within Z Factor, a community drama-based public engagement project implemented in rural Zimbabwe. Quantitative data were collected through a cross-sectional survey (N = 60) using an adapted Community Attitudes to Mental Illness scale. Qualitative data comprised transcripts and video recordings from seven community-authored drama performances. Data sources were analysed and integrated to examine convergence, complementarity, and divergence in community perceptions of psychosis and pathways to care. Results Survey responses showed heterogeneous and contradictory attitudes. Most respondents rejected exclusion, with 80% disagreeing that people with mental illness deserve to be locked away, yet expressed ambivalence about autonomy, risk, employment, and care pathways. 58% agreed that people with mental illness should be treated like minors, 59% disagreed that they could work like any other person, and 77% agreed that community reintegration supports recovery. Drama narratives contextualised these patterns through seven themes: crisis-based perceptions of psychosis, carer burden and delayed help-seeking, elder-led family decision-making, accessibility and familiarity in pathway choice, trust and reassurance, expectations of rapid recovery, and medication as limited, inaccessible, or insufficient. Conclusions Community perceptions reflected the interplay among stigma, caregiving responsibilities, treatment expectations, structural constraints, and cultural explanatory frameworks rather than a single belief system. Help-seeking was shaped by accessibility, familiarity, trust, and coexistence of biomedical, traditional, and faith-based care systems. Participatory arts-based approaches can generate contextually grounded insights into psychosis stigma and pathways to care, stressing the need for collaborative, family-centred, and culturally responsive mental health engagement approaches.

items.title: Why access to health services is hard work: negotiating access in a cross-sectoral mental health program in Denmark.
items.abstract: Even in universal healthcare systems structured around principles of free and equal access, inequity in health continues to increase. This study explores how access to healthcare services is constructed in the intersection between individual experiences, organisational arrangements, and broader structural conditions. Using the analytical concept of candidacy, we examine how health and social care professionals and people seeking and receiving care negotiate access in everyday practice. Empirically, the study is based on a critical case study of a novel intersectoral care model for people with severe mental illness implemented in three Danish municipalities. The study draws on an ethnographically inspired design, including 34 individual interviews with people receiving care and health and social care professionals, three focus group interviews with health and social care professionals, and 15 observations of home visits and staff meetings. We show that, even after formal inclusion in a program designed to support access, people receiving care still had to work hard to engage with health and social care professionals, communicate symptoms and care needs, and sustain their eligibility for care. We argue that the candidacy framework helps explain access as an ongoing negotiated process across individual, organisational, and structural levels.

items.title: Composite sleep patterns and the allergy-related composite outcome among American and Chinese older adults: exploration of depressive symptoms as a potential mediator.
items.abstract: Background Sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms commonly co-occur in older adults, but their associations with heterogeneous allergy-related outcomes and the role of depressive symptoms remain unclear. Methods We analyzed 1,562 participants aged ≥60 years from NHANES 2005-2006. A composite sleep pattern combined sleep duration, trouble sleeping, and diagnosed sleep disorders. The allergy-related composite outcome comprised elevated total immunoglobulin E and seven questionnaire-assessed disease or symptom outcomes. Survey-weighted logistic regression evaluated associations. Depressive symptoms were assessed with a modified 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8), and statistical mediation examined indirect associations through its continuous score. We also conducted a complementary longitudinal analysis in 6,146 Chinese older adults from CHARLS. Results Poor versus healthy sleep was associated with higher odds of the allergy-related composite outcome (OR 2.100; 95% CI 1.328-3.322), wheeze (OR 2.148; 95% CI 1.296-3.559), and sneeze (OR 1.636; 95% CI 1.135-2.357). The estimated indirect association through depressive symptoms represented 22.5% of the total association. In CHARLS, impaired sleep quality was associated with incident asthma (OR 1.689; 95% CI 1.254-2.275), and the corresponding indirect association through depressive symptoms represented 28.3% of the total association. Conclusion Poor sleep was associated with heterogeneous allergy-related outcomes among US older adults, while CHARLS provided complementary longitudinal evidence for incident asthma. Depressive symptoms statistically accounted for part of the observed sleep-allergy association.

items.title: Antiretroviral therapy regimens initiated during pregnancy and risks of adverse perinatal outcomes.
items.abstract: Objective Antiretroviral therapy prevents mother-to-child HIV transmission during pregnancy. We estimated risks of adverse perinatal outcomes following postconception initiation of DTG/FTC/TAF, EFV/FTC/TDF, DTG/FTC/TDF, and DTG/3TC/TDF. Design Observational emulation of a target trial using population-based birth outcomes surveillance data from Botswana. Methods We emulated the IMPAACT 2010/VESTED trial protocol in Botswana's surveillance data and compared the risk of a composite outcome - stillbirth, preterm birth, or small-for-gestational-age birth - among individuals initiating DTG/FTC/TAF, EFV/FTC/TDF, or DTG/FTC/TDF at 14-28 weeks' gestation. After benchmarking results against the trial, we added DTG/3TC/TDF and evaluated individual outcomes (stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, very preterm birth, very-small-for-gestational-age birth, low birthweight, high birthweight, neonatal death). Results Adjusted risk of the composite outcome was 30.3% (unadjusted n = 83/278) for DTG/FTC/TAF, compared with 34.3% for EFV/FTC/TDF (1378/4042; risk difference -4.1% [95% confidence interval (CI) -10.6 to 2.4] and 34% for DTG/FTC/TDF [741/2,173; -3.7% (-10.3 to 2.9)]. All three risks were slightly higher than estimated in the trial. DTG/3TC/TDF showed a similar adjusted risk [34.7%; 1,008/2,883; -4.8% (-11.1 to 1.6)]. Risks of individual outcomes were generally comparable across regimens. Conclusion Our observational study findings for the composite outcome were comparable to the IMPAACT 2010/VESTED trial in a real-world programmatic setting and enabled evaluation of additional regimen and broader set of outcomes. In settings where randomized trial data are limited, well designed observational emulations of trials using nonrandomized data can provide informative evidence. As Botswana expands use of TAF in pregnancy, these results provide reassuring evidence supporting its safety.

items.title: Has Political Psychology Successfully Engaged with Social Identity and Group Psychology?
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter charts Katherine Reynolds’s engagement with political psychology through the lens of social identity and self-categorization theories, which emphasize how group membership shapes cognition, emotion, and behavior. It explains that individuals possess both personal and social identities, and that shifting salience between these identities’ influences prejudice, stereotyping, and political attitudes. Reynolds demonstrates that group-level psychological processes, rather than individual traits alone, account for social phenomena like discrimination, system justification, and collective action. It also shows how political behavior and leadership hinge on shared social identities, especially in contexts of social change, persuasion, and group mobilization. Finally, the chapter argues that political psychology must fully embrace group psychology to address urgent global challenges, stressing that a deeper understanding of social identity processes is essential for fostering behavioral change and sustaining democratic societies.

items.title: Carnivorous marsupials as model systems: four decades of ecological insights from Chris Dickman’s dasyurid research
items.abstract: Australia’s dasyurid marsupials comprise an ecologically diverse radiation of predators whose variation in body size, habitat use, diet and life-history strategies has made them powerful model systems for ecological research. Over more than four decades, Chris Dickman used dasyurids to address fundamental questions concerning competition, species coexistence, population dynamics and resource limitation, reproductive strategies, community assembly and environmental variability. His early research on Antechinus transformed Australian mammal ecology beyond descriptive natural history. He used manipulative field experiments to demonstrate asymmetric interspecific competition and identify behavioural interference, food limitation and resource partitioning as mechanisms promoting coexistence. Subsequent studies linked photoperiodic regulation of reproduction, multiple paternity and sexual selection to the evolution of male semelparity, while ecological and genetic studies revealed previously unrecognised biodiversity, culminating in the description of Antechinus agilis. Chris later expanded the spatial and conceptual scale of his research from interactions between closely related species to the organisation of whole communities and predator guilds. Comparative studies of arid-zone dasyurids demonstrated species-specific responses to habitat and climatic gradients, while long-term monitoring in the Simpson Desert revealed contrasting demographic responses to rainfall, temperature and vegetation across successive boom-and-bust cycles. The work using the Simpson Desert system ultimately extended ecological theory beyond mammalian interactions to competition between dasyurids and insectivorous reptiles. Collectively, Chris’ research established dasyurids as internationally important model systems and demonstrated how rigorous field experimentation, comparative ecology and long-term ecological monitoring can link natural history with ecological theory across multiple spatial and temporal scales. His work continues to provide an enduring conceptual framework for understanding ecological processes and conserving Australia’s unique carnivorous marsupials in a rapidly changing environment.

items.title: Development and usability evaluation of a web-based inventory system for small retail enterprises
items.abstract: Purpose: to develop a web-based inventory system for Toko Hardi Grosir Manisan and evaluate its functional performance and usability using black-box testing and the system usability scale (SUS). Method: this study employed a user-centered design approach within the human–computer interaction (HCI) framework, involving user requirements analysis, interface design, system development, functional testing using black-box testing, and usability evaluation using the system usability scale (SUS). The collected data were analyzed descriptively to assess system functionality and usability. Findings: showed that all 13 black-box testing scenarios passed, achieving a 100% pass rate. The SUS evaluation yielded an average score of 77.0, exceeding the benchmark of 68 and indicating above-average perceived usability based on the illustrative dataset. Implications: a practical solution for improving inventory management in small retail businesses by reducing reliance on manual records, facilitating stock monitoring, and improving inventory reporting. Originality: lies in integrating web-based inventory system development, black-box testing, and SUS-based usability evaluation within the specific operational context of a confectionery wholesale business, Toko Hardi Grosir Manisan.

items.title: Capacity-First Philosophy of Psychology
items.abstract: Abstract This paper aims to show that a neo-Aristotelian version of capacity-first philosophy of mind is fruitfully applied to a question which is specific to philosophy of psychology, namely: What counts as an adequate explanation in psychology? Drawing on Kenny, Glock and Schellenberg, the paper argues that the neo-Aristotelian capacity view is built around a set of criteria for the classification of capacities. All capacities are classified according to (1) possession-, (2) exercise-, (3) vehicle-, (4) opportunity-, (5) enablement- and (6) successful employment- criteria. These classification criteria are used to reconstruct the process of de-intellectualizing explanations of psychological phenomena. De-intellectualization targets theoretical assumptions about the circumstances in which the various criteria for classifying capacities are satisfied. The capacity approach offers a tool for regimenting the process of de-intellectualization. It also illustrates the contrast between de-intellectualization and Dennett’s homuncular functionalism. Rather than offering nothing more than conceptual clarity for debates about the metaphysics and epistemology of mind, the neo-Aristotelian capacity view explains why de-intellectualizing explanations is a feature of adequate explanations in psychology.

items.title: Measuring Implicit and Explicit Attitudes Toward Transracial Adoption
items.abstract: Attitudes toward Transracial Adoption, or TRA (i.e., White individuals adopting a child of a different race than their own) have been largely positive in a few experimental studies conducted, with only one study employing an implicit measure, the Implicit Association Task (IAT). The purpose of the current study was to assess the attitudes toward transracial (TRA) families with Black versus Asian children using both explicit (rating tasks) and implicit (Implicit Association Task) measures. In addition, religiosity was tested as a moderator of the attitudes toward TRA adoption. It was found that individuals had much more supportive attitudes toward photos depicting transracial families on the explicit measures as compared to the implicit measure. Additionally, on the IAT, individuals showed a bias toward photos depicting all-White families. When looking at religiosity, it was found that individuals who were more extrinsically religious had a greater preference toward supporting same-race families, while those who were more intrinsically religious showed more support for TRA adoption practices, but only in the condition where photos of a TRA family with a Black child were shown. The study suggests that individuals’ explicit attitudes toward transracial adoption appear supportive, underlying implicit biases favoring same-race families persist, highlighting the need for interventions to address these biases, particularly among extrinsically religious individuals.

items.title: Postcognitivism and the Unfolding of a Music Cognition Research Program: Embodiment, Imagination, and Intersubjectivity in the Latin American South
items.abstract: This narrative review examines a research program in psychology of music developed over two decades in Latin American South, tracing how studies at the intersection of music psychology, developmental psychology, and the philosophy of mind articulated a postcognitivist account of musical experience. The program unfolded in three overlapping phases: a focus on the listener’s imaginative engagement with tonal structure (2004–2009); an expansion toward embodied and intersubjective processes in adult–infant interaction and musical performance (2010–2018); and a consolidation around the second-person perspective and social enactivism (2018–present). The review revolves around five thematic axes: imaginative ontogenesis, metaphorization in adult musical practice, the postcognitivist turn, embodied performance, and second-person social cognition. Across studies of communicative musicality, image-schematic listening, cross-cultural and tango performance, jazz duos, ensembles, and dancing crowds, a recurring finding emerges: embodied engagement with shared musical structure takes stable but idiosyncratic, culturally and stylistically specific forms, rather than converging through a common entrainment mechanism. The program is discussed in relation to predictive processing, the coupling–constitution debate, simulation-theoretic, entrainment, and new-materialist accounts. Its limits—situatedness, the corroborative rather than comparative status of its second-person claims, and an underdeveloped pedagogical line—are acknowledged, and a future agenda is outlined.

items.title: Growing Up Algorithmic
items.abstract: The chapter critically examines how artificial intelligence has transformed children into consumers within the realm of online platforms, toys, and learning systems. It discusses the impact of AI-driven marketing strategies, including recommendation engines and synthetic influencers, on children's preferences and behaviors. The analysis is grounded in theories related to consumer socialization, media psychology, and digital surveillance, exploring how these technologies affect children's cognition, emotional attachments, and decision-making. It highlights concerns over hyper-personalized content, parasocial interactions with AI, and ethical governance regarding data privacy. Additionally, the chapter reviews existing regulatory frameworks, identifies gaps in protecting children, and proposes a holistic approach to understanding the interactions between children and AI. Finally, it advocates for ethical AI design, corporate responsibility, and enhancing AI literacy among parents, contributing to the broader conversation on child rights and digital well-being in an AI-driven era.

items.title: Contrasting isotopic responses of dryland and wetland plants to a century of global anthropogenic changes in nutrient cycling
items.abstract: Abstract. Anthropogenic emissions of carbon dioxide and reactive nitrogen in various forms disrupt the functioning of ecosystems around the world. In Europe, many valuable habitats, particularly wetlands and semi-natural dry grasslands, are under threat from ongoing eutrophication. However, due to contrasting water regimes, the uptake of anthropogenic nitrogen by plants in these ecosystems is different and is also interrelated with an increase in trophic level in both habitats. In our study, we measured the δ15N and δ13C values, as well as the total nitrogen content (TN), of 99 pairs of foliar samples collected from seven species of vascular plants in both dry grasslands and wetlands in Poland. Each pair consisted of a historical sample collected from a herbarium voucher dating from before 1939 (i.e. before artificial fertilisers were widely used in agriculture) and a contemporary sample collected in 2024 from the same species in a similar location. We performed t-tests to determine whether there were significant differences in the means of δ15N, TN and δ13C between samples from the two different habitats. Next, we calculated the differences in δ15N, TN and δ13C between the contemporary and historical samples for each pair. We then tested whether the difference for each species and habitat type was significantly different from zero using 90 % confidence intervals. Using multiple linear regression, we analysed the relationships between differences in δ15N and TN over time and the following factors: habitat type, the proportion of farmland in the surrounding landscape, the consumption of synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, and NOx deposition. δ15N and TN values were lower in dry grassland species than in wetland species, in both the contemporary and historical subsets. For dry grassland species, the mean δ15N value was lower in contemporary samples than in historical ones. For wetland species, the opposite was true. The difference in δ15N values between pairs of samples was positively related to the amount of farmland in the surrounding landscape. The mean TN was higher in contemporary than in historical wetland samples, but not in dry grassland plants. The mean δ13C value, corrected for the Suess effect, was lower in contemporary samples than in historical ones. The mean difference was −0.51 ‰ for dry grassland and −3.85 ‰ for wetland species. Our study revealed that the century of fossil fuel-derived carbon emissions, increased nitrogen input into the environment, and dominance of artificial fertilisers and combustion-derived nitrogen over biological nitrogen sources have not led to consistent responses across habitats and species. While the isotopic composition of nitrogen and carbon in plant tissues in Central Europe has undoubtedly changed, this change is highly context-dependent. Its magnitude and direction are impacted by the type of habitat and the identity and/or ecology of the species. As expected, man-made alterations appear to be more pronounced in wetland environments than in dryland habitats. Furthermore, the source of disruption may differ between the two habitat types. Specifically, wetlands are exposed to a multitude of anthropogenic nitrogen and carbon sources, whereas dry grasslands seem to be predominantly affected by changes in the composition of the atmosphere.

items.title: Fluctuating environments are sufficient to drive substantial variability in species abundance across locations
items.abstract: Species growing in environments that change in time and space will vary in their abundance across locations, even in the absence of persistent location preferences. Here we quantify this non-equilibrium effect by studying a minimal model of a spatially compartmentalised community with time-averaged-neutral competition but location-dependent environmental fluctuations. We analytically derive distributions of two-point inequality, defined as the log-ratio of a species' abundance across a pair of locations. We characterise how the balance of relaxation via migration and fluctuation strength determine the bulk and extreme value statistics of these distributions in the two-patch and infinite-patch cases. We demonstrate the existence of a noise-induced transition to bimodal inequality, which depends on the correlation timescale of the environmental fluctuations. Finally, we discuss the evolutionary benefit of finite migration rates in environments with temporal correlations.

items.title: “There's no shade anymore”: White phosphorus, destruction, and ecologies of displacement and return in south Lebanon
items.abstract: The 2023–2025 escalation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah triggered widespread displacement across South Lebanon while simultaneously generating extensive environmental destruction that continues to undermine prospects for return. This article examines how warfare-induced ecological damage including white phosphorus contamination, bombardment, deforestation, and the destruction of agricultural infrastructure, reshapes displacement trajectories in agrarian borderland communities. Drawing on an interdisciplinary framework integrating environmental displacement theory, critical refugee studies, and political ecology, the study analyzes qualitative interviews with displaced agricultural workers whose livelihoods depend on land, water systems, and biodiversity. The findings demonstrate that displacement in South Lebanon cannot be understood solely as a response to immediate violence, but also to warfare-induced environmental transformation. Instead, environmental degradation including burned olive groves, contaminated soil, damaged irrigation networks, livestock loss, and disrupted agricultural cycles, has destabilized the ecological foundations that sustain rural life. Even where residents physically return, recovery remains partial and uncertain as farmers confront declining soil productivity, crop disease, market distrust, and persistent fears of contamination. Environmental destruction therefore converts temporary evacuation into protracted displacement by eroding the environmental systems that sustain local economies and social reproduction. By foregrounding ecological viability as a condition for return, the article argues that conflict-induced displacement in agrarian regions is shaped not only by security dynamics but by the transformation of landscapes themselves. Durable return, therefore, depends as much on environmental restoration as on the cessation of violence.

items.title: A Subsequence approach to topological data analysis for irregularly-spaced time series
items.abstract: Abstract A time-delay embedding (TDE), grounded in the framework of Takens’s Theorem, provides a mechanism to reconstruct and analyze the state-space representation of time-series data. Recently, topological data analysis (TDA) methods have been applied to study this time series representation mainly through the lens of persistent homology. Current literature on the fusion of TDE and TDA are adept at analyzing uniformly-spaced time series observations. This work introduces a novel subsequence embedding method for irregularly -spaced time-series data. We show that this method preserves the original state space topology while reducing spurious homological features. Theoretical stability results and convergence properties of the proposed method in the presence of noise and varying levels of irregularity in the spacing of the time series are established. Numerical studies and an application to real data illustrates the performance of the proposed method.

items.title: Similarities and differences between solar and stellar flare pulsation processes
items.abstract: Abstract Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) are oscillatory signatures commonly detected in the light curves of solar and stellar flares, offering valuable diagnostics of the underlying magnetic and plasma processes. This review compares the observational characteristics, detection methods and physical interpretations of QPPs in both solar and stellar contexts. Solar flare QPPs, extensively studied in X-rays and extreme-UV (EUV) bands using instruments such as Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES), Spectrometer Telescope for Imaging X-rays (STIX) on-board Solar Orbiter and Fermi, display typical periods of tens of seconds and show correlations with flare duration and magnetic loop length. Stellar QPPs, observed in X-rays and white light by missions such as Kepler, Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and XMM-Newton, exhibit much longer periods—ranging from minutes to hours—consistent with larger-scale magnetic structures in more active stars. Despite differences in scale and observing band, statistical and comparative studies reveal common scaling relations and damping behaviours, suggesting that both solar and stellar QPPs are manifestations of the same fundamental mechanisms, probably magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) oscillations or oscillatory reconnection within flare loops. The comparison underscores a continuity between solar and stellar magnetic activity, linking the solar detailed physical processes to stellar-scale phenomena and providing constraints for future models and surveys. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Transferable mechanisms in the oscillatory processes of solar and stellar flares’.

items.title: Detector for fast wave trains in the solar radio emission
items.abstract: Abstract Quasi-periodic fast propagating (QFP) wave trains observed in the solar corona after some energetic events (solar flares, coronal mass ejections, jets) open possibilities for diagnostics of spatial and temporal scales of the impulsive energy release processes that are absent in the standard model of a solar flare. In addition, the dynamics of the wave trains and their characteristic spatial and temporal signatures allow for localizing the initial energy release volume magenta and to perform fine diagnostics of the transverse structures of plasma inhomogeneities in the solar corona. However, the small number of such events registered significantly limits their promising diagnostic potential. The aim of this paper is to perform an automatic search for fast wave trains in radio data. We apply classifying neural network/machine learning methods. Dynamic radio spectra obtained by Hiraiso radio spectrograph (HiRAS) radio spectrographs within the 20 MHz–2.5 GHz frequency band during 2011 were used. We consider 50 global coronal extreme ultraviolet (EUV) waves as marker events for a more targeted search in HiRAS data. Our automatic detector revealed 50 independent QFP-candidate events with temporal signatures similar to those of the fast wave trains, with 13 candidates connected with the global waves. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Transferable mechanisms in the oscillatory processes of solar and stellar flares’.

items.title: Polarized anisotropic stochastic gravitational wave background search with ground-based detector networks
items.abstract: Gravitational waves admit a Stokes decomposition into intensity ($I$), circular polarization ($V$), and linear polarization ($Q$, $U$), analogous to Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) polarimetry. We implement a full-Stokes maximum-likelihood SGWB map-making analysis for ground-based detector networks, promoting the standard cross-correlation data products used in existing pipelines to a joint reconstruction of $I$, $V$, $Q$, $U$. Applied to LVK O3 data, we constrain the polarized angular spectra $C^{VV}_\ell$, $C^{EE}_\ell$, $C^{BB}_\ell$ and $|C^{IV}_\ell|$. We show that an intensity-only model is biased when polarized sky components are present, since the detector-network Fisher inner product does not generally make the Stokes responses orthogonal. For transient CBC foregrounds, polarized shot noise is not parametrically suppressed relative to ordinary CBC intensity shot noise. The full Stokes framework separates the Stokes sectors while providing access to polarized anisotropies invisible to conventional intensity-only searches.

items.title: Probing flare-associated eruptions on AB Doradus via X-ray absorption variations
items.abstract: Abstract In this work, we investigate eruptive phenomena associated with X-ray flares on AB Doradus using observations from XMM-Newton. Our aim is to detect such events with the help of continuous X-ray absorption. The variation in the hydrogen column density (NH) is used as a primary diagnostic to detect such absorption or spectral hardening in the soft X-ray band below 1–2 keV. These variations may represent the signatures of the eruptive processes associated with flares, such as stellar prominences, failed eruptions or coronal mass ejections. We applied a time-resolved spectroscopy technique to track changes in the absorption parameter during flaring episodes. Our analysis shows statistically significant enhancements in NH, spanning from 0.3 to 3.4×1020 cm−2 during the flare and post-flare intervals. Out of six datasets, two sets containing multiple-overlapped flares show significant fluctuations and the remaining showed no such variations in NH. These variations indicate the presence of dynamic absorbing material along the line of sight and point to ongoing physical processes within the stellar corona. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Transferable mechanisms in the oscillatory processes of solar and stellar flares’.

items.title: Evolution of non-stationary quasi-periodic pulsations in solar flares with Aditya-L1/HEL1OS and GOES
items.abstract: Abstract In the present work, we use a phase-resolved methodology for the detection and characterization of non-stationary quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) in the hard X-ray light curves observed from the High Energy L1-Orbiting X-ray Spectrometer instrument on board the Aditya-L1 mission, complemented by cross-examination using soft X-ray observations from Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites. Our approach combines variational mode decomposition with Hilbert–Huang analysis and wavelet transforms to sharpen transient QPP signatures, extract narrowband amplitude–frequency modulated modes and track instantaneous period drift across various phases of the flares. By applying these tools to pre-flare, impulsive and decay phases and associated intervals, we identify the timing, duration and evolution of statistically significant oscillations and assess their relation to thermal and non-thermal flare components. Finally, we extend the method to the catalogue of non-stationary QPP flares reported by Mehta et al. (Mehta et al. 2023 Mon. Not. R. Astron. Soc. 523, 3689–3698. (doi:10.1093/mnras/stad1619)), where we identify statistically significant QPPs in both impulsive and decay phases for 74 out of 98 flares. Among these, 56.8% exhibit small period drifts, while 43.2% show larger deviations. Positive period drift dominates (73%), indicating a systematic increase in characteristic timescales as flares evolve. A phase–period–duration analysis reveals distinct regimes of non-stationarity, including overlapping multi-mode oscillations, intermittent same-period episodes and strongly evolving multi-modal behaviour. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Transferable mechanisms in the oscillatory processes of solar and stellar flares'.

items.title: Accretion onto a moving black hole for stiff equations of state
items.abstract: We revisit accretion of an asymptotically uniform fluid onto a moving Schwarzschild black hole, the relativistic analog of Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton accretion. Expanding on previous treatments, we focus on relativistic accretion of stiff fluids with adiabatic indices $Γ\geq 5/3$, which is particularly relevant for the treatment of primordial black holes captured by neutron stars. We perform numerical simulations to systematically explore the dependence of the steady-state accretion and drag rates on the asymptotic sound speed $a_\infty$ and relative speed $v_\infty$, and identify different regimes, both subsonic and supersonic, in which these rates either increase or decrease with respect to the spherical accretion rate for $v_\infty = 0$. We propose simple analytical approximations that capture the qualitative features observed in the dependence of the accretion and drag rates on $a_\infty$ and $v_\infty$.

items.title: Normal-field evolution and the breakdown of classical tearing in current sheets
items.abstract: Classical resistive tearing theory assumes a prescribed current-sheet equilibrium, but a finite normal magnetic field can evolve the background on the tearing timescale. For a transversely pressure-balanced Harris profile of initial half-thickness $a$ and asymptotic reconnecting-field magnitude $B_0$, threaded by uniform $B_n$ ($ξ=B_n/B_0$), we derive an exact evolution in ideal magnetohydrodynamics: counter-propagating Alfvenic fronts broaden the neutral layer and generate a central sheet-parallel flow with shear at its flanks. Inner-layer estimates recover $ξ_{\mathrm{crit}}\sim S^{-3/4}$ for breakdown of the classical resistive balance, where $S$ is the Lundquist number based on $a$. Numerical frozen-profile calculations show loss of central resistive dominance and decreasing tearing growth as the neutral layer expands. Eigenfunction comparisons at fixed wavenumber and predominantly Doppler-shifted propagation support a normal-field-modified continuation of classical tearing. The normal field supplies no net perturbation energy. Energy extraction from the reconnecting-field gradient weakens as the sheet broadens. The velocity-gradient contribution becomes comparable when the neutral-layer width approaches the initial sheet thickness, without reversing the decline in growth. For $S=10^6$, $\mathrm{Pr}_m=0$, and $ξ=10^{-4}$, the maximum growth rate falls by a factor of about ten from its initial value at neutral-layer half-width $w\simeq1.59a$, where the growth and broadening times become equal. Only about 0.18 additional upper-envelope e-folds are estimated between this crossing and $w/a=2$, where the growth rate is about 25 times smaller than its initial value. These results support dynamical suppression of further linear amplification over the sampled evolution, even though the instantaneous spectrum remains unstable.

items.title: Phase-drifting with emitting plasma temperature in the quasi-periodic pulsations of an X-class solar flare
items.abstract: Abstract Recent multi-wavelength observations of solar flares have provided new constraints on the physical origin of quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs). In an X-class flare, we detect a short-lived approximately 5-min QPP simultaneously in hard X-rays, extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) and soft X-ray emissions, exhibiting a clear phase-drifting behaviour with emitting plasma temperature. Based on phase-resolved timing analysis, it is found that (i) the QPPs in all diagnostics share nearly identical oscillation periods, (ii) a systematic temperature-dependent phase drifting is present, with the phase delay relative to the hard X-ray emission increases systematically from the hottest to cooler EUV channels, and (iii) the QPP persists for only a few cycles during the impulsive phase. These properties imply that periodic magnetic reconnection, possibly triggered by the leakage of 5-min oscillations from the lower atmosphere, modulates the non-thermal electrons responsible for the leading hard X-ray QPPs. Subsequently, plasma heating and cooling processes manifest sequentially across passbands with different temperature responses, resulting in the observed temperature-dependent phase drifting. These results provide novel observational evidence supporting the use of multi-temperature, multi-wavelength phase relationships to constrain the temporal evolution of flare energy release and the origins of QPPs. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Transferable mechanisms in the oscillatory processes of solar and stellar flares’.

items.title: Accelerated Execution of Bayesian Neural Networks using a Single Probabilistic Forward Pass and Code Generation
items.abstract: Machine learning models excel across applications like medical diagnostics, weather forecasting, natural language processing and autonomous driving, yet their inadequate handling of uncertainty remains crucial for safety-critical applications. Traditional neural networks fail to recognize out-of-domain (OOD) data, often producing incorrect predictions without indicating uncertainty. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a principled framework for uncertainty estimation by providing statistically grounded probabilities alongside predictions. Despite these advantages, BNNs suffer from high computational costs in both training and prediction. Predictions require sampling over weight distributions and multiple forward passes. To address this challenge, the Probabilistic Forward Pass (PFP) serves as an extreme approximation of Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI). While SVI assumes Gaussian-distributed weights without restrictions on activations, PFP extends this assumption to activations. This enables a fully analytical uncertainty propagation, replacing multiple forward passes with a single, more complex forward pass operating on probability distributions. Thus, PFP requires specialized Gaussian-propagating operators absent from standard deep learning libraries. We present an end-to-end pipeline for training, compilation, optimization, and deployment of PFP-based BNNs on embedded ARM CPUs. By implementing custom operators in the deep learning compiler TVM, we develop a dedicated operator library for multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks. Multiple operator implementations, along with manual and automatic tuning techniques, are applied to maximize efficiency. Ablation studies show that PFP consistently outperforms SVI in computational efficiency. For small mini-batch sizes, critical for low-latency applications, our approach achieves speedups of up to 3900 ×. Our results show that PFP-based BNNs achieve performance comparable to SVI-BNNs for uncertainty disentanglement on the Dirty-MNIST dataset and for complex OOD detection on CIFAR-10 against SVHN, all while significantly reducing computational overhead. These findings underscore the potential of combining Bayesian approximations with code generation and operator tuning to accelerate BNN predictions and enable their efficient deployment on resource-constrained embedded systems.

items.title: Learning about learning: A path from spin glasses to artificial intelligence
items.abstract: The Hopfield model, originally inspired by spin glasses, occupies a central place at the intersection of statistical mechanics, neural networks, and artificial intelligence. Despite its conceptual simplicity and broad applicability, it is rarely integrated into the undergraduate physics curriculum. We present the Hopfield model as a pedagogically rich framework that naturally unifies core topics from the undergraduate physics curriculum and that provides a concise introduction based on concepts such as a model's energy function, dynamics, and pattern stability. We discuss practical aspects of its simulation and provide simulation codes. We also propose problems designed to mirror research practice, which can be included in undergraduate classes.

items.title: The shift toward open and reproducible AI research
items.abstract: Abstract The reproducibility crisis has directed the AI research community toward improving documentation practices. Several studies have identified methodological issues, and in response, the most impactful venues in the field have introduced reproducibility checklists. We seek to understand whether documentation practices have changed over time by assessing all published papers at five leading AI conferences over the past decade. Seven reproducibility variables were identified, quality-assured and used to analyse 56,800 publications. Our analysis reveals that in the period 2014 to 2024, documentation practices have improved; papers sharing both code and data increased nearly sixfold, from 11% to 64%. Building on empirical reproducibility rates from a prior study, we estimate – inferred from documentation practices, not direct testing – that reproducibility increased from 28% in 2014 to 64% in 2024. Improvements in documentation practices predate the introduction of reproducibility checklists, suggesting these changes reflect a broader movement toward open science rather than a direct response to formal requirements.

items.title: The psychological effect of gamification mechanism in XR immersive environment on user willingness to behave
items.abstract: With the rapid landing of XR technology in the fields of architecture, education, medical and other fields, how to effectively guide user behavior through interaction design and content mechanism has become the core topic of human-computer interaction research. This paper examines how gamification mechanisms in an XR immersive environment influence users' behavioral intentions. Drawing on self-determination theory as the overarching framework and incorporating spatial narrative structure and the Octalysis framework, it systematically examines the mediating roles of the three basic psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—in the immersive experience. The study uses a combination of literature review and theoretical analysis, and constructs a theoretical model of "gamification elements → psychological needs to meet → willingness to act" through the depth analysis of typical XR cases such as medical training, building space guide, safety education and other types of XR cases. The study suggests that XR's distinctive sense of presence and interactivity may amplify the psychological effects of gamification drivers, such as a sense of mission and progression, while excessive competition and manipulative design may undermine intrinsic motivation.

items.title: iFLiP: accessible and low-cost lifetime fiber photometry for robust longitudinal and quantitative measurements of neural dynamics
items.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime measurements overcome the limitation of widely used intensity-based measurements in quantifying tonic activities and longitudinal changes in neural dynamics. However, while lifetime sensors are rapidly emerging, their applications have been limited by the complexity and expense of required hardware and software. Here, we report a simple, low-cost lifetime fiber photometry system, named iFLiP, that uses entirely off-the-shelf products and can be assembled without specialized expertise. We also develop software that enables turn-key operation. The integrated system can accurately monitor lifetime changes at up to 5000 Hz for days. We demonstrate the utility of iFLiP in monitoring the activity of protein kinase A (PKA) in vitro and in vivo, and uncover striatal subregion- and cell-type-specific PKA dynamics elicited by locomotion in mice. Additionally, multi-day continuous measurements in the basal forebrain reveal previously unappreciated PKA activity associated with sleep/wakefulness. Overall, iFLiP may make lifetime measurements broadly accessible in neuroscience research.

items.title: Aberrant cortical reorganization and astrogliosis underlie memory deficit post-traumatic brain injury: a longitudinal multiscale multimodal study
items.abstract: Integrating high-dimensional neuroimaging data across spatial scales remains a fundamental bottleneck in quantitative neuroscience. Here, we apply emerging analytical techniques including functional connectome gradient mapping and 3D segmentation of whole-brain cellular resolution microscopy data in a mouse model of traumatic brain injury. At the macroscale, longitudinal functional MRI revealed a transition from frontal hyperconnectivity to hippocampal hypoconnectivity and unimodal-transmodal gradient contraction indicating network dedifferentiation. At the cellular scale, deep-learning based segmentation of whole-brain light-sheet fluorescence microscopy volumes quantified regional astrogliosis, neuronal hyperactivity, and single-axon loss undetected by standard diffusion MRI. Multiscale multimodal data integration not only identified quantitative biomarkers predictive of memory performance post-injury but also enabled validation of in vivo modalities against more sensitive ex vivo histology. This study demonstrates a framework for probing complex multi-network cognitive functions and neurological disorders of network dysfunction.

items.title: Neurospirituality Reappraised: Brain Mechanisms of Transcendent Experience and Beyond
items.abstract: Background:Subjective experiences featuring altered self-awareness, temporal perception, or spatial boundaries—termed Non-Ordinary Experiences (NOEs)—occur across clinical neurology, psychiatry, and psychedelic medicine, including in insular ecstatic seizures, meditation, breathwork, hypnosis, and psychedelic therapy. Objective: To synthesize neurobiological and clinical literature on NOEs for neurologists by presenting three heuristic frameworks: 1.A six-dimension phenomenological taxonomy; 2.A tri-level descriptive taxonomy (computational "software", neuromodulatory-autonomic "firmware", and network "hardware"); 3.The Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model, which maps how acute neurodynamic shifts resolve into adaptive growth or clinical distress without reducing existential meaning to neural activity. Methods: Narrative synthesis of systematic reviews, coordinate-based meta-analyses, and key theoretical frameworks sourced via PubMed/MEDLINE. Results: Conflating spirituality, religion, and NOEs causes construct contamination in neuroimaging, compounded by unvalidated single-item measures and non-independent cohorts. An fMRI meta-analysis of meditation (34 studies, N=700) reveals aggregate recruitment of the right rolandic operculum, left insula, supplementary motor area, and hippocampus, arguing against a singular "spiritual center". First-person reports are mapped using a six-dimension schema (experiential content, temporal dynamics, spatial dynamics, volitional dynamics/agency, ownership/embodiment, cognitive stance). Mechanistically, states are organized across three bidirectionally coupled levels: computational inference ("software"), neuromodulatory-autonomic state-setting ("firmware"), and large-scale networks ("hardware"). Five entry routes (meditation, psychedelics, breathwork, hypnosis, focal neurological events) are hypothesized to share shifts in Bayesian precision weighting and network decoupling within the master Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model. Crucially, long-term outcomes (integration vs. distress) are not dictated by acute brain states alone, but are mediated by contextual filtering through the 4E Appraisal Prism (embodied, embedded, enacted, extended dimensions). Conclusions: Neurospirituality bridges network neuroscience, clinical neurology, and person-centered care. Clarifying biological substrates does not resolve existential validity. Clinicians must maintain a strict distinction between biological mechanisms, subjective experiences, and personal meanings (the Epistemological Invariant) to avoid pathologizing adaptive states or romanticizing neurological disease. Key terms: Spirituality; Neuroimaging; Meditation; Hallucinogens; Epilepsy.

items.title: Attachment and Caregiving as Social Allostatic Inference: An Updated Social Neuroscience Account from Single Brains to Dyads
items.abstract: Humans are highly social, and much of that sociality is regulatory: individuals manage the demands placed upon their bodies not only alone but through and with others. Attachment science has pursued how the brain accomplishes this for the better part of a century, and its most recent contribution has been neurobiological. Within the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt) programme, we previously specified a neuroanatomical architecture of two interacting systems and four domain-general modules for organised attachment, extended it to attachment disruption and disorganisation, and moved it from single brains to dyads through hyperscanning as part of Relational Neuroscience. What that work established energetically, through social allostasis, it did not specify computationally. Here we close that gap. Drawing on active inference, allostasis as interoceptive inference, and recent constructs of attachment as prediction, we propose the term social allostatic inference: the attachment system is one predictive-allostatic loop, the four modules are its successive stages, and organised, disrupted, and disorganised attachment are characteristic settings of the precision parameters that govern it. We extend the account to the caregiving system, which shares this architecture but infers rather than senses both the error that initiates its loop and the signal that terminates it. At the level of the dyad, interpersonal neural and bio-behavioural synchrony are read as indices of where regulatory work is invested rather than of bond quality directly. We address persistent misconceptions in trauma-informed practice and set out a measurement programme.

items.title: Translational neuroscience in psychoeducation: Mapping nonmotor circuitry to clinical management in movement disorders
items.abstract: Non-motor symptoms (NMS) affect nearly all patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD)and related movement disorders, with a mean of roughly 8–10 discrete symptoms perindividual. Their effect on quality of life often exceeds that of motor features, yetNMS remain under-recognized and undertreated, partly because patients and caregivers lack a working model of why these symptoms arise in a “movement” disease.This chapter applies neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to that gap andpositions it relative to conventional psychoeducation, health communication, and behavioral science. We propose the Map-Normalize-Differentiate-Navigate (MNDN)workflow as a movement-disorders-specific implementation of the NIPE frameworkdescribed in Chapter 1 of this volume. MNDN is a clinical proposal, not a validatedprotocol: its components are specified so that it can be tested, but its effects on patient outcomes have not been evaluated. Drawing on the tripartite cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop model and multi-transmitter degeneration, we provide modules for seven high-yield NMS: apathy, anxiety, executive dysfunction, REM sleepbehavior disorder, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, psychosis, and fatigue. Eachmodule summarizes the neural systems implicated, at the level of certainty the evidence supports, together with common misattributions, reversible contributors thatmust be excluded, management options and their limits, and patient and caregiverhandout content. We describe delivery formats from 3 to 5 min “micro-NIPE” sessions in routine visits to group and telehealth programs, specify the minimum components, provider competencies, dose, fidelity criteria, and proximal outcomes neededto test MNDN, and examine the ethical risks of neurobiological framing (determinism, oversimplification, over-attribution, and false reassurance), with particular attention to prognostic counseling in REM sleep behavior disorder. NIPE in movementdisorders is designed to reduce self-blame, support accurate symptom attribution, andimprove collaborative management. Whether it does so is an empirical question thatthis chapter aims to make answerable.

items.title: Measuring heart and breath: BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), a wearable open-source physiology recording platform
items.abstract: Psychology and social neuroscience study the biological basis of real-world interactive behaviors, such as dancing or playing music in groups. Autonomic nervous system reactivity, assessed through cardiac and respiratory signals, plays an important role in these behaviors. However, affordable, scientifically validated, research-grade devices for synchronous, real-time physiological monitoring of multiple individuals in natural settings remain scarce. We propose a wearable open-source physiological monitoring device, the BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), that can record cardiac and respiratory signals simultaneously from multiple individuals. B3 can be built cost-effectively using open-source blueprints and software we provide to yield a transparent, flexible option for research-grade physiological data collection. We empirically validated B3 against a widely used reference device in nine participants performing various motor and guided-respiration tasks. Heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV) were derived from electrocardiographic (ECG) signals, while respiratory sensors were evaluated for respiration rate and the accuracy and consistency of exhalation event detection. B3 derived HR and HRV closely matched reference measures across tasks, with high quality ECG recordings and minimal data loss, except during vigorous arm swinging. Respiratory rate and pattern metrics, including exhalation peak timing, also showed strong agreement. The B3 thermistor accurately tracked respiration rate even at higher breathing frequencies, although minor timing offsets occurred during some guided respiration segments. Overall, B3 performed comparably to the reference system for cardiac and respiratory measures, offering an affordable, open-source solution for physiological monitoring in real-world interactive settings.

items.title: Everyone else does it? Self-reported and perceived questionable research practices in music psychology
items.abstract: Questionable research practices (QRPs) may inflate false-positive rates and have been surveyed in psychology, ecology, and education, but not in music psychology. In a survey, 198 researchers who had authored empirical music-psychology work reported how often they had used 22 practices and estimated how many colleagues had used each. Three quarters (75.1%) reported at least one of the 18 practices bearing on false-positive risk, and 82.8% at least one of all 22. The most common were citing irrelevant work to satisfy a reviewer (46.9%) and selecting the most favourable analysis after seeing the results (43.5%). Respondents estimated that colleagues used 20 of the 22 practices more than they did themselves, but this gap is largely produced by the response scale in the survey and is not evidence of under-reporting. Researchers who thought practices were more widespread reported more of them between persons (OR = 2.16, 95% CI [1.74, 2.68]) and within them (OR = 2.62, [2.32, 2.96]), consistent with false consensus as well as descriptive norms. Music-specific practices were reported less often than reporting and analysis practices, though this depended partly on item wording and on whether a practice applied at all. Career stage showed no detectable association with admissions. Researchers reporting more open research practices reported more QRPs, not fewer (OR = 1.28, [1.14, 1.44]), which may indicate differences in disclosure as much as in behaviour. These results provide a first baseline for the field.

items.title: Environment-dependent diversity-stability relationship in microbial communities
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding the biodiversity–stability relationship has been a central challenge in ecology. Classical ecology proposed that diversity stabilize communities by distributing fluctuations across redundant pathways1,2, whereas random-interaction theory predicts that large and complex communities are unstable3,4. Field observations and experiments have reported positive, negative or negligible relationship between diversity and stability5–10. It therefore remains unclear diversity-stability relationship is universal or not and when a particular diversity–stability relationship emerges. Here we show that diversity-stability relationship is not fixed but environment-dependent, by studying bacterial communities under daily dilutions across temperature (10–50 °C) and dilution-rate (10¹–10⁵) gradients. Communities exhibit two distinct fluctuation regimes: collective fluctuations and dominant-species fluctuations. In the collective fluctuation regime, many species interact and fluctuate together, and exhibit a positive diversity-instability relationship and turnover in the most abundant species. In the dominant-species fluctuation regime, only one or a few abundant species fluctuate and exhibit no significant diversity-instability relationship. Single species measurements show that the community fluctuation regime is determined by the balance between species growth and pH-mediated death. We developed a consumer-resource model with pH feedback reproducing both the fluctuation regimes and diversity–stability relationships observed in the experiment. We further tested our theoretical interpretation by performing another experiment tuning the dilution rate to shift between the same two regimes. Our results thus show that two distinct environment-dependent ecological mechanisms and fluctuation regimes lead to different diversity–stability relationships.

items.title: “We Are All Sick”: Sanitation, Structural Neglect, and the Embodied Politics of Informality in Cape Town
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the relationship between sanitation, systemic neglect, and embodied suffering in the RR Section of Khayelitsha, Cape Town. Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with 30 residents and 16 activists, supported by computer-assisted coding in ATLAS. ti 22, it centres the statement of a resident - “We are all sick” - as a lens into perceived illness, infrastructural decay, and environmental degradation. Testimonies reveal how inadequate sanitation systems, including open toilets, bucket disposal, and stagnant wastewater, exacerbate illness and psychosocial stress in densely packed dwellings. Although authorities acknowledge the crisis, the continued classification of the settlement as “temporary” perpetuates inadequate service provision and entrenches vulnerability. Using Urban Political Ecology, the concept of slow violence, and embodied urbanism, the study demonstrates how informality produces material precarity and political marginalisation. Residents’ accounts highlight not only exposure and illness but also fragmented grassroots organising, civic disillusionment, and episodic resistance. These narratives transform private suffering into collective political speech, challenging invisibility and asserting claims to recognition and citizenship. The study contributes to debates on sanitation justice, health equity, and the politics of informality in African cities, advocating for infrastructure to be recognised as a fundamental right of urban citizenship rather than a conditional privilege.

items.title: The Evolutionary Self: Adaptive Prioritization as a Framework for Personality Structure and Change
items.abstract: Abstract Personality psychology has produced increasingly sophisticated accounts of individual differences through trait, motivational, interpersonal, developmental, and evolutionary approaches. Yet an important theoretical question remains: what principles organize these diverse sources of variation into coherent patterns of behavior across situations and over time? This integrative review proposes the Evolutionary Self, a framework that conceptualizes personality as a dynamic system of adaptive prioritization. Whereas existing models primarily describe personality traits, motivational systems, or the processes producing state variation, the Evolutionary Self focuses on how competing adaptive demands are weighted and coordinated when they cannot be simultaneously maximized. Drawing on evolutionary psychology, behavioral ecology, reinforcement sensitivity theory, attachment theory, self-determination theory, interpersonal models of agency and communion, and dynamic approaches to personality, the framework identifies three candidate domains of recurrent adaptive tension: Opportunity–Protection, Control–Accommodation, and Connection–Self-Reliance. These dimensions are not proposed as mutually exclusive psychological systems. Rather, they represent domains in which individuals must coordinate competing adaptive demands. The framework distinguishes capacities, priorities, states, positions, and trajectories. Capacities describe what an individual can potentially do; priorities describe which motives receive greater weight when competing demands become salient; states describe momentary configurations; position describes the person’s characteristic center of gravity; and trajectory describes systematic movement through adaptive space across situations and developmental periods. The model is offered as a theoretical synthesis that generates testable hypotheses concerning personality structure, contextual variability, development, stress response, and behavioral flexibility.

items.title: From Forest to Remedy: Medicinal Plants and Indigenous Therapeutic Knowledge among Naga tribes of Manipur, Indo-Myanmar Biodiversity Hotspot
items.abstract: Abstract Background The Rongmei and Tangkhul Naga tribes of Manipur are forest-dwelling communities that have traditionally relied on medicinal plants for primary healthcare. Ethnomedicinal knowledge has been documented for these tribes in the Tamenglong/Noney and Ukhrul districts, respectively, but populations in the ecologically distinct Churachandpur and Kamjong districts remain undocumented, and no study has applied a quantitative framework to compare the two tribes and prioritize species for pharmacological validation. We documented medicinal plant use among both tribes in these districts and evaluated informant consensus and cross-cultural patterns to inform pharmacological and conservation priorities. Methods Field surveys were conducted from July 2024 to April 2025 across ten villages using multistage sampling. Data were gathered from informal interviews and focus group discussions using modified semi-structured questionnaires, and plants were identified using regional floras and consultation with taxonomists. Relative frequency of citation (RFC), use value (UV), fidelity level (FL), and informant consensus factor (ICF) were used to assess species importance; the Jaccard Index (JI) and Rahman's Similarity Index (RSI) were used to assess cross-cultural similarity in taxa and therapeutic use. Informants were general community members rather than specialized healers, and because each tribe was sampled in a single district, tribal identity, local ecology, interviewer, and sampling intensity could not be disentangled. Effect sizes, an overlap coefficient that adjusts for unequal inventory size, and exact confidence intervals were added to the comparisons Results Among 373 informants (aged 21–86 years), gender, age, and education were not significantly associated with plant-use knowledge in either community. We recorded 131 taxa from 117 genera and 57 families, used to treat 83 human ailments, including a distinctive Rongmei practice of using burnt Goniothalamus sesquipedalis ash for gastritis, fever, and warding off evil spirits. Species overlap between communities was low (JI = 16.03%), and RSI (9.16%) indicated modest concordance in therapeutic use of shared taxa. Plant-part use differed significantly in five of ten categories, though leaves dominated in both. Brassaiopsis glomerulata , Phlogacanthus thyrsiformis , Mikania micrantha , Goniothalamus sesquipedalis , Zanthoxylum acanthopodium , and Clerodendrum colebrookeanum emerged as the strongest candidates for pharmacological screening based on RFC and FL. Several taxa, including Aquilaria malaccensis (Critically Endangered), are of global conservation concern. Conclusion The study documents rich community-level ethnomedicinal knowledge among the Rongmei and Tangkhul Naga and shows that low taxonomic overlap can coexist with substantial agreement in the use of shared plants. Pharmacological validation and safety screening of promising species, targeted conservation of threatened taxa, and community-controlled benefit-sharing are needed to safeguard this cultural and botanical heritage.

items.title: Twenty Years of Agricultural Mechanization Practices in Northern Nigeria: Bibliometric Insights into Research Trends, Productivity, Labor, and Technology
items.abstract: Abstract Agricultural mechanization significantly boosts farm productivity, reduces labor effort, and promotes rural development, especially in developing economies. This study investigated trends in mechanization, productivity, labor, and technology in northern Nigeria. A total of 735 open-access articles published in English from 2004 to 2025 were extracted from the Dimensions.ai database and analyzed using R's Biblioshiny package ver.5.0. The tools of analysis used include co-authorship networks, keyword co-occurrence, citation patterns, co-citation, and word cloud generation, etc. The results show a 20% annual growth rate and a peak in 2025 with 138 publications, reflecting increasing academic, policy interest in mechanization and agricultural modernization. The average citation count was 14.82, highlighting the relevance of the field. Collaboration involved 4,530 authors, with an average of 6.84 co-authors per-paper and 16.55% international partnerships, highlighting global cooperation. Chinese scholars dominate publication volume. With citation analysis, the distribution of research impact by region is seen to be diverse from Asia, Europe, and Africa. Mechanization’s impact on sustainability and livelihoods is illustrated in the research clusters identified and the core themes of agriculture, employment and climate change. The word-cloud analysis reveals that mechanization research in northern Nigeria is multi-faceted, local, and integrative, connecting technology, socio-economics, sustainability and ecology. The results indicate the influence of mechanization in rural development in different ways, so region-specific results are necessary. It is necessary to have policies and investments in local research for effective implementation. Inclusive mechanization policies should promote smallholder farmers, dissemination of knowledge, and resource access in region for sustainable rural development.

items.title: Reevaluating Body Size in Fossil Physeteroids Using Cranial Proportions
items.abstract: Fossil physeteroids exhibited substantially greater diversity in body size and feeding ecology than their extant relatives, yet body-length estimates for many taxa remain dependent on incomplete skeletons and proportional scaling from a limited number of reference species. This study reassesses body-size estimates in fossil physeteroids using a cranial proportion-based framework centered on bizygomatic width (BZW) and condylobasal length (CBL). The reference body lengths of Zygophyseter varolai and Brygmophyseter shigensis were reevaluated using published vertebral measurements, preserved skeletal length, and scale-bar-based skeletal data, and were conservatively set at approximately 6.5 m and 6.0 m, respectively. These revised reference values were then used to generate updated body-length estimates for a broad sample of extinct physeteroids. Revised estimates indicate that large-bodied physeteroids were relatively uncommon. Among the non-kogiid genera examined, only seven reached or exceeded 6 m in estimated total length, whereas Livyatan and Eophyseter were the only fossil genera estimated to exceed 9.5 m. Macroraptorial physeteroids ranged from approximately 4.0–4.3 m in Acrophyseter spp. to approximately 15–16 m in the giant Livyatan melvillei. The results further suggest that large body size evolved under multiple ecological regimes. Some large-bodied physeteroids were macroraptorial predators, whereas others show adaptations consistent with suction feeding or predation on smaller prey. The temporal distribution of giant forms is therefore more consistent with repeated, independent increases in body size than with a single evolutionary trend toward gigantism. However, incomplete preservation and uncertainty in the body lengths of reference taxa remain important limitations. The framework presented here provides a more consistent basis for reassessing body-size diversity in fossil physeteroids and can be refined as more complete cranial and postcranial material becomes available.

items.title: Transparency Is Necessary but Not Sufficient for Trust: Information Leakage and Procedural Overfitting in Supervised Machine Learning for Psychology
items.abstract: Min et al. (2026) provide a timely checklist for improving the transparency and trust of supervised machine learning (ML) research in psychology. I strongly endorse this goal and recognize that their focus on retrospective reporting is both valuable and the appropriate scope for an article. However, I suggest that two related issues warrant greater emphasis in their framework: information leakage and procedural overfitting. Both can produce optimistic estimates of model performance despite apparently transparent reporting. I propose two extensions to the checklist: reporting requirements that make information leakage auditable and prospective specification of key analytical decisions through preregistration. I argue that these additions would further strengthen the ability of readers and reviewers to evaluate the trustworthiness of supervised ML analyses in psychology. Moreover, comprehensive guidelines that do not sufficiently emphasize these issues may create unwarranted confidence that threats to valid model evaluation have been ruled out, allowing information leakage or procedural overfitting to remain undetected.

items.title: More Visibility for Diversity? A Systematic Review of LGBTQ+ Representation in Educational Psychology Journals
items.abstract: Students identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or otherwise non-heterosexual or non-cisgender (LGBTQ+) are increasingly represented. However, they still face additional challenges in educational settings, so Educational Psychology needs to research these issues. In this preregistered systematic scientometric literature review, we investigate (a) the extent of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology journals, (b) common themes and trends, and discuss systematic gaps for future research. After searching all 41,992 articles on ERIC, published in the most impactful (Q1 and Q2) Educational Psychology journals, we combined scientometric-quantitative and qualitative methods to review 68 eligible articles. We found a surge in publications from 2000 onward, driven by special issues. For almost half of these high-impact journals, we found no published articles on LGBTQ+ issues on ERIC; most publish only a few per thousand, even though this topic falls within their scope. Most often, these articles were empirical, correlational, and US-based, with inconsistent measures of LGBTQ+ identities. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified seven research themes and highlighted pertinent research gaps. To strengthen the evidence base in the field, future research should conduct rigorous longitudinal and intervention studies with culturally diverse samples and adhere to open science standards.

items.title: Artificial Agents as Leaders and Followers: An Integrative Role-Congruity Review
items.abstract: Artificial agents such as algorithms, virtual agents, and robots increasingly occupy organizational roles as leaders, followers, and partners. However, evidence on how people evaluate these nonhuman role occupants is mixed. We systematically review 107 empirical studies across management, psychology, engineering, and computer science through a role-congruity lens. A consistent pattern emerges: Artificial agents in leader roles face role incongruity, driven largely by perceived deficits in morality (e.g., fairness, trustworthiness). Agents in follower roles are evaluated as largely congruent with role expectations. Agents in partner and teammate roles show conditional congruity that depends on task context and design-based social cues (e.g., appearance, voice). We integrate these patterns into the Artificial Agent Role Congruity (AARC) model, a conceptual model that extends role congruity theory to artificial agents: perceived role (in)congruity occurs when observers compare role prescriptions with the attributes they ascribe to an agent from its design-based cues along a task dimension (competence, assertiveness) and a social-emotional dimension (warmth, morality). Based on this synthesis, we outline theoretical extensions, an agenda for future research, and guidance for managers and designers deploying artificial agents in organizational roles.

items.title: Avoiding the worst leaders is more important than getting the best
items.abstract: Society and organizations invest heavily in selecting the best leaders 1, and existing research shows a positivity bias by focusing on the bright side of leadership 2–4. Yet, according to Popper 5, the central question of institutional design is not who should rule, but how to prevent bad leaders from doing too much damage. This raises the question of which approach is more consistent with human psychology: Aim for the best leaders, or avoid the worst? We provide robust evidence for an “avoid-the-worst” principle in human leadership preferences. Although text analyses indicated that the top 100 business schools emphasize good leadership far more than the prevention of bad leadership, actual employee experiences from 9.9 million Glassdoor reviews show that people mentioned their leader 70% more often in the negative than positive section, and negative leader mentions predicted company ratings 1.5 times more strongly. Providing causal evidence, five high-powered experiments across 40 countries (N = 51,433) revealed that people were more willing to sacrifice time and money to avoid a bad leader than obtaining a good leader—across morality and competence, hypothetical and incentivized choice, ideology and culture. People care more about avoiding the worst leaders than getting the best.
