items.title: Mutualism in socio-semantic networks: structural correlates of publication output across ecosystem approaches to health
items.abstract: Abstract While existing scientometric research has examined how individual network position and team composition affect citation-based performance, less is known about how the structural configuration of socio-semantic networks relates to collective publication output. We propose that publication output is associated with configurations that foster mutual visibility between research topics (memes) and author communities. Drawing on mutualistic network theory from ecology, we hypothesise that lower bipartite modularity (H1) and higher nestedness (H2) are associated with higher publication output. We analyse 6,406 publications across three ecosystem approaches to health (EcoHealth, One Health, Planetary Health) over 18 approach × period observations (2004–2023), linking author communities to 20 research topics identified by Latent Dirichlet Allocation. Our analyses show an empirical asymmetry: bipartite modularity is negatively and robustly associated with publication output (Spearman ρ = −0.79, p < 0.001; robust across four community detection algorithms and under leave-one-out by approach), whereas weighted nestedness shows a positive but non-significant association ( ρ = +0.39, p = 0.11), in a direction consistent with H2 but without statistical support at the cell level. The modularity result supports the H1 component of the framework: low modularity — author communities touching multiple topics — fosters mutual visibility between authors and themes. Given the observational design, we report these as field-level patterns, not causal mechanisms. The non-significant association for H2, combined with marked algorithmic variability, invites reconsidering how nestedness is operationalised in socio-semantic contexts. By integrating social and semantic dimensions within a mutualistic framework, this approach complements existing scientometric tools.

items.title: Characterizing social-ecological transformation trajectories in the Western Indian Ocean
items.abstract: Abstract Marine social-ecological systems (SES) face unprecedented pressures, demanding approaches designed to create more sustainable interactions within and between those systems. Transformation theory offers frameworks for understanding and documenting systemic change, but its empirical testing in marine contexts remains limited. This study analyzes three case studies involving marine transformations in the Western Indian Ocean region: bycatch mitigation in South African fisheries, fisheries co-management in Tanzania, and regional pelagic fisheries’ management. Each process was documented following Olsson's framework (preparing for change, navigating transition, and building resilience) and characterized using selected transformation attributes. Our findings show that the type of outcome a transformation produces is closely linked to its entry point (practices, views, and structures). Practices-oriented transformation achieved rapid, measurable gains, but limited spillover into underlying values. Views-oriented transformation achieved broader, deeper change across dimensions but unfolded more slowly. Structures-oriented transformation, in the absence of shared values among actors, produced the shallowest and most contested change. Local and national initiatives achieved deeper transformation than regional governance, which faced greater barriers from competing interests and institutional inertia, highlighting the role locally-driven action can play in advancing transformation.

items.title: Effect of Positioning On Financial Performance of Tour Firms In Kabale District, Uganda
items.abstract: This study examined the effect of positioning on the financial performance of tour firms in the Kabale, Uganda, focusing on value proposition, target audience and content strategy. A cross-sectional quantitative research design was employed, targeting 140 registered tour firms. Stratified random sampling produced a sample of 120 respondents drawn from tour, marketing, and finance managers. Primary data were collected using structured questionnaires designed on a 5-point Likert scale. Instrument validity was ensured through expert review, pilot testing, and content validation, while reliability was confirmed with Cronbach’s alpha values above 0.85. Ethical procedures, including informed consent and confidentiality, were observed. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 27, with descriptive statistics summarizing trends and simple linear regression testing hypotheses at a 5% significance level. Findings revealed that community engagement, such as timely information sharing and feedback, significantly predicted financial performance (R² = .126, p < .001). Market positioning emerged as the strongest predictor, accounting for 27% of the variance (R² = .270, p < .001), with firms using targeted messaging and audience segmentation to enhance competitiveness. Overall, the results demonstrate that social media marketing is a key driver of profitability, revenue growth, and return on investment among tourism enterprises. The study concludes that tour firms can leverage social media as a cost-effective and interactive tool to strengthen customer relationships and improve financial outcomes. It recommends greater use of user-generated content, adoption of advanced analytics, and diversification of strategies across platforms to maximize returns.

items.title: Controlling ammonia in aquatic environments: a critical review linking monitoring, prevention, and recovery
items.abstract: Abstract Ammonia is a key inorganic nitrogen species connecting aquatic chemistry, ecosystem toxicity, and atmospheric particulate formation. In water, environmental risk is not governed solely by total ammonia nitrogen (TAN), but by the speciation equilibrium between NH $$_3$$ 3 and $$\text {NH}_{4}^{\,\,+}$$ NH 4 + , controlled by pH, temperature, and hydrological variability. Increasing nitrogen loads from wastewater effluents, anaerobic digestion residues, and agricultural activities generate short-term concentration peaks that are difficult to capture by conventional monitoring and complicate regulatory management. At the same time, tightening discharge limits and circular-economy policies require strategies that both mitigate environmental impacts and enable nutrient recovery. However, ammonia is still typically addressed separately in environmental chemistry, agricultural management, and wastewater engineering, preventing coordinated mitigation. Here, we review environmental ammonia in aquatic systems using an integrated chemical–environmental–technological perspective. The major points are the following: (i) chemical speciation governs toxicity, volatilization, and environmental transport more strongly than total concentration alone; (ii) analytical monitoring approaches, from colorimetric and ion-selective electrode measurements to sensors and passive sampling techniques, are essential for interpreting environmental exposure and guiding regulation; (iii) upstream measures, including controlled-release fertilizers and urease inhibitors, reduce emission peaks at the source; (iv) physicochemical and biological treatment processes such as air stripping, membrane contactors, adsorption, and nitrification enable ammonia removal and recovery from wastewater and digestate; and (v) recovered ammonia can serve as a secondary nitrogen resource within circular nutrient management. Integrating monitoring, prevention, treatment, and reuse provides a framework for data-driven ammonia control across environmental and engineered water systems.

items.title: Effects of Ageratina adenophora invasion on soil multifunctionality and microbial networks of Pinus yunnanensis forest in the Panxi region, China
items.abstract: The Panxi region of southwestern China, an important ecological barrier in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, is severely invaded by Ageratina adenophora , yet the effects of this invasion for soil functioning remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we selected Pinus yunnanensis forest plots with slight or heavy A. adenophora invasion, to investigate the effects of invasion on soil multifunctionality and microbial networks. Additionally, we selected heavily invaded plots co-occurring with the nitrogen-fixing tree Alnus cremastogyne to investigate whether co-occurrence with nitrogen-fixing tree mitigates the negative effects of invasion on soil multifunctionality. The results of this study are as follows. First, heavy invasion by A. adenophora significantly reduced soil multifunctionality, and although microbial network stability increased, this functional decline was associated with the modular and functionally constrained architecture of the networks. Second, the coexistence of nitrogen-fixing tree A. cremastogyne significantly mitigated the invasion-related loss of soil multifunctionality. This mitigating effect was underpinned by increased microbial network complexity and connectivity. Third, random forest analyses identified microbial network complexity as the most important biotic predictor of soil multifunctionality, whereas its network complexity was strongly associated with soil nutrient availability and microbial cohesion. Overall, our findings suggest that microbial network complexity may play a more critical role than diversity or stability in maintaining soil multifunctionality following plant invasion. Our study provides critical empirical evidence for managing invasion pressure and preserving soil health in this ecologically vital region.

items.title: Avoidance without flight: actor and timescale in the spatial responses of an arboreal primate to human presence
items.abstract: Abstract Animals that share landscapes with people must balance the avoidance of human disturbance against the costs of avoidance itself, and movement is the currency in which this trade-off is paid. Because the distance between an animal and a person is a joint property of two trajectories, however, a change in that distance need not reflect movement by the animal. We examined how an energy-conservative, time-minimizing primate, the mantled howler monkey ( Alouatta palliata ), responds spatially to a recurring and mobile human presence in an agroforestry landscape, decomposing the response according to who moves and over what timescale. Using 3,116 synchronous 15-min records of group and nearest-worker locations, worker numbers, worker activity and sound levels collected across 112 days, we analysed the probability and geometry of movement, partitioned changes in monkey–worker distance into monkey- and worker-generated components, and modelled day-scale space use against daily disturbance dose. Groups moved in only 14% of intervals, and the probability of moving was unrelated to worker numbers, sound level or proximity to workers. When groups did move, their movements were not oriented away from the nearest worker (mean resultant length = 0.08), a result robust to day-level dependence, to permutation tests preserving within-day trajectory structure, and to correction for effective sample size. Approximately 63% of the magnitude of change in monkey–worker distance was generated by the worker’s rather than the monkeys’ movement. Over whole days, groups maintained greater distance from workers when more workers were present (≈21% per standard deviation of daily worker number) without any increase in their own travel. This day-scale separation was itself substantially human-generated: it persisted when monkey positions were held fixed, was absent when worker positions were held fixed, and was attenuated by controlling for the kind of work being done. Reactive flight is therefore not how these monkeys respond to people, and the separation that does emerge over longer timescales cannot be attributed to the monkeys without further evidence. Energetic constraint remains a plausible framework for the absence of costly avoidance movement, but it is not tested here. Our results show that proximity-change metrics can overstate active avoidance when the human party is itself mobile. Significance statement Wild animals increasingly live among people, and avoiding human disturbance is widely assumed to mean moving away from it. But moving is costly, especially for animals that conserve energy by resting most of the day, and the distance between an animal and a person depends on both of them. Studying an arboreal monkey with exactly this energy-conserving lifestyle, we separated two things usually conflated in studies of avoidance: whether an animal actively moves away when a person is near, and whether it ends up further from people over longer periods. The monkeys did not flee: they were no more likely to move when workers were numerous or close, and when they did move their movements were not aimed away from workers. Most of the moment-to-moment change in how far apart they were came from the people moving. On days with more people the groups were further away, but much of that separation, too, was produced by where the work happened rather than by the monkeys relocating. Avoidance can be far less active than proximity measures suggest.

items.title: Water management in flood-prone areas using nature-based solutions: an AI-assisted systematic review and thematic analysis
items.abstract: Nature-based solutions (NbS) are increasingly used to reduce flood risk and improve water management in flood-prone areas. However, research remains fragmented across disciplines, regions, and scales, making it difficult to identify research trends, knowledge gaps, and priorities. This study presents an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted systematic review of peer-reviewed articles published between 2016 and 2025, retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, a large language model (LLM) was used to screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review by the research team. A structured dataset was developed through LLM-assisted data extraction and human validation. Semantic clustering and LLM-assisted synthesis were then used to identify research themes and summarize implementation conditions, benefits, limitations, and research needs. A total of 185 studies were included, which were predominantly published between 2021 and 2025. Nine research themes emerged, with urban green infrastructure for runoff mitigation, spatial planning and decision support, and catchment and hydraulic modeling accounting for 47.6% of the studies. Research was concentrated in the United Kingdom, China, and the United States, with limited representation from Africa and Latin America. The evidence relied mainly on scenario modeling and short monitoring periods, while social equity, public acceptance, and maintenance outcomes were rarely assessed using standardized metrics. While literature reviews have been previously done on the topic of NbS for flood-prone water management, to our knowledge, this is the first review of NbS for flood-prone water management to combine LLM-assisted screening, data extraction, and synthesis with semantic clustering and human validation. The study provides a thematic evidence map, examines temporal and geographic research trends, and presents a reproducible workflow to support future environmental evidence synthesis.

items.title: ECOLOGIES OF WELL-BEING: LINKING FOREST BIODIVERSITY, INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE AND HOUSEHOLD RESILIENCE IN KAKAMEGA TROPICAL RAINFOREST ECOSYSTEM
items.abstract: Forest biodiversity and indigenous ecological knowledge are interconnected socio-ecological assets that sustain the livelihoods and resilience of forest-dependent communities. However, environmental degradation, biodiversity loss, and socio-economic transformation increasingly threaten these systems and the well-being they support. This study examined the relationship between forest biodiversity, indigenous knowledge, and household resilience among communities surrounding Kakamega Tropical Rainforest, Kenya. Specifically, it explored indigenous knowledge of forest resource use, assessed the contribution of medicinal plants and non-timber forest products to livelihoods and health, evaluated the role of forest-based foods in food security, and examined community participation in biodiversity conservation. Guided by Firey's Theory of Resource Use and the Sustainable Livelihoods Approach, the study employed a mixed-methods cross-sectional design involving 384 households. Quantitative data were collected using structured questionnaires, while qualitative data were generated through key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, and qualitative data were analyzed thematically. The findings indicate that indigenous ecological knowledge remains central to the sustainable use and conservation of forest biodiversity, supporting household resilience through healthcare, nutrition, income generation, and cultural continuity. Indigenous conservation practices also enhance community stewardship and sustainable forest management. However, declining biodiversity and the erosion of indigenous knowledge pose significant challenges. The study concludes that integrating indigenous knowledge into biodiversity conservation and forest governance can strengthen household resilience and sustainable development. It recommends documenting indigenous knowledge, conserving indigenous plant species, and promoting community-based forest management and participatory conservation policies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Free Flap Monitoring in Reconstructive Surgery: A Review
items.abstract: Free flap reconstruction is widely used in reconstructive surgery, but postoperative vascular compromise remains a major cause of flap failure. Early detection of arterial insufficiency and venous congestion is essential for timely intervention and flap salvage. Conventional monitoring is limited by observer variability, flap accessibility, and assessment frequency. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support more consistent and continuous surveillance. This review examines the diagnostic performance, clinical utility, implementation challenges, and research priorities of AI-based postoperative free flap monitoring. Applications include smartphone photography, serial clinical images, thermal imaging, near-infrared spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, and other monitoring signals. Tasks encompass classification, segmentation, severity grading, and longitudinal prediction, distinguishing detection of existing perfusion abnormalities from prediction of subsequent compromise. Emerging studies report promising performance in identifying impaired perfusion; however, diagnostic accuracy alone does not establish clinical effectiveness. Limitations include small or single-center cohorts, image-level data leakage, class imbalance, inconsistent reference standards, limited external validation, and insufficient evidence of improved flap salvage. Performance may vary with flap location, tissue characteristics, skin pigmentation, image quality, and monitoring protocols. Intraoral and buried flaps pose additional accessibility challenges. Safe implementation requires standardized data acquisition, transparent alert thresholds, clinician oversight, privacy protection, and clear escalation pathways. AI may complement established clinical assessment, but routine adoption requires multicentre validation and prospective evidence of clinical benefit. Future studies should prioritize patient-level performance, detection time, false-negative events, unnecessary alerts, workload, flap salvage, and patient outcomes.

items.title: Ecological structuring of biosynthetic potential across terrestrial soil-associated Streptomyces genomes
items.abstract: Streptomyces populations represent one of the richest reservoirs of microbial specialized metabolites, although the ecological organization of their biosynthetic diversity remains insufficiently resolved at large genomic scales. In the present study, 14,597 publicly available genome assemblies were initially screened. Environmental metadata associated with each genome were subsequently retrieved from the corresponding NCBI BioSample records and systematically curated to retain genomes originating from terrestrial soil-associated environments while excluding marine, freshwater, clinical, laboratory, industrial, and other non-terrestrial sources. Standardized climatic and edaphic variables were examined using principal component analysis (PCA), K-means clustering, and Kruskal–Wallis tests to evaluate ecological differentiation across terrestrial soil-associated Streptomyces populations, with false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment applied to inter-cluster comparisons. PCA revealed pronounced environmental structuring, with Principal Component 1 (PC1) explaining 44.3% of the total variance and Principal Component 2 (PC2) contributing 31.1%, together accounting for 75.4%. K-means clustering resolved three environmentally coherent groups with distinct soil and climatic profiles. Significant differentiation was detected for soil pH, rainfall, temperature, soil organic carbon, and clay content, with adjusted p -values below 0.001. Genome mining using GECCO (GEne Cluster prediction with COnditional Random Fields) revealed extensive biosynthetic diversity dominated by polyketide- and non-ribosomal peptide-associated gene clusters. Total biosynthetic richness also differed significantly among ecological groups (Kruskal–Wallis statistic = 7.28, p < 0.05). This study provides a large-scale ecological-genomic framework linking environmental differentiation with biosynthetic organization across terrestrial soil-associated Streptomyces populations, advancing understanding of soil microbial and metabolic diversity.

items.title: ILLEGAL MANGROVE EXPLOITATION IN JOLO SULU: BASIS FOR PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT
items.abstract: This study explored the lived experiences and perceptions of local government officials, community representatives, and affected individuals regarding illegal mangrove exploitation in Jolo, Sulu. Specifically, it examined their awareness of mangrove protection laws, the underlying causes of illegal extraction, its environmental and socioeconomic impacts, the effectiveness of existing policies and interventions, the challenges encountered in conservation, and strategies for strengthening mangrove protection. The study employed a qualitative research method using a phenomenological design. Seventeen participants were purposively selected, comprising eight local government officials, six community representatives, and three affected individuals. Data were gathered through face-to-face interviews using a researcher-made, semi-structured interview guide validated by experts. The interview data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis approach. The findings revealed that participants generally understood mangrove protection laws and recognized the ecological and socioeconomic importance of mangrove ecosystems. However, illegal exploitation persisted due to poverty, limited livelihood opportunities, cultural practices, inadequate environmental awareness, community tolerance, and weak law enforcement. Mangrove destruction contributed to coastal erosion, flooding, increased vulnerability to natural hazards, declining fisheries productivity, biodiversity loss, and disrupted household livelihoods. Existing interventions, including law enforcement, monitoring, mangrove rehabilitation, environmental education, livelihood assistance, and community participation, had contributed to greater awareness and conservation involvement. Nevertheless, their effectiveness remained constrained by inadequate resources, limited monitoring capacity, economic dependence on mangrove resources, weak institutional coordination, and climate-related threats. The study concludes that sustainable mangrove conservation requires an integrated and community-responsive approach combining stronger law enforcement, continuous environmental education, adequate institutional support, sustainable alternative livelihoods, active community participation, and climate-resilient conservation measures. These strategies may help reduce illegal mangrove exploitation and protect the environment, livelihoods, and safety of coastal communities in Jolo, Sulu.

items.title: Modelling habitat suitability for multiple priority weed species to predict invasion hotspots for strategic management in complex landscapes
items.abstract: Abstract Established weeds require ongoing, costly management to reduce harm to agricultural and environmental values. Heterogeneous landscapes that encompass substantial variation in land use, vegetation and topographic conditions are often under threat from multiple long-established weeds, whose simultaneous management presents strategic and tactical challenges. Systematic monitoring of weed populations provides more detailed insights into invasion threats than the more readily available presence-only data. We leveraged six years of weed density monitoring and high-resolution environmental data to model habitat suitability for four high-priority weeds across the Australian Capital Territory. We developed habitat suitability maps for African lovegrass, Chilean needlegrass, serrated tussock grass and St John’s wort. Maps were then standardised and combined to derive potential multi-species invasion hotspots and explore patterns of secondary invasion threat. While some species shared environmental predictors such as elevation, each responded to distinct combinations and interactions among environmental predictors. Overall, we found approximately 71% of the study area was suitable for multiple weeds to exceed low densities, but only 11% was sufficiently suitable for two or more species to reach high densities. In those invasion hotspots, habitat suitability was often highest for St John’s wort, and where suitability was highest for either of the other three weeds, St John’s wort typically posed the second highest invasion threat. These findings could improve management efficiency by focussing integrated control of multiple co-occurring species in a small number of priority invasion hotspots. Our study demonstrates how spatially explicit models and analyses based on systematically collected weed density data can inform a multi-species, landscape-scale approach to weed management.

items.title: Blue injustice: competing claims for freshwater forage fisheries
items.abstract: Abstract This paper draws on blue justice scholarship to examine how inequalities are intensified as small forage fish move between “fish as food” and “fish as feed,” highlighting distributional justice as a key lens for understanding pressures on fisheries-based households. Forage fish, which can be consumed in diverse forms or diverted into aquafeed (including direct feed and fishmeal), are contested resources among artisanal fishers, fish processors, and small producer fish farmers in Cambodia’s Tonlé Sap region. We show how declining forage fish populations—driven by overfishing, environmental change, and aquaculture’s demand for feed—reshape livelihoods, including women’s post-harvest work, and exacerbate social inequities by redirecting an important food source away from low-income populations.

items.title: Intra- and interspecific variation in growth and heat tolerance traits of saprotrophic fungi isolated from pyrogenic carbon in a frequent fire ecosystem
items.abstract: Fire is an important disturbance in many terrestrial ecosystems across the globe. A byproduct of fire is partially combusted organic matter, or pyrogenic carbon (PyC), which can be difficult for most microbes to decompose. Pyrophilic fungi are fungi that can break down and use PyC, survive through extreme heat, and/or have adaptations to rapidly colonize under postfire conditions. However, only a few fungal taxa have been characterized for their pyrophilic traits. Understanding the growth strategies and pyrophilic traits of fungi found in post-fire environments can help us understand mechanisms of ecosystem recovery from fire and their contributions to carbon cycling. Here, we characterized the pyrophilic traits of seven fungal isolates ( Trichoderma and Mucor species) by testing their ability to grow on different carbon substrates (media containing PyC, sucrose, or water agar). Isolates were also incubated across a range of temperatures to determine if carbon source impacts thermotolerance and if the ability to catabolize PyC co-occurs with higher thermotolerance. We found that PyC-associated fungi exhibited a wide range of growth strategies, and many were able to grow on PyC. However, we found weak evidence for thermotolerance and growth on PyC as coordinated pyrophilic traits. Finally, we also found high intraspecific variation in growth strategies and weak tradeoffs along the fungal economics spectrum growth traits. These results were additionally supported by FT-IR analysis of substrates and fungal tissues, which showed different tissue chemistry based on substrate. Our results highlight the importance of intraspecific variation in carbon use ability and growth strategy as a key area of future research for pyrophilic fungi.

items.title: Macroinvertebrate diversity patterns in floodplain wetlands under fragmentation, northwest China
items.abstract: Wetlands are among the most diverse and dynamic ecosystems on Earth. Meanwhile, they have experienced habitat loss and degradation worldwide, leading to biodiversity declines. As a primary driver of wetland loss and degradation, fragmentation can pose profound impacts on natural environmental regimes of floodplain wetlands. Here, we investigated the composition of macroinvertebrate assemblages in the Heihe Floodplain, Northwest China comparing wetlands with connection to rivers (i.e., riverine wetlands) and those isolated from rivers (i.e., lacustrine wetlands), with the wetland type used as a proxy for hydrological connectivity. We observed evident differences in species composition and community structure of macroinvertebrates between riverine and lacustrine wetlands. Three indicator species ( Palaemon sp., Radix sp., Gyraulus sp.) were identified for lacustrine wetlands, whereas none were detected for riverine wetlands. Compared to lacustrine wetlands, riverine wetlands had significantly lower taxonomic and functional richness, but they had significantly higher mean local contributions to taxonomic and functional beta diversity, as well as more heterogeneous communities at regional scale. Our study highlights the need for a balanced wetland conservation strategy that protects lacustrine wetlands with high local diversity while also maintaining or restoring appropriate hydrological connectivity to promote regional biodiversity recovery and enhance ecosystem service functions. It also underscores the importance of incorporating functional traits and beta diversity into environmental monitoring and conservation planning to safeguard wetland biodiversity and associated ecosystem functions and services.

items.title: Persistence of sedimentary DNA in burrowing marine benthos: evidence from the decapod Upogebia major
items.abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis is an increasingly important tool for surveying marine organisms. Requiring only small environmental samples, eDNA analysis enables efficient assessment of the occurrence and distribution of target taxa based on eDNA detection and concentration. This approach is particularly effective for organisms difficult to observe and collect conventionally. However, knowledge of eDNA persistence in the environment remains limited. A better understanding of taxon-specific eDNA persistence is essential for accurate interpretation of eDNA data. Burrowing benthic organisms are suitable targets for eDNA-based surveys because they are difficult to collect and observe directly, making field surveys time-consuming and labor-intensive. However, little is known about the persistence of their eDNA. Because burrowing benthos remain in close contact with sediments, their eDNA is expected to occur predominantly in sediments as sedimentary DNA (sedDNA). Therefore, we evaluated the persistence of sedDNA in a tank experiment with burrowing decapod Upogebia major , a species widely distributed in tidal flats throughout East Asia. The results suggest that, at least under tank conditions, the sedDNA of this species can persist in sediments for at least 30 days and up to 50 days without substantial changes in concentration. Three explanations are possible: (1) the amount of sedDNA produced by U. major may have greatly exceeded its rate of degradation, resulting in very slow degradation; (2) bacterial activity, one of the drivers of sedDNA degradation, may have been lower under tank conditions than under natural field conditions; and (3) the burrows may have functioned as a continuous source of sedDNA, allowing sedDNA to be intermittently released from the burrows even in the absence of animals. Collectively, these factors may have contributed to the long-term persistence of sedDNA without substantial changes in its concentration. However, the detection frequency and concentration of sedDNA varied among sampling locations and days. Both differences in the behavior of U. major and the low mobility of the sediment, which limited sediment mixing and redistribution of sedDNA, likely influenced this variability. This study provides new insights into the dynamics of sedDNA in burrowing benthos and highlights the importance of considering its persistence when interpreting sedDNA data.

items.title: Pre-service biology teachers’ motivational responses to the sustainable digital vegetation mapping program design: A pre-implementation study
items.abstract: Plant awareness disparity (PAD) poses a challenge to botany education. However, students’ evaluations of instructional designs before implementation remain underexplored. This study aimed to describe pre-service biology teachers’ motivational responses to the Sustainable Digital Vegetation Mapping Program (SDVMP) and integrate these responses with their qualitative perceptions. A convergent mixed-methods design was employed involving 122 Biology Education students at Universitas Sriwijaya who had completed a Vascular Plant Botany course. Before completing the instruments, participants reviewed an infographic presenting the proposed SDVMP design. Quantitative data were collected using an adapted 34-item Instructional Materials Motivation Survey (IMMS) based on the four ARCS dimensions. Qualitative data were obtained through one open-ended question, and 109 responses were analysed thematically. The overall IMMS mean was 3.28 (SD = 0.36; α = 0.96). Satisfaction (M = 3.34) and Relevance (M = 3.34) had nearly identical mean scores, followed by Attention (M = 3.26) and Confidence (M = 3.19). Eight themes emerged, with Appeal and Innovation (77.06%), Relevance and Usefulness (42.20%), and Program Clarity and Organization (33.94%) being the most prominent. Sustainability and Green Campus appeared in 20.18% of responses. Overall, students perceived the SDVMP design positively in motivational terms. However, these responses reflect preliminary evaluations of the infographic rather than evidence of program effectiveness or a reduction in PAD. The findings can inform formative refinement of the program design and provide a basis for evaluating its effectiveness after implementation.

items.title: From cultural realization to psychological resilience: traditional Chinese folk songs, well-being, and intergenerational knowledge transmission in indigenous ethnic minority communities
items.abstract: Introduction Folk songs such as Zhuang antiphonal singing, Dong Grand Song, Miao Feige, and Hua’er singing preserve cultural knowledge and ancestral traditions among ethnic minority communities in southern and southwestern China. However, their potential role as psychological resources remains insufficiently examined. This study investigated the association between cultural realization, psychological resilience, cultural identity, and meaning-making, considering the moderating roles of intergenerational transmission engagement and community cultural vitality. Methods A convergent mixed-methods design was employed. A total of 520 participants from six communities representing four folk-song traditions completed standardized and newly developed instruments. Quantitative data were analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis and a moderated mediation model with a multilevel extension. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 36 participants and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results Cultural realization was positively associated with psychological resilience, both directly and indirectly through cultural identity and meaning-making. The indirect association through cultural identity was stronger among participants with higher engagement in intergenerational transmission. Community cultural vitality was positively associated with resilience; however, its cross-level moderating effect was not supported. Given the inclusion of only six communities, this finding remains inconclusive. Qualitative analysis identified four themes: ancestral dialogue, collective singing as a coping mechanism, living pedagogy, and fragile communal recovery. Discussion The findings suggest that traditional folk songs may function as culturally embedded psychological resources by supporting cultural identity, meaning-making, and resilience. Nevertheless, the cross-sectional, self-reported design precludes causal conclusions, and the observed associations may partly reflect selection into singing. Further longitudinal and multilevel research involving more communities is needed to clarify these relationships.

items.title: Marine heatwave exposure is changing unevenly across Scottish aquaculture sites
items.abstract: Introduction Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are an increasing climate hazard for coastal aquaculture, yet regional assessments may not resolve how exposure varies across the locations where farms operate. Methods Here, we analysed daily ~5-km OSTIA sea surface temperature data from 1990 to 2025 at the locations of 361 active Scottish finfish and shellfish farms, represented by 218 unique grid cells, and compared satellite temperatures with in situ records from eight farms. We used principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering to describe long-term MHW exposure, and mixed-effects models to assess temporal changes. Results Two broad exposure profiles were identified. Cluster 1 was characterised by higher mean, maximum and cumulative intensity, whereas differences in event duration and frequency between clusters were smaller. Temporal trends, however, differed more strongly. MHW frequency increased at similar rates in both clusters, while event duration, cumulative intensity and severity increased more rapidly in Cluster 2. Between 1990 -2019 and 2020 -2025, estimated event duration increased by 44.6% in Cluster 1 and 89.9% in Cluster 2, while cumulative intensity increased by 50.0% and approximately 127.5%, respectively (cluster × period, p < 0.001). The estimated probability of a Severe or Extreme event rose from 2.2% to 26.2% in Cluster 2, compared with 1.8% to 6.1% in Cluster 1 (cluster × period, p < 0.001). Mean event intensity changed comparatively little. Discussion These findings show that MHW exposure across Scottish aquaculture is multidimensional, spatially uneven and changing at different rates through time. The resulting hazard -exposure landscape helps bridge regional MHW assessments and individual-farm monitoring, providing a foundation for more targeted monitoring and future assessment of aquaculture vulnerability and climate risk.

items.title: The effect of rural tourism on rural prosperity: evidence from China on agricultural labor productivity, incomes, and household food consumption
items.abstract: Policy support in China has disproportionately favored rural tourism as a core pillar of rural revitalization. However, its net effect on agricultural labor productivity, rural income, and household consumption remains empirically untested. This study examines how rural tourism expenditure affects these three dimensions of rural prosperity and evaluates alternative policy instruments to maximize developmental benefits. The analysis employs a dynamic autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) simulation model using annual Chinese data from 1994 to 2023. The findings reveal that an increase in rural tourism expenditure significantly reduces agricultural labor productivity, rural household income, and rural household consumption in both the short run and the long run. A positive shock to rural tourism expenditure similarly generates a negative response across all three outcomes, with the effects persisting over the forecast horizon. These results suggest that the net effect of rural tourism expansion on rural prosperity is consistently negative, challenging the conventional assumption that rural tourism serves as an unconditional driver of rural development. The findings call for conditional tourism subsidies, complementary investments in agricultural capital, and spatially differentiated rural development policies that safeguard agricultural livelihoods while permitting tourism to develop only where it does not displace farming.

items.title: Associations between stand structure and the predictability of multiple forest carbon pools in the transition zone between the Qinghai–Tibet and Loess Plateaus
items.abstract: Introduction Complex mountain forests in the transition zone between the Qinghai–Tibet and Loess Plateaus are characterized by strong topographic heterogeneity and marked stand structural variation. These conditions may lead to differences in the predictability of forest carbon pools. However, the role of stand structure in shaping the predictability of multiple forest carbon pools remains insufficiently understood. Methods In this study, we used field survey data from 90 plots (77 forest plots and 13 shrubland plots) collected in 2024-2025 in the Taohe National Nature Reserve, Gansu Province, together with vegetation indices, topographic, climatic, soil, and stand structural variables, to develop random forest models for multiple forest carbon pools. For plot-scale modelling, 77 forest plots were used, and soil carbon was assessed at 0–60 cm depth. We assessed the composition, predictability, and major predictors of biomass, soil, litter, deadwood, and ecosystem carbon densities. Results The mean ecosystem carbon density was 306.79 Mg C ha -1 , with soil carbon and biomass carbon accounting for 71.5% and 24.9%, respectively, suggesting that these two pools comprised the dominant carbon pools. Plot-scale random forest models showed clear differences in predictive performance among carbon pools. Biomass and ecosystem carbon densities were predicted with relatively high accuracy, with cross-validated R2 values of 0.766 and 0.659, respectively. Litter carbon density showed moderate predictability, whereas soil and deadwood carbon densities were poorly predicted. Biomass carbon density was primarily associated with stand volume proxy, tree height, and basal area proxy, whereas ecosystem carbon density was mainly associated with tree height, stand volume proxy, and stand age. Spatial random forest models showed relatively poor predictive performance. Discussion These differences in predictive performance indicate that stand structural variables were closely associated with the predictability of biomass and ecosystem carbon densities. Overall, carbon density predictability in complex mountain forests showed clear component dependence. Component-specific modelling of multiple forest carbon pools helps reveal differences in their key predictors, predictive performance, and uncertainties associated with spatial extrapolation, and may provide useful information for forest carbon monitoring, spatial pattern characterization, and carbon management zoning in the Taohe Reserve.

items.title: Dark Energy Survey Year 6 Results: improved mitigation of spatially varying observational systematics with masking for the MagLim++ lens sample
items.abstract: As photometric surveys reach unprecedented statistical precision, systematic uncertainties increasingly dominate large-scale structure probes relying on galaxy number density. Defining the final survey footprint is critical, as it excludes regions affected by artefacts or suboptimal observing conditions. For galaxy clustering, spatially varying observational systematics, such as seeing, are a leading source of bias. Template maps of contaminants are used to derive spatially dependent corrections, but extreme values may fall outside the applicability range of mitigation methods, compromising correction reliability. The complexity and accuracy of systematics modelling depend on footprint conservativeness, with aggressive masking enabling simpler, robust mitigation. We present a unified approach to define the DES Y6 JOINT footprint, integrating observational systematics templates and artefact indicators that degrade mitigation performance. This removes extreme values from an initial footprint, leading to the final JOINT evaluating the DES Y6 lens sample MagLim++ on this footprint, we enhance the Iterative Systematics Decontamination (ISD) method, detecting non-linear systematic contamination and improving correction accuracy. While the mask’s impact on clustering is less significant than systematics decontamination, it remains non-negligible, comparable to statistical uncertainties in certain w(theta) scales and redshift bins. Supporting coherent analyses of galaxy clustering and cosmic shear, the final footprint spans 4,031.04 deg^2, setting the basis for DES Y6 1x2pt, 2x2pt, and 3x2pt analyses. This work highlights how targeted masking strategies optimise the balance between statistical power and systematic control in Stage-III and -IV surveys.

items.title: Kratos-polrad: Novel GPU system for Monte-Carlo simulations with consistent polarization calculations
items.abstract: Abstract Polarized radiation serves as a vital diagnostic tool in astrophysics, providing unique insights into magnetic field geometries, scattering processes, and three-dimensional structures in diverse astrophysical scenarios. To address these applications, we present Kratos-polrad, a novel GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo Radiative Transfer code built upon the heterogeneous computing framework of Kratos, designed for self-consistent and efficient polarization calculations. It utilizes a comprehensive treatment of the Stokes parameters throughout photon propagation, featuring grain–lab frame transformations using quaternion algebra and a consistent analytical integration of polarized extinction and emission within each cell, which are useful in modeling radiative transfer processes with scatterings by aligned dust grains. The code implements two-step polarimetry imaging that decouples Monte Carlo sampling of scattering physics from imaging geometry, enabling efficient synthesis maximizing the utilization of photon packets. Extensive validation against analytical solutions and established codes demonstrates accurate treatment of diverse polarization phenomena, including self-scattering polarization, dichroic extinction in aligned dust grains, and complex polarization patterns in twisted magnetic field configurations. By leveraging massive GPU parallelism, optimized memory access patterns, and analytical approaches for optically thick cells, Kratos-polrad achieves performance improvements of ∼102 times compared to CPU-based methods, enabling previously prohibitive studies in polarimetric astrophysics.

items.title: Identifying heating processes in simulations with an entropy-based scheme: A single jet episode in a galaxy cluster
items.abstract: Understanding heating processes in galaxy clusters is essential for predicting the regulation of radiative cooling and star formation and for clarifying the mechanisms underlying active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback in cool-core clusters. We investigated the processes through which AGN jets deposit heat into the intracluster medium (ICM) by tracking passive entropy scalars in magnetohydrodynamic simulations. This allowed us to systematically disentangle the contributions from different heating channels. We successfully validated this method with several idealized tests, including turbulent heating, heating by anisotropic Braginskii viscosity, dissipative and adiabatic heating by shocks using in situ shock-detection methods, as well as cosmic-ray heating through the excitations and damping of Alfvén waves. Using this methodology, we simulated single-epoch outbursts of high-power jets with varying densities in a cluster environment. Light jets produce wider bubbles, displacing a larger fraction of the gas in the cluster's core, whereas comparatively denser jets propagate more efficiently to larger distances without significantly disturbing the central region. During early evolution, shock heating of the ICM prevails irrespective of jet density. At later times, light jets primarily heat the ICM through turbulently induced heating (which includes dissipation of vortices emerging from a turbulent cascade and mixing gas of different temperatures) and compressible dissipation of sound waves and very weak shocks, while denser jets continue to dissipate most of their energy via shocks. Particularly, turbulently induced heating by solenoidal-shear motions prevails inside the cocoon, whereas shocks and acoustic compressions dominate outside. In light jets, the forward shock weakens rapidly, whereas dense jets can sustain strong bow shocks to large distances. This heating estimator allows us to identify the dominant heating mechanism responsible for resolving the cooling flow problem in future self-regulated AGN jet simulations.

items.title: Nexae in caverna: The secular evolution of disks via collectively excited, transient spiral structure
items.abstract: Using the hydrodynamical (fluid) approximation, we present a self-consistent theoretical framework that couples the origin, evolution, and decay of spiral structures to the secular dynamical evolution of their host galactic disks. Our approach highlights nonresonant spiral excitation through azimuthal forcing that leverages mild, pervasive gradients in the disk's mass and angular momentum distributions, structural features we term ``cavernae.'' These cavernae are weaker but more widespread than the sharp features behind traditional groove mode excitation and are commonplace in exponential disks. We discuss how nonresonant features combine with the other responses in exponential disks -- resonant dressing, steady waves, and groove modes -- to produce a global, evolving spiral ``nexum'' that transports angular momentum and reshapes the disk. Using expressions for spiral torques, angular momentum transport, and heating, we demonstrate that global spirals are intrinsically self-limiting; the angular momentum changes and heating they generate rapidly quench their own growth, dictating a finite lifetime for any single spiral episode. A succession of transient episodes, each with properties adjusted to the changed disk conditions, lays the pathway to long-lived spiral activity. This behavior suggests that the character of secular evolution shifts over time. We find that the short-lived, high-multiplicity (high-m) spirals that dominate in dynamically cold disks induce widespread, impulse-like nonresonant heating, yet with a low ratio of heating to radial migration. As the disk warms, these high-m features are suppressed, leading to steadier, lower-m spirals that heat the disk progressively more efficiently near discrete resonances. In this light, the dynamical coldness of many disk galaxies observed today requires a past dominated by high-m transient perturbations, whereas warmer, more compact systems reflect an advanced stage of secular evolution regulated by transient, low-m spirals. Ultimately, the heating and reshaping produces stable (featureless), centrally concentrated but disky, rotating early-type galaxies.

items.title: Ion composition of the Earth plasmasphere observed by the PEP JEI and RPWI instruments on the JUICE spacecraft
items.abstract: Abstract. During the first Earth gravity assist maneuver of JUICE on 20th August 2024 the spacecraft passed through the Earth plasmasphere for about 2 hours. Before closest approach at a distance of 2.1 RE the Jovian Electron and Ion spectrometer JEI of the PEP instrument suite was switched on for 40 min in an ion mode test configuration. The high plasma density of about 3000/cm3 (observed by the RPWI plasma wave instrument) led to a negative charging of the spacecraft which allowed a rare observation of the cold and dense plasmaspheric ion populations. Since the ions are only corotating with the Earth at a velocity of about 1 km/s at this distance the observed ion speed is dominated by the spacecraft velocity of about 8 km/s. For this reason ions with different mass appear at different energies in the energy spectrum observed by the JEI sensor. In addition the spacecraft potential leads to specific filtering of ion masses in the observed angular distribution. By calculating the sensor response function for these specific observing conditions it is possible to quantify densities of the different ion species. But this response calculation depends critically on the response of the JEI channel electron multipliers to the ion velocity and mass. Since the sensor was operated with a low post-acceleration further laboratory calibrations may be needed for this specific setup. Still we can already conclude from the observations that ions with mass >4 amu/q contribute at least 30 % to the observed total ion density. A flux peak observed in the energy spectrum at 15 eV can only be explained by the presence of heavy molecular ions with mass ~30 amu/q. Molecular ions have only been rarely detected in the outer Earth plasmasphere. The observations indicate that the JEI sensor can also be used to achieve ion composition measurements in the exospheres of the Jovian moons.

items.title: SN 2023rve: A Type II Supernova with No Nebular Oxygen
items.abstract: Abstract We report on multiband photometric and spectroscopic observations of SN 2023rve, a nearby Type II supernova (SN II) discovered in galaxy NGC 1097 ( D = 15.4 ± 3.2 Mpc). Nearby SNe II provide constraints on late-stage evolution and progenitor mass loss, in particular the role of circumstellar material (CSM) in shaping SN II observables. SN 2023rve peaks with an absolute V -band magnitude of −17.1 and declines at a rate of 0.90 ± 0.02 mag/50 days during the plateau. The bolometric light curve implies a 56 Ni mass of 0.0064 M ⊙ . Using hydrodynamic light-curve modeling, we infer an intermediate-mass progenitor (∼14–18 M ⊙ ), a low explosion energy of 0.27 × 10 51 erg, and a dense CSM component with radial extent of 2900 R ⊙ and density parameter of 10 18 g cm −1 . This supports growing evidence that enhanced pre-SN mass loss influences the diversity of SNe II. The nebular spectra of SN 2023rve show narrow He i lines and an absence of [O i ] lines unprecedented among Type II SNe. Comparison with other SNe II shows that only two other known objects, both with higher velocities, lack oxygen signatures at similar epochs, <10% of the sample. The lack of oxygen emission combined with low explosion energy, a long plateau, and a small synthesized nickel mass may be consistent with partial fallback of material onto the compact remnant. We also discuss alternative explanations for the suppressed oxygen emission, including dust formation, oxygen–calcium mixing, and ongoing CSM interaction.

items.title: New framework for lightning-fast gravitational wave analysis of pulsar timing data
items.abstract: Pulsar timing array data analysis is computationally expensive, limiting the complexity of models which can be studied. As pulsar timing datasets and their respective models grow in size and sophistication, faster and scalable inference methods are essential. In this paper, we accelerate pulsar timing analyses by sampling in the space of Fourier coefficients instead of analytically marginalizing over them. Previous studies have shown the Fourier space induces a complex, high-dimensional posterior geometry, from which it is generally difficult to sample. We show that under an appropriate coordinate transformation the Fourier coefficients approximately follow a standard normal distribution, and may be efficiently sampled using a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo scheme. Under this coordinate transformation, for datasets of size and complexity comparable to the NANOGrav 15-year release, the new method produces converged posterior distributions for a range of models which include inter-pulsar correlations, stochastic, and deterministic signals in approximately 15 minutes on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. By comparison, the legacy pulsar timing analysis software \texttt{ENTERPRISE} would require months of computation on a CPU cluster to analyze comparable datasets under the same joint stochastic and deterministic models.

items.title: Companion architectures of sub-Saturns: Distinct migration pathways across the Neptunian landscape
items.abstract: Close-in sub-Saturns (4.0, _⊕ łeq R_ łeq 8.5, _⊕) are distributed unevenly across the period--radius plane: They are depleted in the Neptunian desert at periods P łesssim 3.2,d, accumulate in a narrow overdensity at P ≃ 3.2--5.7,d (the Neptunian ridge), and thin out in the savanna at P ≳ 5.7,d. R p R We tested whether sub-Saturns in different landscape regions have systematically different planetary companion architectures, as expected if desert and ridge planets arrived through high-eccentricity migration and if savanna planets migrated quiescently. We compiled 90 sub-Saturns in 86 systems with both transit and radial velocity (RV) data, constructed per-system RV and transit injection-recovery completeness maps, and combined them into detection probability surfaces for companions. From these maps we derived completeness-corrected occurrence rates for different companion types with a joint Poisson occurrence model. Companion architectures differ significantly across the landscape. Nearby companions (P_ < 200,d) accompany comp -4.3 ^ +3.2 % of savanna sub-Saturns but only 36_ -14 ^ +16 % of desert and ridge sub-Saturns. This contrast is driven almost entirely by small (M_ < 20, _⊕) companions, accompanying 88.2_ comp M -5.5 ^ +4.2 % of savanna but only 29_ -14 ^ +17 % of desert and ridge sub-Saturns, while medium-mass and giant companions within 200,d are rare (łesssim 13%) everywhere, so the sub-Saturn typically dominates its inner system. Moreover savanna sub-Saturns reside in compact multi-planet systems. These contrasts are robust to crosscuts in sub-Saturn radius, bulk density, eccentricity, and host-star properties. Desert and ridge sub-Saturns reside in dynamically emptied systems whose nearby companion rates resemble those of hot Jupiters, while savanna sub-Saturns inhabit compact multi-planet systems resembling those of warm Jupiters. This parallel supports two migration channels within a single population: high-eccentricity migration delivering planets to the desert and ridge, and quiescent disk migration or in situ formation populating the savanna.

items.title: Infrared spectroscopy of gas-phase hydrogenated and methylated pyrenes: From laboratory spectra to the simulated 3.4 μm emission band
items.abstract: Observations of the aromatic infrared (IR) emission band at 3.3 μm often reveal satellite emission features in the 3.4 -- 3.6 μm range. While the 3.3 μm band is attributed to the CH stretching vibration of polycylic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the satellite bands, particularly its prominent 3.4 μm component, is assigned to aliphatic CH stretching vibrations in hydrogenated and methylated PAH-like species. We derive state-of-the-art IR emission spectra for aliphatic-containing pyrene derivatives and compare them with astronomical observations. This will help us to refine our understanding of the contribution of these species to the 3.4 μm emission band. Infrared spectra (1.4--25 μm) of gas-phase hydrogenated pyrenes (dihydropyrene, tetrahydropyrene, and hexahydropyrene), methylated pyrene, and pyrene were recorded at temperatures ranging from 373 to 673 K, depending on the species. The band profiles were analysed using a multi-component fitting tool, and empirical anharmonicity laws were derived to quantify the evolution of the band positions and widths with temperature. The obtained spectral data were combined with the results of a Monte Carlo emission model to simulate the emission spectra following UV-photon absorption, up to the dissociation limit (łesssim6 eV). The resulting synthetic spectra were then compared with astronomical spectra including James Webb Space Telescope observations of the Orion Bar region (PDRs4All program). Based on these state-of-the-art simulated spectra, we show that 1,2,3,6,7,8-hexahydropyrene matches all the constrains to fit the red component of the 3.4 μm band observed at 3.403 μm. While 1-methylpyrene may also contribute to the underlying emission plateau, its lack of a strong IR band complicates detection in observed spectra, unlike hexahydropyrene. All experimental spectra and their temperature-dependent analyses are available in the new cosmicPAH-IRDB database of anharmonic IR spectra.

items.title: Time-dependent Accretion Disks in Tidal Disruption Events: Long-term Light Curves
items.abstract: Abstract The time-dependent accretion disk has been applied to explain the light curves observed in tidal disruption events (TDEs). Radiation pressure instability is expected to be an important factor that can shape the evolution of the accretion disk. In this paper, we upgrade the time-dependent disk model in Guo & Qiao by incorporating an index μ (with the stress tensor ∝ p μ p gas 1 − μ , where p = p gas + p rad ) for the modified viscosity, and a parameter f w for the strength of the wind. Meanwhile, we adopt a more realistic fallback rate to inject into the disk. After systematically testing the effects of the newly incorporated parameters, we find that f w can affect the time when the instability occurs, while μ can influence the occurrence and variation magnitude of the radiation pressure instability. When μ 0.4, the light curves can show oscillations caused by the instability, or drop steeply when the instability occurs and become flat in the late-time evolution, which mainly occurs when the viscous viscosity parameter α is small, or the impact parameter β is small. Since the drop in magnitude can be modulated by μ , we apply these “decay-to-flatten” light curves to some optical/UV observations in TDEs with different magnitudes of decline. Finally, we discuss the potential application of our model to some special TDEs that show oscillations in the light curves.

items.title: Will a supernova explode in CD-3011223?
items.abstract: Accretion of He-rich matter onto a low-mass carbon-oxygen white dwarf in a binary system with a He-rich donor may lead to an explosive event at the level of a type Ia supernova ( albeit with a low peak luminosity and peculiar nucleosynthesis. Recently, the possibility of this occurring in the context of certain binaries with He-accreting white dwarfs has been questioned, with the suggestion that if the effects of rotation are accounted for in the evolution of the accretor, the latter would not explode. It could instead become a white dwarf with a massive He-buffer. We investigate the expected evolution of the currently detached binary ̧dth harboring a 0.74, carbon-oxygen white dwarf and a 0.47, donor with a He-burning core and a very thin H-envelope (Δ M_H=6 , 10^ -4 We used the stellar evolution code FuNS to compute the evolution of ̧dth up to the epoch when the two components come into contact and through the RLOF phase of the donor. With respect to our earlier study of the system PTF J2238+743015.1, we also included the transport of angular momentum due to magnetic instabilities in the accretor interiors (`magnetic model'). During the H-accretion phase, the effects of rotation in the accretor are negligible. In the `magnetic model', the angular momentum deposited by the accreted matter is very efficiently redistributed along the whole WD due to magnetic instabilities, so that the angular velocity of the accreted layers remains very low. During the He-accretion phase, the accretor experiences two very strong He-flashes, which result in the ejection from the binary system of a large part of the matter previously accreted. The system ends its life as a carbon-oxygen core capped by a massive He/C/O-envelope (Δ M_ ̊m env ≃ 0.194, and an extremely low-mass companion that is remnant of the donor, as in the rotating model, and not including the effects of magnetic field. The system ̧dth cannot be regarded as the potential progenitor of an SN Ia. This conclusion is equally applicable to all detached binary systems having similar component masses and orbital periods.

items.title: Volcanic satellites and ion escape in the magnetospheres of ultra-cool and brown dwarf stars
items.abstract: Radio emissions at gigahertz frequencies of ultra-cool dwarf and brown dwarf stars suggest the presence of radiation belts not unlike Jupiter's. We investigate the possibility that the inferred magnetospheric plasma at the primary star is sourced by an active planet or via ion escape, which we modeled as a weak ionospheric outflow. We consider indirect methods to estimate the magnetospheric plasma mass flow from auroral radio emission and apply them to the ultra-cool dwarf LSR J1835+3259. We find that an ionospheric outflow on the order of 10^5 kg s -1 $ is a viable source if the ionospheric effective Pedersen conductance is lower than ∼ 0.003 mho. On the other hand, a tidally heated volcanic satellite with the same mass and radius as Io and an orbit with a semimajor axis smaller than ∼ 10 stellar radii, whose eccentricity ($e ∼ 10^ -3 ) is maintained by perturbations by other planets in the system, is found to be a viable source of magnetospheric plasma without strong limitations on the ionospheric conductance. The volcanic satellite scenario is also naturally in sync with the recent finding that ultra-cool dwarfs with distant substellar or stellar companions are remarkably more likely to be detected as radio emitters.

items.title: The triple nature of the PSR J0435+3233 system
items.abstract: The recent pulsar timing ephemeris of PSR J0435+3233 indicates that this millisecond pulsar (MSP) has a spin-down rate that is much higher than observed in other MSPs and challenges our understanding of the formation and evolution of MSPs. We propose that this system is a hierarchical triple, and that the high spin-down rate is caused by varying acceleration due to a tertiary in a wide orbit. We use pulsar timing methods with radio and γ-ray observations of PSR,J0435+3233 to determine the system properties. We find that a hierarchical triple timing model describes the timing observations of PSR,J0435+3233 and that this results in the detection of γ-ray pulsations back to the beginning of the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) data in 2008. The intrinsic spin-down rate remains uncertain, as it correlates with the parameters of the outer orbit, but large spin-down rates are excluded, and the intrinsic rate is at least two orders of magnitude lower than the observed rate, in line with other Galactic MSPs. We identified a star located 11 mas from the pulsar position as the optical counterpart to the tertiary companion. From the 1.5-2.5,kpc distance and colours, we infer that the tertiary is a 1.2,M_⊙ F-type main-sequence star. Along with the pulsar binary, it orbits the common centre of mass with an eccentric (e ≈ 0.6) wide (≈ 70 yr) orbit that is likely seen at a low orbital inclination. We conclude that PSR J0435+3233 is a hierarchical triple system. We discuss the motivation and prospects for the continued study of this system. Spectral measurements of the outer star in addition to continued astrometric measurements will yield mass ratio and inclination estimates, while continued pulsar timing may yield a tighter constraint on violations of the strong equivalence principle than are currently obtained from PSR J0337$+$1715.

items.title: New universal relations for magnetized neutron stars
items.abstract: Unlike the neutron-star mass--radius relation, which depends sensitively on the internal stellar structure through the equation of state of dense nuclear matter, certain neutron-star properties obey approximately universal relations that exhibit only weak dependence on the equation of state. In this paper, we explore new universal relations for magnetized neutron stars. We focus on a purely poloidal dipolar magnetic-field configuration and treat the effects of the magnetic field perturbatively to second order in the field strength. After appropriately normalizing the relevant quantities by the stellar mass and the magnetic-field strength at the pole, we first identify an exact universal relation between the magnetic dipole moment and stellar compactness. We then find approximate universal relations among the magnetic dipole moment, magnetically-induced stellar quadrupole moment, and ellipticity, with fractional variations due to the equation of state at the level of O(10%). We support these numerical findings with analytic estimates for Newtonian polytropes, which reproduce the observed behavior. Among the newly discovered relations, the one connecting the magnetic dipole moment and stellar quadrupole moment may be particularly useful for the analysis of gravitational-wave signals from binaries containing magnetized neutron stars.

items.title: An updated census of the Vast Polar Structure member galaxies
items.abstract: The Vast Polar Structure (VPOS) is a thin, planar arrangement of dwarf galaxies oriented almost perpendicular to the Milky Way (MW) disc. Since its discovery, the census of VPOS member galaxies has progressively expanded thanks to continuous findings of new dwarfs in the vicinity of the MW and increasingly precise measurements of their phase-space coordinates. In this work, we present the largest census to date of VPOS member galaxies, building on a sample of 73 MW dwarfs for which positional and kinematic data are available in the literature. Based on their orbital poles, we identify 22 VPOS members. We note that the majority of VPOS member galaxies are co-rotating, while only three systems are counter-rotating (Bootes III, Kim 1, and Sculptor). Our revised census increases the known VPOS member population by nearly 50%, introducing Delve 4, Kim 1, Kim 3, Eridanus III, Pictor II, and YMCA-1 as new on-plane dwarfs. From this updated census, we revise the structural parameters of the VPOS, confirming its planar (c/a =0.27) and remarkably thin (15 kpc) nature.

items.title: Disk survey in the Serpens star-forming region: Environmental effects in nearby star-forming regions
items.abstract: The external environment where protoplanetary disks are embedded regulates disk evolution. External irradiation, which heats and evaporates gas, as well as frequent stellar encounters, which truncate disks, can reduce disk sizes and masses. Disk surveys in nearby star-forming regions with various environments can help us understand how external environments impact disk evolution. The Serpens star-forming region, which is thought to be dense but not highly irradiated by massive stars, is an ideal laboratory for studying the dynamical effects on disk properties. We aim to study how dynamical interactions modify disk dust masses by comparing the Serpens star-forming region (distance sim400 pc) with other nearby star-forming regions through their disk masses and 3D stellar densities. We surveyed 321 class I to III young stellar objects in Serpens using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at a resolution of ∼ 0. We measured disk dust masses from millimeter observations under the optically thin assumption and recomputed the 3D stellar density using Gaia data. We applied the same method to other nearby star-forming regions for direct comparison with Serpens. The cumulative disk dust mass distribution of Serpens is similar to those of similarly aged nearby star-forming regions, such as Lupus and Taurus. Along with a reassessment of the 3D stellar density, it suggests that Serpens is not likely to have experienced strong tidal truncation capable of producing lower disk dust masses. We also find that the low disk dust mass tension in Ophiuchus and Corona Australis can be resolved when only disks explicitly identified as members of young (1-2 Myr) sub-clusters are considered. Disks without Gaia identifications, especially in Ophiuchus, are spatially clustered in the 2D projected sky plane and less massive than nearby disks with Gaia identifications. This may trace the effects of tidal truncation in denser environments at earlier evolutionary stages.

items.title: The fading hierarchy of Galactic open clusters
items.abstract: Galactic open clusters (OCs) provide a record of both hierarchical star formation and the subsequent dynamical evolution of the Milky Way disk. We used the two-point correlation function to characterize the spatial and kinematic clustering of OCs in the solar neighborhood, considering their 3D distributions and their projections onto the Galactic plane, as well as subsamples divided by age, mass, and survey volume. We quantified clustering through fractal dimensions (D_f) and characteristic correlation scales. We find that the youngest clusters have D_f comparable to those measured in the interstellar medium, which suggests they retain part of the hierarchical structure of their natal molecular clouds. The clustering strength then decreases systematically with age and becomes weak on a characteristic timescale of order 100 Myr. This evolution is scale-dependent: the excess correlation at tens of parsecs fades more rapidly than the weaker correlation at hundreds of parsecs. By contrast, we find only a weak dependence of the clustering properties on OC mass and volume. Using the same OC sample, we derived an observational calibration between projected and 3D D_f, providing an observational benchmark for comparing the Milky Way with studies of external galaxies, where only projected measurements are available. The OC population exhibits characteristic spatial and kinematic clustering scales of approximately 370 pc and 11 ̨ms, respectively. These results support a picture in which young OCs inherit a spatial hierarchy from star formation and progressively lose their spatial correlations through subsequent evolution.

items.title: CHEX-MATE: X-ray surface brightness discontinuities across a representative cluster sample
items.abstract: We analyzed the presence of X-ray surface brightness (SB) discontinuities, such as shocks and cold fronts, in the intracluster medium (ICM) of the 116 galaxy clusters from the CHEX-MATE sample. These features arise from accretion-related processes, including the merging of subclumps onto the main cluster halo and the sloshing of cold gas in a higher-entropy environment. We identified these structures in the XMM CHEX-MATE maps by examining both the SB residuals, obtained by subtracting a cluster model from the observations, and the gradient variations across X-ray images. We validated our method with an extensive analysis and comparison of the discontinuities described already in the literature. Our analysis reveals 66 discontinuities, 32 of which are newly detected, in 48 objects (∼41%). We find that discontinuities in relaxed systems tend to be closer to the core, weaker, and less aligned with the global X-ray morphology compared to those in disturbed systems. Using wavelet-based temperature maps, we provide a preliminary classification of these discontinuities, proposing the occurrence of eight putative shocks and 34 cold fronts. Furthermore, about 48% of the systems with extended radio emission show evidence of ICM discontinuities; conversely, ∼88% of the objects with detected discontinuities have an associated diffuse radio emission. This work also explores the limitations of using XMM data, characterized by relatively low spatial resolution, for detecting and analyzing such features, highlighting the challenges and potential biases introduced by instrumental constraints.

items.title: Examining Temporal Characteristics of Galactic Cosmic Rays in the AMS-02 Era
items.abstract: Abstract The energy spectra of Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) serve as critical probes of their astrophysical origins and propagation mechanisms through the interstellar medium. Among the key physical processes shaping the observed spectra, solar modulation, driven by turbulent heliospheric magnetic fields and the variability of the solar wind, plays a dominant role in modifying GCR fluxes within the inner heliosphere. The recent release of time-dependent flux measurements for He, Li, Be, B, C, N, and O by AMS-02 provides unprecedented precision to investigate solar modulation phenomena. In this study, we demonstrate that Li, Be, B, C, N, and O nuclei exhibit solar modulation parameters consistent with those of protons (p) and He within a modified force-field approximation (FFA) framework incorporating rigidity-dependent modulation potentials. By positing that GCRs with the same charge sign share solar modulation parameters, we further forecast daily fluxes of Ne, Mg, and Si from 2011 to 2020.
