items.title: What Patients See Before They See the Surgeon: Bariatric Surgery on TikTok.
items.abstract: BackgroundTikTok is a rapidly growing audiovisual social media platform and an emerging source of health information, including bariatric surgery content that may influence patients' expectations before consultation with clinicians. This study aimed to characterize the engagement patterns and themes of bariatric surgery-related TikTok videos to inform clinical practice.MethodsA comprehensive search identified the 10 most frequently used bariatric-related hashtags on TikTok. For each, the 10 most liked videos (n = 100) were extracted. Videos were included if they contained English, Spanish, or Portuguese content referencing bariatric surgery. Quantitative engagement metric analysis and qualitative thematic analysis were performed.ResultsMost videos were created by patients (92%) and most creators were female (83%). Content was overwhelmingly positive (79%) and focused primarily on vertical sleeve gastrectomy (61%), with limited representation of alternative procedures. No videos meaningfully discussed risks or differences between surgical options. The most common themes included body image and identity (59%), often with before and after images, and lifestyle adaptation (19%). Educational and promotional content was significantly longer (74.8 seconds, Kruskal-Wallis test: P = 0.002) without a statistically significant difference in engagement.DiscussionBariatric surgery content on TikTok is characterized by patient-generated, visually driven narratives that emphasize transformation and empowerment, with limited discussion of risks or procedural complexity. These findings suggest TikTok may shape narrow perceptions of bariatric surgery for patients. Clinicians should address social media-shaped expectations when counseling patients and use short-form, visually engaging, and patient-partnered content when posting educational content on TikTok to enhance engagement.

items.title: Association of Antihypertensive Medications with Orthostatic Hypotension among OIder Adults.
items.abstract: Background Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is common among older adults actively prescribed hypertension pharmacotherapy. Associations between antihypertensives and OH are inconsistent, due to differences in drug classes and OH assessment protocols. Methods Three supine and six standing blood pressures (BPs) were measured over 6 minutes, timed to initiate immediately (0 minutes) and 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 minutes after standing. OH was defined as a drop of systolic/diastolic BP ≥ 20/10 mmHg upon standing from the supine position. OH phenotypes were initial (immediately after standing), early (within 3 minutes), late (after 3 minutes), and sustained (during 6 minutes of standing). Participants were asked about orthostatic symptoms experienced during OH assessment. We investigated associations of antihypertensive classes with OH phenotypes and orthostatic symptoms via multivariable logistic regression. Results Of 863 participants (mean age 84 years), 41% had initial, 24% early, 18% late, and 17% sustained OH; 81% used antihypertensive medications. First-line antihypertensives (renin angiotensin aldosterone system blockers, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and thiazide diuretics) were not associated with OH or orthostatic symptoms. Among non-first-line, alpha blockers were significantly associated with initial OH (OR 1.80, 95%CI 1.07, 3.01) and orthostatic symptoms during postural change (OR 2.64, 95%CI 1.34, 5.23), whereas combined alpha-beta blockers were significantly associated with early, late, or sustained OH (2.24 [1.15, 4.37], 2.50 [1.21, 5.17], 2.99 [1.41, 6.30], respectively) and experienced symptoms while standing (3.08 [1.10, 8.65]). Conclusions First-line antihypertensives are not associated with OH among older adults, which does not support their discontinuation in the setting of non-neurogenic OH.

items.title: The Magnusian generator for dissipative systems and application to leading 2.5PN radiation-reaction dynamics
items.abstract: A bstract The Magnusian is a phase-space function that generates finite-time evolution through nested Poisson brackets. It is related to several familiar generators of classical dynamics, including the radial action, the eikonal phase and related quantities. In this work, we extend the Magnusian framework to systems with dissipation and nonlocal-in-time interactions using the in-in formalism, also known as the Schwinger-Keldysh or Galley formalism. This framework is particularly natural for binary dynamics, where integrating out the mediating gravitational field can produce both dissipative radiation-reaction effects and hereditary, nonlocal-in-time interactions. We derive the generalized Magnusian and show that it continues to generate finite-time evolution. As an application, we construct the Magnusian for Newtonian bound motion subject to the leading 2.5PN radiation-reaction force. The resulting generator defines a discrete evolution map from one cycle to the next and describes the evolution of the system in agreement with numerical solutions.

items.title: Gate-Based Feature Importance in Simulation-Based Inference for EEG: A Cautionary Tale
items.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) provides a powerful way to fit mechanistic models to data, but offers little insight into which information in the data shapes the inferred parameter values. It could therefore benefit from robust and inexpensive interpretability methods. Learned weighting mechanisms such as feature gates provide a potential route to low-cost interpretability, although their interpretation assumes that predictive training reveals which inputs drive performance. We examined this assumption in a computational neuroscience setting, where neural posterior estimation (NPE) is used to infer four physiological parameters of a dynamical model of interacting neuronal populations (Jansen-Rit). We tested whether the learned gate weights captured feature importance by comparing them with a retrain-based ablation benchmark, in which each feature was removed in turn and the NPE retrained. We considered two jointly trained gates: independent sigmoid weights and competing softmax weights. If these reliably reflect feature importance, they should align with the ablation-based estimates. Across nine independent training seeds, however, gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman's rho approximately -0.61 for sigmoid gating and -0.56 for softmax gating). The feature that ablation identified as most important, total signal power, was among the features the gate down-weighted most, despite gating costing negligible predictive accuracy. These results extend a pattern previously documented for attention mechanisms in natural language processing and for explainability methods in electroencephalography (EEG) deep learning to the simulation-based inference setting, and suggest caution when interpreting learned gate weights as measures of causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.

items.title: The medium is the message: How neurometabolic entanglement generates conscious experience
items.abstract: Most neuroscientific accounts of consciousness assume that conscious experience is constituted by the information conveyed between neurons. The physical-chemical details of the metabolic and physiological processes that convey this information are correspondingly presumed to be relevant only insofar as they support the organization of information processes. We describe an alternative perspective that denies this presumed independence of the processing of neural information and the metabolic-physiological details of these processes. We call this alternative paradigm the theory of neuro-metabolic entanglement (NME). NME proposes that mental experience exemplifies the inseparability of the organization of neural information processes from the constraints imposed by the material-energetic properties of the neural medium itself. Central to this account is a recursive, Möbius-like loop of neural connections that entangles patterns of forebrain information processing with midbrain regulatory systems that modulate forebrain metabolism. This enables patterns of neural activity to indirectly modify the global distribution of metabolic resources underlying these information processes. It also constitutes a bottleneck that integrates diverse neural processes into an adaptively relevant unitary experience organized in terms of the global redistribution of metabolic support. Computational models of neural function cannot treat energy supply as a fixed background parameter; our proposed Möbius-like loop of neuro-metabolic entanglement offers a framework for future models in which neural activity is dynamically and recursively modulated by the network's own metabolism. Recognizing this entanglement is a first step toward dissolving the explanatory gap highlighted by the so-called "hard problem" of consciousness.

items.title: Quasi-Localization of Short-Wavelength Perturbations in Softened Laplace-Lagrange Chains
items.abstract: We examine the long-term evolution of localized eccentricity perturbations in a softened Laplace-Lagrange chain. The secular coupling between mass elements is long-ranged, suggesting that any disturbance imposed at a single radius should disperse rapidly across the chain. We show that this expectation fails once the secular interaction is regularized by a finite softening length $β$: while broad eccentricity profiles propagate smoothly, as textbook secular theory anticipates, narrow profiles remain confined to their launching site for millions of secular periods. The origin of this quasi-localization lies in the dispersion relation of the softened chain. The group velocity of eccentricity waves collapses by orders of magnitude on spatial scales below the softening length, so that narrow perturbations project almost entirely onto a nearly flat sector of the band, where little differential precession is available to disperse them. Propagating the initial wavenumber spectrum through the dispersion relation reproduces the retained fraction of angular momentum deficit across the full range of perturbation widths with no adjustable parameters. The confined perturbation is flanked by an apsidally polarized (oppositely-aligned) response, which we show to be the real-space imprint of this spectral projection. The softening length therefore sets a dynamical scale below which eccentricity perturbations spread only on timescales far longer than the secular period.

items.title: Simulations of a Conducting Sphere Moving through Magnetized Plasma II: Effect of Internal Magnetic Fields and Enhancement of Alfvénic Drag
items.abstract: Magnetic interaction between astrophysical objects can play an important role and produce electromagnetic radiation in various systems, ranging from planet-moon and star-planet systems to binary compact objects. We extend our previous numerical study of an ideal magnetized plasma flowing past a conducting sphere to the case where the sphere is magnetized. Such a flow generates magnetic disturbances and produces a drag force on the sphere. We examine the drag coefficient as a function of the strength and orientation of the conductor's internal magnetic field relative to the background magnetic field. We find that a strong internal magnetic field that is aligned with the background field significantly enhances the drag coefficient compared to the unmagnetized case; this enhancement is related to the increased magnetic flux that connects the conductor and the open, external field region. We also explore how the drag coefficient changes as the flow transitions from the sub-Alfvénic to the super-Alfvénic regime. Our results suggest that magnetic interaction may play a larger role in orbital evolution of some binary systems than previously expected.

items.title: Ellipsoidal Modeling Framework for TNOs: the triaxial shape of (50000) Quaoar and its implications for Weywot and the dynamical environment
items.abstract: The three-dimensional shapes of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) are notoriously difficult to determine due to their slow orbital motion and minimal variations in aspect angle over human timescales. To overcome this geometric degeneracy, we developed a versatile modeling framework capable of deriving ellipsoidal shapes by simultaneously combining stellar occultations and rotational light curves, including parameterizations of localized surface albedo. We applied this methodology to the large TNO (50000) Quaoar, jointly modeling 37 stellar occultation events and two photometric datasets. Our MCMC analysis demonstrates that Quaoar is best represented by a triaxial shape with equatorial semi-axes $a = 620.7^{+3.3}_{-2.8}$ km and $b = 546.5^{+6.0}_{-5.6}$ km, and a polar semi-axis $c = 511.5^{+5.3}_{-5.5}$ km, yielding a bulk density of $1.663 \pm 0.127$ g cm$^{-3}$. By isolating Quaoar's barycentric motion from the astrometric offsets, we determined the mass of its satellite, Weywot, to be $(1.485 \pm 0.360) \times 10^{18}$ kg, corresponding to a system mass ratio of $q = 0.0012 \pm 0.0003$ and a satellite bulk density of $0.95 \pm 0.60$ g cm$^{-3}$. Furthermore, dynamical simulations using the derived triaxial gravitational field reveal that potential additional satellites can only maintain stable orbits beyond 2.4 Quaoar radii, as inner bodies would be strongly perturbed. Regarding the ring system, particles at the location of the secondary ring (Q2R) location exhibit libration associated with the 5:7 spin-orbit resonance (SOR). Similarly, particles at the location of the main ring (Q1R) location show libration of the 2:6 SOR angle for orbital eccentricities larger than 0.2, providing a plausible mechanism for the azimuthal width variations observed in Q1R.

items.title: The Pandora SmallSat: post-launch operations and mission update
items.abstract: The Pandora SmallSat is a NASA flight project designed to study the atmospheres of exoplanets. Transmission spectroscopy of transiting exoplanets provides our best opportunity to identify the makeup of planetary atmospheres in the coming decade, and is a key science driver for HST and JWST. Stellar photospheric inhomogeneity due to star spots, however, has been shown to contaminate the observed spectra in these high-precision measurements. Pandora will address the problem of stellar contamination by collecting long-duration photometric observations sampled over a stellar rotation period with a visible-light channel and simultaneous spectra with a near-IR channel. These simultaneous multiwavelength observations will constrain star spot covering fractions of exoplanet host stars, enabling star and planet signals to be disentangled in transmission spectra to then reliably determine exoplanet atmosphere compositions. Pandora will observe exoplanets with sizes ranging from Earth-size to Jupiter-size and host stars spanning mid-K to late-M spectral types. Pandora was selected in early 2021 as part of NASA's inaugural Astrophysics Pioneers Program. Herein, we present an overview of the mission, including the science objectives, operations, the observatory, science planning, and upcoming milestones as we prepare for launch readiness in 2025.

items.title: A Technical Reanalysis of the Viking Carbon Assimilation-Pyrolytic Release Experiment
items.abstract: The 1976 Viking Carbon Assimilation-Pyrolytic Release (CAPyR) experiment tested whether carbon from $^{14}$CO$_2$ and $^{14}$CO entered Martian soil during a 120-hour incubation in a form retained during a 120 $^\circ$C purge but released by pyrolysis at 635 $^\circ$C. Untrapped radioactivity was measured as Peak 1; material retained in an organic vapor trap was oxidized and measured as Peak 2. Net Peak 2 was intended to represent synthesized reduced organic carbon. Seven of nine usable incubations at Chryse and Utopia Planitia yielded significant net Peak 2 signals, including the dark U1 run. An underreported Viking Lander 2 gas leak introduces uncertainty into U1-U3. The C1 signal corresponds to approximately 10 or 30 pmol of carbon, assuming derivation entirely from CO or CO$_2$, respectively. We reassess these results in light of the possible presence of perchlorate salts in Viking soils. Oxidation of fixed organic radiocarbon during pyrolysis could have shifted label from Peak 2 to Peak 1, a perchlorate-specific effect not considered in previous CAPyR analyses. Hubbard's (1979) mineral-substrate experiments produced abiotic Peak 2 signals without reproducing the heat sensitivity. No demonstrated abiotic mechanism has reproduced all CAPyR observations under Mars-relevant conditions. The observations remain consistent with a biological carbon-assimilation system whose relevant activity survives C5's 120 $^\circ$C/90 $^\circ$C pretreatment but is strongly impaired by C2's 175 $^\circ$C pretreatment. Together with the Labeled Release experiment, CAPyR suggests oxidative and reductive chemistry in separate aliquots from common Martian soil acquisitions. Metabolically active life combines these processes; a quantitative abiotic explanation of their combined heat-labile response patterns remains to be demonstrated.

items.title: OGLE-2012-BLG-0563: Relative Proper Motion Constraint from Keck Follow-up finds the correct Lens
items.abstract: We present Keck/NIRC2 adaptive optics imaging results of planetary microlensing event OGLE-2012-BLG-0563. We find that the OGLE-2012-BLG-0563L planetary system consists of a 1.12 +/- 0.09 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting a 0.81 +/- 0.04 solar-mass host star at a distance of 5.49 +/- 0.56 kpc from the Sun. This event has a lens-source separation of 23.28 +/- 0.48 mas, which is the smallest lens-source separation measured to date with Keck AO data. We find that the incorrect solution - which identifies the Northeast (NE) star as the source star - is favored if one only considers the discovery paper, the Fukui et al. (2015) solution, or an unconstrained model. However, by performing an image-constrained light curve model fit using the relative proper motion direction constraint from the Keck follow-up data, we demonstrate that the correct solution identifies the NE star as the lens star. The discrepancy in the unconstrained models is driven by systematics in the FTS and MOA B & C data, alongside the impact of the relative proper motion direction constraints. This outcome offers two important lessons for future Roman data analysis: (1) thoroughly verify systematics across all passbands and identify the precise origin of chi-squared differences, and (2) utilize image-constrained light curve modeling incorporating relative proper motion direction constraints to identify the correct lens.

items.title: The physical and chemical structure of Titan's upper atmosphere: energy balance, photochemistry and Jeans escape
items.abstract: Titan's upper atmospheric layers provide a unique opportunity to study how photochemistry, photoionisation, haze microphysics and escape processes shape its atmospheric chemical structure, providing a unique benchmark for understanding these processes in exoplanets. Using a 1D first-principles approach, we extend the Kompot model to simulate Titan's upper atmosphere and investigate its thermal and chemical structure, and Jeans escape. We performed self-consistent simulations of Titan's upper atmosphere, above the dense haze layer, over a 1D radial grid by solving the coupled hydrodynamics, thermal and photochemical kinetic, and energy balance equations. We considered heating by stellar X-ray and ultraviolet (XUV) and infrared (IR) radiation, and cooling due to radiative emission of methane (CH4) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN). We also included additional nineteen photochemical and 117 thermal reactions to Kompot's standard chemical network. Our modelled atmospheric temperature structures lie within the observed variability of Titan's atmospheric temperature profile. Our simulations reproduce observed nitrogen (N2) and CH4 densities in the upper atmosphere, and abundance of minor chemical species also broadly agree with observationally derived abundances. Near the exobase, our CH4 mixing ratio overlap with Cassini-Huygens results, and our model H2 mixing ratios also exhibit broad agreement with observations. Our simulations suggest no significant thermal loss of CH4, even under the conditions of an early Sun's XUV environment.

items.title: The coupled impacts of atmospheric dynamics and cloud microphysics on hot Jupiter atmospheres. I. An application to WASP-43b
items.abstract: Understanding the influence of cloud-circulation feedback on planetary climates is crucial to interpreting solar system and extrasolar planet observations. Hot Jupiter phase curve observations have reported westward optical phase curve offsets and weak absorption features, which may be explained by the presence of clouds. JWST observations have also revealed tentative silicate cloud absorption features in emission and transmission spectroscopy. While a number of 3D atmospheric dynamics models of hot Jupiters and microphysical models describing cloud formation exist, few combine these two approaches. To help elucidate the impact of clouds on hot Jupiters, we introduce a post-processing scheme with the 3D GCM ADAM with SPARC (formerly SPARC/MITgcm), the 1D microphysical cloud model CARMA, and the radiative transfer code PICASO. We first simulate the cloud-free atmosphere of WASP-43b with ADAM, then incorporate resulting thermal profiles into CARMA to simulate WASP-43b's cloud structure, and finally generate phase-dependent emission spectra from our results with PICASO. By comparing to JWST observations, we infer that WASP-43b has a cloudy nightside, a mostly clear morning and evening limb with patchy clouds, and a clear dayside at the level of the photosphere. Our microphysical model predicts the condensation of five cloud species, including silicates, but overestimates the cloud opacity at all phases compared to observations, requiring additional modeling to explain. The results from this post-processing setup are promising for more meaningful characterization of WASP-43b's atmosphere, and will serve as a comparison baseline for our upcoming indirect coupling of both models, as well as for other future studies.

items.title: EXPRESS: How error rates scale with chance rate among dogs following human pointing gestures, and why it matters.
items.abstract: Humans use pointing gestures to communicate with dogs. However, efforts to study how dogs receive this communicative signal have produced ambiguous results. Prior work presenting a choice between two options has shown that dogs choose the pointed-to option at above chance levels, but just barely. With only two options, the high probability of choosing correctly by chance weakens the signal. After replicating the 2-option task, we changed the task's parameters by presenting dogs with six options. We compared two models that make divergent, quantitative predictions on how the success rates will relate on the two tasks. One model stresses that multiplying the options should reduce the number of correct choices made by chance at a higher rate than instances of genuine communication. A second model that involves no understanding of referents, but just a systematic shift in attention, predicts the effect size to remain constant irrespective of the number of options. Dogs chose the location pointed to at barely above chance rates in both the 2-choice and 6-choice tasks. This pattern discourages the view that dogs understand the referential aspect of human pointing. Additional patterns that become visible with more than two options bolster this interpretation. Dogs chose the correct side of the arena and succeeded on second choices disproportionately more often. Dogs succeeded with far and near locations at similar rates. These results challenge the view that dogs interpret human pointing as referring to a specific object, which has implications for claims that point-following evinces intentional capacities among dogs.

items.title: Comparing the coherent point drift algorithm to sliding semilandmark and weighted spherical harmonic whole-bone three-dimensional shape analyses.
items.abstract: The ability to quantify 3D morphologies is critical for anatomical research; however, setting up high-density landmark sets and positioning them on all specimens can represent a substantial challenge. The coherent point drift (CPD) algorithm, a technique for registering two point clouds based on the Gaussian mixture model, was recently used to investigate human variation; however, its performance has yet to be compared to other 3D shape analysis methods. Here we compare the results of a CPD analysis to a sliding semilandmark and weighted spherical harmonic (SPHARM) analysis of the same 60 human and African ape calcanei and a CPD analysis and SPHARM-sliding analysis (a combination SPHARM and sliding semilandmark analysis) of 40 primate third manual proximal phalanges (mPP3s) to determine methodological comparability. Additionally, we run a CPD analysis on a small but wide-ranging sample of primate ulnae to demonstrate its utility for proximodistally long and mediolaterally narrow long bones. All specimens were surface or micro-CT scanned. All calcanei were subjected to a CPD analysis with 2000 semilandmarks, a sliding semilandmark analysis with 1007 semilandmarks, and a SPHARM analysis. All mPP3s underwent a CPD analysis with 2500 semilandmarks and a SPHARM-sliding analysis with 2562 semilandmarks. For the ulna, a CPD analysis with 1252 semilandmarks was run. Shape variation for all analyses was summarized using (separate) principal component analyses (PCAs). Results of the respective analyses for the calcaneus and mPP3 were compared by calculating the maximum and root mean square distances (RMSD) between average taxon shape configurations (scaled based on centroid size) generated from each analysis. All three calcaneus analyses separate taxa along the first two PCs, with humans separating from African apes along PC1 and chimpanzees and gorillas separating across PC2. For the two mPP3 analyses, the three great ape taxa consistently separate along PC1, and Papio separates from the other taxa along PC2. The average RMSD between CPD and sliding semilandmark analyses for the calcaneus was 0.24 mm, and 0.21 mm between CPD and SPHARM analyses. For the mPP3, the average RMSD between CPD and SPHARM-sliding was 0.14 mm. These results indicate that CPD is a comparable 3D shape analysis method to these other approaches. The CPD analysis was also able to place a semilandmark set on primate ulnae ranging from gorillas to tarsiers and capture morphological variations including shaft curvature, relative olecranon process length, and overall robusticity. CPD analyses are less time intensive than sliding semilandmark analyses; however, the sliding semilandmark analysis was better able to capture variation surrounding the borders of the articular facets (although differences were relatively minor), suggesting that these analyses may be better suited when the researcher is interested in a specific anatomical feature. CPD did capture edges better than SPHARM analyses; however, this is likely not an issue for small, relatively round bones such as carpals and most tarsals. In sum, CPD produces similar results to sliding semilandmark, SPHARM, and SPHARM-sliding approaches and has benefits for analyses of long bones with complex morphologies or among taxa that exhibit large amounts of morphological variation.

items.title: Architecture of the Norrin signaling complex and structure-guided surrogate design.
items.abstract: Norrin binds Frizzled 4 (FZD 4 ), tetraspanin 12 (TSPAN12) and low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 (LRP5) to regulate angiogenesis and the integrity of the blood-brain barrier and inner blood-retina barrier (BRB). Aberrant Norrin signal causes retinopathies, BRB defects and deafness. Therapeutic mimetics of Norrin are currently in clinical trials for eye diseases. To characterize the mechanism of Norrin signal biogenesis, we determined the structure of a Norrin-FZD 4 -TSPAN12-LRP5 signaling complex using a de novo designed FZD 4 binder as a 'protein glue'. Our structure shows that two curved Norrin homodimers bridge two FZD 4 -TSPAN12 heterodimers. LRP5 LA3 simultaneously interacts with TSPAN12 and two Norrin homodimers, positioning the cytosolic FZD 4 and LRP5 tails for signal activation. On the basis of our findings, we designed FZD 4CRD -LRP5 LA3 bispecific binders that act as Norrin surrogates. Our signaling assays showed that oligomerization of the Norrin surrogate enhances signaling potency. Thus, this work reveals how the Norrin signal is generated and may assist in the development of Norrin/Wnt mimetics.

items.title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes.
items.abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase 1,2 . The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain 3 . Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A 4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons 6 . Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.

items.title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits.
items.abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes 1,2 . Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes 3 ; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies 4 , we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51 + and CD51 - astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51 + and CD51 - astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51 + astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51 + astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51 + astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.

items.title: Functional architecture of the human insula.
items.abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain 1,2 , interoception 3,4 and feelings 5,6 , yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula 7-10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal-posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral-posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior-polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

items.title: SIK3 controls synaptic localization of NMDA receptors by phosphorylating GluN1.
items.abstract: Synaptic NMDA-type glutamate receptors (NMDARs) are central components of all neural computations. NMDAR levels critically vary between synapses but how the synaptic localization of NMDARs is controlled remains unclear. Here we show that SIK3, a serine-threonine protein kinase, localizes to synapses where it phosphorylates the obligatory NMDAR subunit GluN1 at a single site. This single phosphorylation event controls NMDAR recruitment to synapses. Genetic deletion of SIK3 severely and selectively decreases synaptic GluN1 levels by ~60% without altering AMPA-type glutamate receptor levels or inducing major transcriptional changes. Pharmacological inhibition of SIK3 impairs synaptic NMDAR responses within 45 minutes. Mutating the SIK3-phosphorylation site inhibits GluN1 synaptic recruitment. 'Sleepy', a gain-of-function mutation in SIK3 that increases sleep, selectively enhances synaptic NMDAR levels by increasing GluN1 phosphorylation. Thus, SIK3 phosphorylation of GluN1 provides a key signal for recruiting NMDARs to synapses.

items.title: A corticohypothalamic circuit that mediates maternal awakening to pup cries.
items.abstract: Maternal caregiving requires sensory vigilance to ensure offspring survival, particularly during sleep. Infant cries are salient sensory cues that reliably trigger maternal arousal and caregiving responses in both humans and dams, but the underlying neural circuitry remains poorly defined. Here we identify a corticohypothalamic circuit in mice that mediates maternal awakening in response to pup calls. We show that layer 6 (L6) neurons in the temporal association cortex and ectorhinal cortex (TeA/Ect) projecting to the preoptic area (POA) exhibit enhanced responsiveness to pup calls after the transition to motherhood. This enhanced responsiveness is mediated by increased expression of dopamine receptor D1 (Drd1) in TeA/Ect → POA neurons. Additionally, we reveal a pathway from the auditory thalamus to L6 TeA/Ect neurons that transmits pup cues during sleep. Together, these findings identify a dedicated neural circuit that grants infant cries privileged access to arousal systems, likely representing a fundamental adaptation for caregiving across mammals.

items.title: Evolution towards higher unitary conductance in mammals makes BK channels more efficient and precise.
items.abstract: The large-conductance calcium-activated potassium (BK) channel plays a critical role in neuronal excitability and spike timing precision. Mammalian BK channels are distinguished by an exceptionally high unitary conductance (~250 pS), while invertebrates exhibit a significantly lower unitary conductance. We confirmed the evolutionary trend to high unitary conductance and used computational models to examine how differences in unitary conductance affect calcium activation of BK channels and influence neuronal dynamics. We show that mammalian BK channels are activated more efficiently by calcium and generate stronger repolarizing currents than lower unitary conductance channels. Channels with lower unitary conductance require greater channel density in the cell membrane, leading to stronger competition for calcium and reduced activation. In contrast, high unitary conductance channels minimize competition, enabling more effective activation and repolarization. Incorporating these channel properties into a neuronal model revealed that mammalian-type BK channels enhance spike-timing precision, consistent with the evolution of fine motor control and advanced neuronal processing in mammals.

items.title: Changes in Comorbid Obsessive-Compulsive and Restrictive Eating Disorder Symptoms in Eating Disorder Focused Family Therapy.
items.abstract: Objective Restrictive eating disorders (EDs) are highly comorbid with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and comorbidity is associated with worsened outcomes. However, it is unclear if (1) Maudsley family therapy (FT-AN) for restrictive EDs reduces comorbid OCD symptoms, and (2) if higher baseline OCD symptoms merely reflect higher severity or are associated with inhibited ED treatment. Method Participants with restrictive EDs (Anorexia Nervosa, Atypical Anorexia Nervosa, or other specified feeding and eating disorders) received FT-AN as part of an intensive day program or outpatient services in London from mid-2024 through January 2026. Nonparametric Wilcoxon signed-rank tests examined pre/post differences in ED, OCD, and general impairment symptomology. Linear regressions investigated the effect of baseline OCD scores on changes in ED symptoms across treatment. Results Across FT-AN, ED pathology and weight improved while OCD pathology and general impairment did not. After excluding likely under-reporters, OCD symptoms and overall functioning did significantly improve. More severe OCD impairment at baseline did not impair, and in fact was related with more ED improvement. However, more severe ED and OCD symptoms at baseline were both associated with less change in weight. Together, these results suggest that worsened outcomes among patients with OCD represent higher initial severity rather than treatment inhibition. Discussion FT-AN's effects on ED symptoms are likely not directly inhibited by, but also do not appear to fully target, OCD symptoms. Future research should examine efficacy and optimal timing of incorporating OCD-specific treatments into care.

items.title: Depression in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease: Clinical manifestations, biomarker evidence, and predictive implications.
items.abstract: Depression is one of the earliest and most frequent non-motor symptoms in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease (PD), often preceding motor signs by years to decades. This review synthesizes epidemiological, neuroimaging, biomarker, and genetic evidence to clarify whether depression is a risk factor, a direct prodromal manifestation, or both. Meta-analyses consistently show a two-fold increased risk of subsequent PD in individuals with depressive symptoms or major depressive disorder (MDD), with the highest risk occurring within 1-2 years of diagnosis but persisting for up to 25 years. Late-onset depressive syndrome (after age 50-60) is associated with dopaminergic deficits on dopamine transporter imaging in 24-79% of cases, supporting it as a prodromal symptom, whereas early-onset depression may act through shared genetic vulnerability or chronic inflammatory pathways. Neuroimaging in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) reveals that depression correlates with caudate atrophy, frontostriatal white matter disruption, and brainstem monoaminergic dysfunction, but not simply with nigrostriatal denervation. Depression frequently coexists with RBD, autonomic dysfunction, and olfactory impairment, likely reflecting shared brainstem pathology. Genetic forms of PD (GBA1, SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN) show variable depression prevalence, providing mechanistic insights into lysosomal, inflammatory, and proteostatic pathways. Emerging evidence implicates IL-17A, sIL-2R, and α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation as convergent points linking depression and prodromal α-synucleinopathy, with gut-brain axis dysfunction potentially amplifying this process. Current Movement Disorder Society prodromal PD criteria include depression but have limited sensitivity in general populations. No disease-modifying trials have tested whether treating prodromal depression alters phenoconversion risk. We conclude that proximal, late-onset depressive syndrome is a robust prodromal marker, while distant or early-onset depression, including MDD, identifies a chronically elevated risk population. Future studies should integrate multimodal biomarkers and test therapeutic interventions in prodromal cohorts.

items.title: The Roles and Uses of Extracellular Vesicles in Neuroimmunologic Diseases.
items.abstract: Neuroimmunology is a field of neurology focused on the diagnosis and treatment of diseases where the immune system causes inflammation or injury to the nervous system. This includes diseases such as multiple sclerosis, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, autoimmune encephalitis, autoimmune ataxia, stiff person syndrome spectrum disorder, and neuro-rheumatologic diseases such as neuropsychiatric lupus. Over the past couple decades, there have been significant advancements in the diagnostic methods for several neuroimmunologic diseases. Despite these achievements, major needs remain for additional methods to facilitate earlier diagnosis, monitor disease activity and treatment, and elucidate disease mechanisms to aid in the development of novel or tailored treatment strategies. Currently, there is often a trade-off between the invasiveness of neurodiagnostic testing and the level of detail that can be obtained from the test without causing an iatrogenic injury. Here, we discuss the potential of extracellular vesicles (EVs), especially CNS-derived EVs obtained from peripheral blood, as a promising avenue for advancing research and clinical care in neuroimmunology. This article provides a review of the key clinical features and approaches to care for the most common neuroimmunologic diseases. We identify gaps that remain in our current understanding of these conditions. We then highlight how ongoing research in the EV field may address these existing gaps. Finally, we examine the challenges that must be overcome before EV analysis can be more widely adopted in both research and clinical care in this field.

items.title: Comparative neuropathological evaluation of pT217 immunoreactivity in human and transgenic mouse tauopathies.
items.abstract: Tau phosphorylation at threonine 217 (pT217) has been increasingly recognized as a biomarker for Alzheimer disease (AD), but its neuropathological distribution and the performance of available antibodies remain to be fully characterized. In this study, we performed a comparative evaluation of a recombinant rabbit monoclonal anti-pT217 antibody (mAb) using immunohistochemical and biochemical analyzes in human and transgenic mouse tauopathies and compared results to those of a commercially available anti-pT217 antibody and the AT8 antibody. In rTg4510 mice, the anti-pT217 mAb detected pathological tau aggregates with high sensitivity, including hyperphosphorylated tau species identified by biochemical fraction. In human postmortem brain tissues (AD, Pick disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration), quantitative image analysis demonstrated labeling of a broad range of tau lesions, including neurofibrillary tangles, neuropil threads, tufted astrocytes, astrocytic plaques, and Pick bodies. The overall detectability was comparable to that of AT8 and similar to or modestly > that of a representative commercial anti-pT217 antibody. These findings indicate that pT217 is widely present across tauopathies and suggest that the recombinant anti-pT217 mAb provides a sensitive and reproducible tool for neuropathological assessment. Together, these results provide a framework for evaluating anti-pT217 antibodies in neuropathological studies.

items.title: Effect of a Nutritional and Culinary Support Intervention on Food-Related Quality of Life During Chemotherapy.
items.abstract: Context Chemotherapy adversely affects nutritional status and the eating experience in patients with cancer, yet its impact on food-related quality of life (QoL) remains underexplored. The CANUT guide was developed to provide practical nutritional, sensory, and culinary support during treatment. This study aims to evaluate the effect of the CANUT intervention on food-related QoL in patients undergoing chemotherapy. Secondary objectives included health-related QoL, dietary intake, and anthropometric and functional parameters. Method In this RCT, 209 patients with cancer receiving chemotherapy were randomly assigned (1:1) to an intervention group (dietary counselling supported by the CANUT guide) or control group (standard care). Food-related QoL was assessed using the ALT-QVA score, reflecting chemotherapy-related sensory alterations, meal experience, digestive discomfort, and adaptive dietary behaviours. Health-related QoL (EORTC QLQ-C30), dietary intake (24-hour recall), anthropometry, and handgrip strength were collected. Outcomes were measured at baseline and after four chemotherapy cycles. Longitudinal analyses used linear mixed-effects models. Results Food-related QoL declined over time (-2.85±0.53, P 75% of patients below recommendations at both time points. Anthropometric and functional parameters remained unchanged. Conclusion The CANUT intervention did not improve food-related QoL or nutritional outcomes in a population mostly consisting of women with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy. This highlights the need for more integrated, comprehensive, and multimodal strategies addressing sensory alterations and individual characteristics of patients during chemotherapy (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05027490).

items.title: Suppression of Tau-tubulin kinase 1 mitigates tau phosphorylation, and Aβ mediated neurotoxicity via altered kinase network.
items.abstract: Tau-tubulin kinase-1 (TTBK1) is a neuron-specific serine/threonine tau kinase that is highly expressed in the entorhinal and hippocampal regions and phosphorylates microtubule-associated protein tau at sites relevant to Alzheimer's disease (AD), thereby contributing to early tau pathology. Targeting TTBK1 can be a promising therapeutic approach for AD, although how suppression of TTBK1 may change neuronal functions is poorly understood. Here we show the proteome and phosphoproteome analysis of murine primary cortical neurons transduced with adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing short hairpin RNA (shRNA) targeting murine Ttbk1, using tandem mass tag and data independent acquisition liquid chromatography/mass-spectrometry. Suppression of TTBK1 expression by shRNA transduction increases expression of neuronal intermediate filament proteins and V1-domain subunits of the vacuolar H + -ATPase, suggesting the regulatory roles of TTBK1 on cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal activity. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces phosphorylation of TTBK1 and MAP1A as well as increases phosphorylation of neuronal intermediate filament proteins, indicating the regulation of microtubule-related proteins and axonal stabilization. Phosphosite-specific signature analysis identifies the kinases regulated by TTBK1 including AD-related cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) and AKT1. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces CDK5 activator p25/p35 ratio and pT231 phospho-tau level, consistent with the reduced activity of CDK5. Finally, silencing of Ttbk1 reduces amyloid-β-induced neurotoxicity in vitro. These results suggest a close functional relationship or coordinated regulation among TTBK1 and other kinases in maintaining axonal homeostasis via phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins, and mediating amyloid-β toxicity, thus emphasize TTBK1 as an emerging therapeutic target of AD.

items.title: Thalamocortical dysconnectivity shapes cortical hierarchy disruption across illness durations in schizophrenia.
items.abstract: Background Schizophrenia is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of circuit-level dysfunction. However, how thalamocortical abnormalities differ across cohorts with varying illness durations and relate to large-scale cortical hierarchical organization remains unclear. Methods We analyzed resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 1,223 patients with schizophrenia and 1,224 matched healthy controls across 12 datasets. The datasets were grouped as early-, middle-, and late-stage cohorts. Connectivity gradient mapping was applied to characterize thalamocortical organization, and computational modeling evaluated simulated hierarchical changes after modifying thalamic-salience connectivity. Results We identified a schizophrenia-relevant sensorimotor-salience-association axis that captures systematic differences in thalamocortical abnormality profiles across the stage cohorts. Along this axis, case-control effects in association regions were positive in the early-stage cohort but negative in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, whereas sensorimotor regions showed the converse pattern. This cross-cohort pattern was accompanied by reduced cortical hierarchical separation in cohorts with longer illness duration. In contrast, salience-related thalamic regions showed negative case-control effects in all three stage cohorts, with larger effect sizes in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, and these alterations were associated with clinical symptoms. Computational modification of thalamic-salience connectivity increased simulated cortical hierarchical differentiation, particularly in the middle-stage cohort. Conclusions These findings indicate that thalamocortical dysconnectivity, centered on disrupted thalamic-salience interactions, is associated with systematic differences in cortical hierarchical organization across cohorts. The cross-cohort pattern of salience-related abnormalities highlights thalamic-salience coupling as a circuit-level link to cortical hierarchical differentiation and a candidate for future mechanistic and interventional investigation.

items.title: Brain NaV1.5 fine-tunes neuronal excitability to facilitate female-directed social behavior in male mice.
items.abstract: Background The voltage-gated sodium channel Na V 1.5, an essential subtype for cardiac action potential generation, is also enriched in limbic regions of the brain, but its function in the central nervous system remains poorly understood. Methods We performed RNAscope, immunostaining, electrophysiology, fiber photometry, Scn5a knockdown, and behavioral testing to dissect the functional role of Na V 1.5 in the brain. Results Na V 1.5 channels are enriched in neurons of posterior bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNSTp) and accumulated at the axon initial segment. Activation of these tetrodotoxin-resistant channels lowers action potential threshold and accelerates spike initiation at relatively hyperpolarized levels of membrane potential (V m ). In vivo fiber photometry showed that BNSTp Na V 1.5-expressing neurons in male mice were recruited by salient social stimuli and exhibited hyperpolarizing V m dynamics during social contacts. Scn5a knockdown selectively attenuated neuronal responses to female chemosensory cues, and disrupted sex preference and female-directed behaviors. Conclusions These findings identify Na V 1.5 as a V m state-dependent regulator of BNSTp neuronal excitability, and reveal an unexpected role of this channel subtype in female-cue processing and female-directed social behavior in males.

items.title: The Impact of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists on Post-Anesthetic Pulmonary and Gastrointestinal Adverse Events: A Target Trial Emulation Using Multinational Database.
items.abstract: Objective Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) delay gastric emptying, raising concerns about perioperative aspiration and postoperative complications. This target trial emulation aims to evaluate the association between the use of GLP-1 RAs and the risk of postoperative pulmonary and gastrointestinal adverse events in patients undergoing general anesthesia. Methods Data was utilized from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. The study analyzed data from January 1, 2023, to December 31, 2023. Patients aged 20 years or older who underwent general anesthesia were included. These patients were divided into two groups: those using GLP-1 RA and those who were not. Propensity score matching was used to balance baseline characteristics. The primary outcome measures were the incidence of pulmonary and gastrointestinal adverse events within one-month post-anesthesia. Hazard ratios were calculated using Cox proportional hazards regression models to estimate the risk of these adverse events associated with GLP-1 RA use. Results A total of 21,948 patients were included after matching. Patients who used GLP-1 RAs demonstrated a significantly lower risk of pulmonary adverse events (HR 0.682 [0.496-0.938]). Secondary outcomes further revealed a reduction in the risk of postoperative respiratory failure, as well as postoperative hospitalization and emergency department revisits. However, there was a marginally increased risk of gastrointestinal adverse events in the GLP-1 RA group (HR, 1.034 [1.003-1.067]). Conclusions The use of GLP-1 RAs prior to general anesthesia was not associated with higher risk of pulmonary adverse events. A slight elevation in gastrointestinal risks was observed, although the signal remained modest.

items.title: Diagnostic classification of ASD improves with positively sparsified DTI inter-regional correlation and graph-theoretical artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition characterized by impairments in social interaction and behavioral functioning. ASD diagnosis primarily relies on behavioral assessments and can vary across individuals. In this study, an ASD diagnostic model was developed using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) derived inter-regional correlations, graph-theoretical analysis and artificial intelligence. Initially, the DTI data from 283 individuals (154 ASD and 129 typically developing) were preprocessed using a standard pipeline. Subsequently, DTI-derived parameters were extracted from 50 white matter (WM) regions. Inter-regional correlations were computed between DTI-derived parameters using Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC), Biweight midcorrelation coefficient, and Spearman rank correlation coefficient. The resulting fully correlated matrices were subsequently decomposed into positive and negative correlation matrices. These matrices were sparsified at different threshold levels to construct graph networks. Nine graph-theoretical features were calculated for each WM region, yielding 450 features, which were fed as input to artificial intelligence models, including logistic regression, support vector machine (SVM), random forest, extreme gradient boosting, and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network. The highest average 5-fold classification accuracy of 90.47% was achieved using 75 features derived from a positively correlated PCC network thresholded at 0.2 and SVM. The most discriminative features were eigenvector and pagerank centrality of the cingulum (cingulate gyrus) left, and eigenvector centrality of the superior corona radiata left, inferior cerebellar peduncle right, and cingulum (cingulate gyrus) right. These findings indicate that positively sparsified DTI inter-regional correlation networks combined with graph-theoretical analysis and artificial intelligence provide a promising framework for accurate ASD classification.

items.title: Plasma miR-21-5p, miR-195-5p, and clusterin profiles in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and their relationship with cognitive function.
items.abstract: Cognitive impairment is a debilitating aspect of multiple sclerosis (MS), and reliable blood biomarkers to assess it are still scarce. MicroRNAs such as miR-21-5p and miR-195-5p, together with clusterin, are involved in neuroinflammation and synaptic plasticity, which suggests a potential role in MS. The aim of the study was to investigate the relationship between plasma clusterin, miR-21-5p, and miR-195-5p expression and cognitive performance in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (pwRRMS). The study included 30 treatment-naïve pwRRMS, 30 pwRRMS on disease-modifying therapy (DMT), and 30 healthy controls. Plasma clusterin was determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, relative expression levels of the miRNAs were determined using real-time quantitative PCR, and cognitive performance was assessed using the Brief International Cognitive Assessment for MS. In silico network analysis was performed to explore the regulatory architecture of the miRNA-CLU axis. miR-21-5p expression was significantly elevated in treatment-naïve pwRRMS, while miR-195-5p was downregulated across all pwRRMS compared with controls and these differences persisted after adjustment for age and sex. Plasma clusterin levels were similar across groups. Neither the miRNAs nor clusterin significantly correlated with cognitive impairment status or adjusted BICAMS scores. Cognitive impairment in the pwRRMS on DMT group was associated with higher lesion burdens. In silico analysis positioned miR-21-5p, miR-195-5p, and clusterin among genes involved in neuroinflammatory pathways, generating cellular-level hypotheses; their circulating levels primarily reflected systemic inflammatory activity. In this cohort, magnetic resonance imaging lesion burden showed a stronger association with cognitive impairment than circulating biomarkers, and these findings warrant validation in larger multi-center studies.

items.title: Systematic Review of Clinical Utility of Multimodal Imaging in Infectious Posterior Uveitis. Multimodal imaging in Uveitis (MUV) Taskforce Report 12.
items.abstract: Topic To systematically evaluate the clinical utility of multimodal imaging (MMI) for the diagnosis, activity assessment, longitudinal monitoring, and detection of complications in the five most prevalent infectious posterior uveitides. Design Systematic review and evidence-based quality appraisal. Participants Original research studies published between January 2018 and September 2025(primary cohort) and 2012-2017(supplemental cohort) evaluating MMI in ocular toxoplasmosis(TOXO), cytomegalovirus retinitis(CMVR), ocular tuberculosis(TB), syphilitic uveitis(SYPH), and acute retinal necrosis(ARN). Methods MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane, and Scopus were systematically searched. Independent reviewers extracted reported imaging findings and clinical utility statements for: color fundus photography (CFP), fundus autofluorescence (FAF), optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), indocyanine green angiography (ICGA), and OCT angiography (OCTA). Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), and certainty of evidence was graded using a bespoke consensus-based scheme informed by GRADE principles. Main outcome measures (1)reported imaging findings for each entity and modality; and (2)statements of clinical utility for diagnosis, detection of disease activity, longitudinal monitoring, and detection of complications. Results Among 122 included studies (82 primary and 40 supplemental), the primary studies contributed 5,522 individual patient examinations and 574 imaging statements, while the supplemental studies provided corroborating evidence. Overall, 366 clinical utility statements were identified across the four prespecified domains, including 30 statements supporting synergistic MMI strategies. CFP, including studies using ultra-widefield imaging, achieved high certainty for diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring in four of five entities (4/5, 80%), with moderate certainty in ARN. OCT achieved high certainty across all four clinical utility domains for four of five entities (4/5, 80%), with lower certainty in ARN owing to its limited evidence base. FFA achieved high certainty for complication detection in three of five entities. FAF achieved high certainty for disease activity in four of five entities. OCTA achieved high certainty in at least one domain for two of five entities, whereas ICGA achieved high certainty in at least one domain for only one of five entities. Conclusions Substantial evidence exists regarding the imaging findings and clinical utility of MMI in infectious posterior uveitis. Combined MMI enables integrated structural, vascular, and choroidal assessment beyond conventional clinical examination.

items.title: The ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of Molecular Targets, version 2 (ESCAT v2): an evidence-based framework for ranking alterations as actionability and resistance biomarkers in precision oncology.
items.abstract: Background Since the publication of the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of Molecular Targets (ESCAT) in 2018, precision oncology has evolved substantially. Tumour-agnostic therapy approvals, expanding real-world evidence datasets, and the clinical recognition of genomic resistance biomarkers have created the need to revise the original framework. Methods The ESMO Precision Oncology and Taxonomy Committee convened an international expert panel to revise the ESCAT classification. Through iterative review of the evolving evidence-base, structured feedback rounds, and consensus discussions, the panel developed an updated actionability scale and a novel resistance scale. The revision followed three principles: explicit grading of uncertainty within actionable tiers, formal inclusion of tumour-agnostic eligibility criteria, and systematic classification of resistance biomarkers to complement sensitivity designations. Results ESCAT version 2 (ESCAT v2) introduces several substantive changes. Tier I is restructured into three categories, proven, inferred, and extrapolated, that carry the same clinical directive but differ in the level of certainty within the supporting evidence. The guideline introduces formal tumour-agnostic gating criteria, the ESMO Tumour-Agnostic Classifier and Screener (ETAC-S). Tier II is refined into three sub-tiers graded by prospective interventional evidence, high-quality real-world or non-prospective evidence, and replicated case-level evidence. Tier X is subdivided into alterations that are tested and found not to be predictive (X-A) and biomarker-therapy matches in which the therapy lacks meaningful activity in the biomarker-defined population (X-B). A parallel four-level resistance scale ranges from clinically validated resistance (contraindication) to preclinical or computational evidence (research use only). Conclusions ESCAT v2 provides a comprehensive, evidence-graded framework for interpreting actionability and resistance biomarkers in cancer, enabling more nuanced communication among clinicians, patients, regulators, and researchers while preserving a clear directive to act when evidence supports patient benefit.

items.title: Suicidality during intranasal (es)ketamine treatment: A retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: Background Intranasal (es)ketamine has shown efficacy in therapy of treatment-resistant depression (TRD). However, its effects on suicidality have not been fully elucidated. Methods We conducted a retrospective longitudinal cohort study of 80 patients affected by TRD, treated with intranasal (es)ketamine. Suicidality was assessed using item 10 of the clinician-rated Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) and item 9 of the Beck-Depression-Inventory-II (BDI-II). We measured patient- and transition-level fluctuations of suicidality, tested temporal clustering using mixed-effects logistic regression, examined associations between non-suicidal depressive symptom change and suicidality worsening, and explored baseline predictors. Results Mean suicidality ratings decreased modestly. Upward and downward category transitions occurred at similar frequencies across treatment (MADRS: 57 increases and 50 decreases across 767 valid transitions, 7.4% vs. 6.5%; BDI-II: 22 and 23 across 741 transitions, 3.0% vs. 3.1%). At least one upward transition occurred in 38.8% on MADRS and 21.3% on BDI-II. Transient elevations were more frequent than sustained elevations. Sustained elevation occurred at 15.0% on MADRS and 7.5% on BDI-II. Increases did not cluster by treatment phase. MADRS, but not BDI-II, upward transitions were associated with concurrent and lagged worsening in non-suicidal depressive symptoms. Higher baseline suicidality showed the most consistent association with later worsening across both measures. Two serious adverse events occurred, including one suicide. Conclusions In this routine-care cohort, suicidality decreased on average, with no evidence of treatment-phase-specific worsening. Nonetheless a minority of patients showed transient or, less often, sustained increases in suicidality, supporting necessity of continuous suicidality monitoring throughout (es)ketamine treatment.

items.title: Enhancing diagnostic and prognostic prediction of child psychopathology via multivariate predictive modeling: Where are we and where do we need to go?
items.abstract: Advances in computational science and machine learning provide an opportunity to improve access and quality of mental health care in the near-term. Applications of these tools to child dysregulatory psychopathology and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder are of particular interest because they are common and place high burden on healthcare systems; early identification and effective treatment can alter life-long trajectories. The successful development and validation of predictive tools would allow clinicians to 1) efficiently and accurately screen for diagnoses, even in settings with limited behavioral or mental health training; 2) allocate scarce behavioral health resources; 3) work more effectively with children and families around risk-benefit decisions; and 4) initiate tailored treatment plans before crises emerge. Yet this work is challenging. Here, we outline some of what we see as the most pressing conceptual, practical, and computational challenges. We propose potential paths to move the field forward by leaning into individual variation not as noise, but as predictive information; considering novel phenotypic features that have traditionally been outside the scope of diagnostic practice, such as cognitive and temperament-based emotional features; and enhancing cross-disciplinary collaboration, including with patient and provider stakeholders, to ensure robust model development and evaluation that directly addresses clinical goals. We provide specific recommendations for rigorously testing internal and external validation and addressing clinical utility to enhance clinical translation. As the field undertakes this work, careful thought about who is being helped and who is being potentially left behind because of limitations of existing data sources and limits on generalizability will be critical.

items.title: Early electrical stimulation promotes functional recovery after volumetric muscle loss.
items.abstract: Volumetric muscle loss (VML) overwhelms the inherent regenerative capacity of skeletal muscle, causing persistent functional deficits with no routinely effective therapies. Electrical stimulation (ES) is a promising regenerative cue, but its sustained delivery during the acute post-injury window has been limited by the electrochemical performance of available stimulation electrodes and by the repeated anesthesia that needle-electrode delivery requires for each session, which constrains daily dosing in rodent models. Here, we report a fully implantable bioelectronic system in which nanoporous platinum (NanoPt) modification of multistrand stainless-steel electrodes provides the high charge storage and injection capacities required for safe, repeatable stimulation in a rat tibialis anterior VML model. Electrochemical characterization confirmed that the porous NanoPt surface lowered impedance, increased charge storage and injection capacities, and remained stable over 48 h of continuous stimulation in muscle-mimicking phantom tissue. The electrode platform enabled daily therapeutic stimulation and electromyographic recording in awake, freely moving animals, removing the per-session anesthesia that percutaneous needle-electrode delivery requires during the early dosing window. Animals receiving ES during the acute post-injury period (10 sessions over days 0-14) showed sustained functional improvement, reaching 90% of baseline torque at 8 weeks compared to 71% in unstimulated controls, reflecting enhanced remodeling of the injured muscle rather than synergistic compensation. Histological analysis revealed early increases in vascularization, pro-regenerative macrophages, and satellite cells that accompanied, and temporally preceded, the functional gains. By coupling a biomaterial-enabled electrode platform to a defined stimulation regimen, this work identifies the acute post-injury period as a therapeutically actionable window and provides a basis for combining bioelectronic interventions with engineered scaffolds and other regenerative biomaterials for traumatic muscle loss. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Severe traumatic muscle injuries cause permanent weakness because lost muscle is not regrown and no biomaterial-based therapy reliably reverses the deficit. Electrical stimulation is a promising regenerative cue, but the electrode materials and procedures required for daily stimulation during the brief post-injury healing window have remained elusive. Here, nanoporous platinum-modified electrodes provide the electrochemical stability and charge-handling capacity needed to deliver sustained daily stimulation in awake animals, without the per-session anesthesia required by needle-electrode approaches, in a rat model of volumetric muscle loss. Two weeks of immediate post-injury stimulation restored near-normal limb strength while enhancing vascularization, pro-regenerative macrophages, and satellite-cell activity. This biomaterial-enabled bioelectronic platform identifies the acute post-injury period as a therapeutic window and a basis for combining electrical stimulation with regenerative biomaterials.

items.title: Caffeine attenuates Aβ-induced hippocampal dysfunction alongside changes in adenosine receptor-linked GABA handling and neuronal excitability.
items.abstract: Synaptic and circuit dysfunction in the hippocampus is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease, involving disturbances at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Adenosine receptors (ARs) regulate hippocampal glutamatergic and GABAergic signaling. Caffeine, a non-selective AR antagonist, has well-established neuroprotective actions. We examined whether caffeine attenuates amyloid-β (Aβ)-induced changes in neuronal viability, GABA handling, intrinsic excitability and synaptic excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, and whether these functional effects occur alongside changes in AR and GABA transporter 1 (GAT-1) protein abundance. Primary mouse hippocampal cultures were exposed to Aβ 1-42 (1nM) and/or caffeine (0.1, 1, 25, and 50µM) for culture-based assays, whereas acute hippocampal slices were exposed to Aβ 1-42 (100nM) and/or caffeine (25µM) during whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from CA1 pyramidal neurons. In cultures, Aβ increased neuronal death, confirming previous reports, and caffeine co-treatment attenuated this effect. Total GAT-1, A1R and A2AR protein levels were unchanged, whereas Aβ reduced neuronal A1R immunoreactivity; this reduction was not observed with caffeine co-treatment. Radiometric assays identified treatment-associated differences in 1-h 3 H-GABA accumulation and basal 3 H-GABA outflow, including a non-significant trend toward increased accumulation after Aβ exposure and reduced accumulation in the Aβ+caffeine condition. In slices, Aβ flattened the frequency-current relationship and transiently reduced the E/I ratio, whereas these changes were not observed during caffeine co-application; subsequent caffeine exposure restored firing output after 30min of Aβ exposure. Further experiments are required to establish if changes in A1R immunoreactivity or radiometric GABA handling contribute to the electrophysiological effects.

items.title: Dynamic roles of embryonic glial cells in octopus brain development.
items.abstract: Coleoid cephalopods, such as octopus, squid, and cuttlefish, have evolved remarkably large nervous systems with neuron numbers comparable to those of small mammals. Despite this, little is known about how these nervous systems develop, which genetic programs drive the formation and diversification of their neural cells, and what factors contribute to evolutionary brain expansion. This study combined single-cell multi-omics with spatial expression analysis to uncover the cell types and the regulatory mechanisms underlying nervous system development and evolution in Octopus vulgaris. We discovered an early embryonic glial cell population that is distinct from neurogenic progenitors and defined by orphan nuclear receptor 4a (nr4a), distal-less homeobox (dlx), and prospero homeobox (pros) regulons. Their spatial distribution and dynamic transcriptional profile during embryogenesis indicated that these cells might orchestrate cell migration, axon guidance, and brain patterning before expressing neuronal markers or differentiating into mature glia. Comparison of embryonic glial transcriptional signatures across two cephalopods, a gastropod, and Drosophila revealed shared expression of nr4a, dlx, and pros in mollusks, while embryonic glia in Drosophila expressed pros, dlx, repo, ttk, and gcm but not nr4a. Intriguingly, the overall gene expression profile of cephalopod embryonic glia has diverged from that of Pomacea canaliculata (golden apple snail), whose glia do not express guidance or patterning genes. Together, these findings identified a conserved embryonic glial cell type in mollusks that might have acquired new functions in coleoid cephalopods to organize neuronal migration and wiring in their expanded brain.

items.title: Protein arginine methylation promotes global 3'UTR shortening in proliferating cells.
items.abstract: Protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs) are promising anti-cancer targets, but their tumorigenic mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that arginine methylation drives global 3'UTR shortening, thereby promoting oncogenic short isoforms. Inhibition of asymmetric dimethylation reverses this shift, with combined inhibition of asymmetric and symmetric dimethylation (DMAi) producing an even greater effect across human cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and activated murine T cells, while also counteracting the shortening induced by reduced CFIm25 expression. Arginine methylation promotes PCF11 association with the cleavage and polyadenylation machinery, enabling efficient processing of weak proximal poly(A) sites within transcripts characterized by high GC content, large distances between alternative poly(A) sites, and a position-dependent sequence code. These findings establish physiologic roles of PRMTs in promoting 3'UTR shortening, which could be exploited for patient stratification of PRMT-targeting therapies in oncology and immune-related diseases.

items.title: Usability and Acceptance of a Social Robot in People With Multiple Sclerosis: Comparative Cross-Sectional Study.
items.abstract: Background Socially assistive robotics (SAR) is an emerging field integrating robotics, medicine, cognitive and social sciences, and neuroscience. Its potential in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains largely unexplored, although MS affects sensory-motor, cognitive, and psychological domains where SAR could offer substantial benefits. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the usability of a humanoid robot in people with MS, compare it with age-matched healthy individuals (HIs), and explore usability predictors. Automated written-language analysis was tested as a complementary approach. Methods In this 2025 cross-sectional study at the Italian MS Foundation laboratory, 20 people with MS (mean age 51.4, SD 11.0 years; n=13, 65% female; mean education 13.0, SD 3.4 years) and 20 age-matched HIs (mean age 47.3, SD 10.1 years; n=12, 60% female; mean education 14.8, SD 2.2 years) completed 4 predefined tasks with the robot Pepper. Usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS). Attitudes toward robots, robot-related factors, and task-related effort were measured with the General Attitudes Towards Robots Scale (GAToRS), Godspeed questionnaire, and NASA-TLX, respectively. Psychological variables (eg, personality traits from the Italian Ten-Item Personality Inventory [I-TIPI]) and clinical characteristics for people with MS (eg, cognitive functions via the app DIGICOG-MS, upper-limb difficulties with the Arm Function in Multiple Sclerosis [AMSQ]) were collected. Written responses to open-ended questions were analyzed using natural language processing (NLP). Results SUS scores exceeded the standard cut-off in both groups, with no between-group differences (people with MS: mean 81.00, SD 12.31; HIs: mean 77.75, SD 11.24; r =0.14, 95% CI 0.01-0.42; P =.39), indicating high usability. People with MS reported more negative attitudes toward robots at the societal level (GAToRS S-: r =0.36, 95% CI 0.08-0.63; P =.02) and judged Pepper as more anthropomorphic ( r =0.42, 95% CI 0.15-0.67; P =.007) and intelligent ( r =0.37, 95% CI 0.09-0.61; P =.02) than HIs. Anthropomorphism was strongly associated with visuospatial memory (DIGICOG-MS: ρ=-0.632, 95% CI -0.84 to -0.26; P =.003) and relatively strong with both verbal memory (DIGICOG-MS: ρ=-0.504, 95% CI -0.77 to -0.08]; P =.02) and agreeableness (I-TIPI: ρ=0.491, 95% CI 0.06-0.77; P =.03). Exploratory forward stepwise regression showed that conscientiousness (I-TIPI: B =2.064, 95% CI 0.679-3.449), negative personal attitudes toward robots (GAToRS P-: B =0.169, 95% CI 0.033-0.306), and perceived upper-limb difficulties (AMSQ: B =0.169, 95% CI 0.033-0.306) explained 64% of SUS variance (adjusted R ²=0.568); task-related frustration (NASA-TLX: B =-1.497, 95% CI -2.276 to -0.719) explained 48% (adjusted R ²=0.451). NLP analyses revealed no between-group differences in lexical productivity or sentiment-lexicon coverage. Conclusions This study provides first preliminary evidence that people with MS perceive a social robot as highly usable, comparably to HIs, suggesting MS-related challenges may not hinder human-robot interaction. Psychological factors, prior attitudes toward robots, and clinical characteristics were associated with user experience in the MS group. Future research should explore whether integrating these measures with language-based approaches informs tailored interventions in MS.
