items.title: A Reverse-Gold Theorem: Positive-Data Identification by Substrate-Bounded Contrastive Learners
items.abstract: Gold's theorem shows that no learner can identify an arbitrary language in a superfinite class from positive presentations alone. We prove a positive result of a different shape. Fix an innate \emph{recursive contrast operator} $R$ mapping any string to a finite set of structurally bounded perturbations of it, and a discriminative scorer of bounded capacity trained by InfoNCE-style contrastive estimation \citep{vandenoord2018,macollins2018} on self-generated perturbations. Under a faithfulness condition relating operator, scorer, and target, the trained scorer achieves \emph{PAC conditional identification} from positive data alone: with high probability it ranks all but an $\varepsilon$-fraction of positives above every out-of-language perturbation in their own orbit, with sample complexity polynomial in the capacity, the orbit size, the score bound, and $1/\varepsilon$. The negatives are constructed by the learner, not supplied by an oracle, and no global normalizing constant over strings is ever computed. The misranking bound follows from the geometry of the contrastive loss---per-example loss floors plus a definite loss increment under misranking---yielding an $\varepsilon^{-2}$ rate, together with an explicit approximation gap that quantifies the cost of in-language (``colliding'') perturbations and vanishes for orbit-pure operators. The ranking guarantee lifts to a global membership classifier under a margin condition, and the same operator composed with the learned scorer is a normalization-free Metropolis--Hastings generator. We instantiate the hypotheses for substitutable context-free languages \citep{clarkeyraud2007} and the subregular classes \citep{heinz2010,hayashikamigaito2025}, and state an open conjecture locating the construction in the mildly context-sensitive hierarchy.

items.title: System-evolutionary view of RNA presence in living cells
items.abstract: Our guiding question for this article was: How did RNA adjust its life when the RNA world era came to an end? RNA has its practical execution side in the whole-cell systems setup serving critical functions in metabolism, compartmentalization, and in the RNA-DNA-Protein network, coupling information handling and different events of macromolecule production into a self-sustaining loop. Aligning with current views of cooperation we find that RNA life is distributed across a population of information-bearing entities persisting by compatibility, with DNA serving as a long-term memory and proteins offering the catalytic reach. We suggest that the reproduction-survival axis, relevant to higher organisms, is also manifested by RNA in many forms, including RNA-primers, mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs. Each of these have contrasting, highly adapted molecular phenotypes. Ultimately, we wish to emphasize the evolutionary narrative where RNA did not lose in exchange for DNA genes or otherwise. Ultimately, RNA just changed strategy and in its various forms has an active and critically important presence in all cells at all times.

items.title: White dwarf pollution in wide binaries I: the effects of stellar evolution
items.abstract: Context. Atmospheric pollution in white dwarfs is interpreted as evidence for the accretion of rocky material from remnant planetary systems. Wide binary companions can influence the delivery of planetary material onto white dwarfs, making it essential to understand the interplay between stellar evolution and binary perturbations. Aims. We investigate how uncertainties in stellar mass-loss histories affect the dynamical evolution of remnant planetary systems in wide binaries, and assess their relative importance compared with binary perturbations in driving the accretion of rocky material onto white dwarfs. Methods. We perform REBOUND N-body simulations incorporating time-dependent stellar parameters interpolated from MESA evolutionary tracks and tidal interactions, following the dynamical evolution up to the white dwarf stage. We explore two stellar-evolution models with distinct mass-loss histories for wide binary systems hosting a Jupiter-mass planet and a planetesimal disc, spanning a range of binary architectures. Results. The adopted stellar-evolution model has only a minor effect on the survival of the planet, mainly affecting the timing and efficiency of planetesimal delivery during the white dwarf stage. Instead, the architecture of the binary primarily controls the pollution outcome: wider binaries produce the highest rates of accretion onto the white dwarf, consistent with the observed prevalence of polluted white dwarfs in wide binaries. Moreover, planetesimal reservoirs remain long-lived, with survival times increasing with binary separation, enabling Gyr-long metal pollution. Conclusions. Our results suggest that the architecture of wide binaries, rather than uncertainties in stellar evolution, is the dominant factor controlling the dynamical delivery of rocky material onto white dwarfs.

items.title: FAUST XXXII. Chemically layered structures and ionisation in the disk and envelope of NGC 1333 IRAS 4C
items.abstract: Recent molecular line observations with high spatial resolutions have revealed vertical chemical stratification in Class I/II disks (i.e. chemical composition changing with height in the vertical direction of the disk), as well as a radial variation of ionisation rates. However, such chemical layered structures in Class 0 disk and envelope systems have been investigated only for limited objects, such as L1527. In the context of the ALMA Large Program FAUST, we report the results of molecular line observations toward the disk and envelope around the low-mass Class 0 protostar NGC 1333 IRAS 4C in the Perseus Molecular Cloud. Previous observations have shown that the disk rotation axis of this object is largely tilted to the line of sight, making it suitable for studying the molecular abundance distribution as a function of disk height. We found that the molecules known as gas density tracers such as C18O and H2CO are distributed around the disk midplane. In addition, molecules known as tracers of photochemical reactions such as CCH and c-C3H2 are distributed in the low-density upper layers of the disk, unlike the distribution in L1527. Moreover, the column density ratio of HCO+/CO derived from the H13CO+ and C18O line emission suggests that the ionisation degree and the ionisation rate vary with the disk radius and they are larger in the outer region of the disk and envelope.

items.title: Systematic Uncertainties in Rocky Exoplanet Reflected Light from Incomplete Laboratory BRDF Measurements
items.abstract: The first observations of short-period rocky exoplanets have initiated the era of terrestrial exoplanet characterization. The interpretation of these observations relies on forward models used in atmospheric and surface retrieval frameworks. While atmospheric modeling is supported by extensive laboratory datasets of molecular opacities, the experimental basis for rocky surface characterization remains limited. Most reflectance libraries of planetary analog materials provide spectra measured at a single illumination and viewing geometry, constraining the spectral behavior but not its full angular scattering properties. We show that incomplete angular coverage in laboratory bidirectional reflectance measurements introduces an intrinsic systematic uncertainty in the interpretation of rocky exoplanet observations. We demonstrate that multiple combinations of photometric parameters can reproduce the same laboratory reflectance spectrum while predicting different angular scattering behaviors and disk-integrated observables. We propagate this non-uniqueness to reflected-light phase curves, geometric albedos, and planet-star contrast ratios between $0.5$--$1.7\,μ$m, representative of the spectral range targeted by future direct-imaging missions such as the HWO. We find that single-geometry laboratory spectra produce large uncertainties in predicted signals, particularly at small phase angles. Simplified assumptions adopted in exoplanet studies, such as isotropic scattering can additionally introduce systematic biases. Using multi-angular laboratory measurements from the Bloomsburg University Goniometer dataset, we show that the uncertainty in predicted observables collapses once angular scattering behavior is directly constrained. Our results demonstrate that multi-angular measurements are required to construct physically predictive reflected-light models of rocky exoplanets.

items.title: Saturation Level of the Streaming Instability
items.abstract: In proto-planetary disks, gas turbulence can cluster dust grains and catalyze the formation of planetesimals. This process depends on the strength of the turbulence. Here, we evaluate the turbulence strength that is induced by the streaming instability. Based on the amount of free energy available, we estimate the viscous parameter to be alpha ~ St Pi^2 f(epsilon), where St (< 1) is the Stokes number of the streaming grains, Pi is the dimensionless pressure gradient, and f (epsilon) is an explicit function of epsilon, the local dust-to-gas density ratio. This estimate explains the results of many previous studies, and is also supported by our additional tailor-made simulations. We discuss two easy applications of our result, one is a self-consistent dust scale height, one is the astrophysical relevance of a pressure bump. Lastly, while this work allows one to characterize the streaming turbulence, we emphasize our current inability to connect the strength of turbulence to the formation of planetesimals.

items.title: A Solar Optical Clock
items.abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.

items.title: Solar System Surface Technosignatures: Searching for Signs of Artificial Design on Extraterrestrial Terrain
items.abstract: Artificial radio emissions have historically been a major focus of technosignature searches. Here, we apply an anthropological lens to expand this scope to surface technosignatures: non-random, intentional patterning on planetary terrain, similar to long-lasting human-made landscapes and monuments on Earth. On geologically inactive bodies such as the Moon and Mars, artificial traces and patterns could potentially remain visible for hundreds of millions of years. We discuss two recent developments that make this search timely: high-resolution imaging datasets, such as those produced by the HiRISE camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and ML-based anomaly-detection methods. Finally, we list two possible approaches to developing a model capable of searching for these surface technosignatures: a supervised and an unsupervised one. Complemented by LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar, and reflectance spectroscopy, these methods would enable the first quantitative upper limits on surface technosignatures while yielding ancillary benefits for planetary science.

items.title: Astrocytic glutamate transporter loss drives chemoreflex hyperactivity and cardiorespiratory dysfunction in a heart failure model.
items.abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Breathing instability and exaggerated chemoreflex activation contribute to adverse HF outcomes, yet the central mechanisms linking respiratory control to cardiac dysfunction remain poorly defined. The retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) is a key brainstem chemosensory region regulating ventilatory and autonomic output, but whether glial dysfunction within this circuit contributes to HF pathophysiology is unknown. We hypothesized that loss of astrocytic glutamate transporter 1 (GLT-1) in the RTN disrupts glutamate homeostasis, producing chemoreflex hyperactivity and cardiorespiratory dysfunction in HF. In a rat model of nonischemic HF, reduced astrocytic GLT-1 expression in the RTN was accompanied by extracellular glutamate accumulation and heightened excitability of chemosensitive neurons. These changes were associated with exaggerated central chemoreflex responses, breathing instability, autonomic imbalance, and impaired cardiac function. Astrocyte-specific GLT-1 restoration normalized RTN glutamate levels, reduced central chemoreceptor neuron hyperexcitability, stabilized breathing, and improved cardiac performance. Systemic riluzole, an FDA-approved glutamate-modulating drug, similarly reduced RTN glutamate accumulation and attenuated chemoreflex-driven respiratory instability. These findings identify loss of astrocytic GLT-1-mediated glutamate homeostasis in the RTN as a mechanism contributing to cardiorespiratory dysfunction in HF and support pharmacological targeting of brainstem glutamate homeostasis as a therapeutic strategy requiring further investigation.

items.title: Vaccines targeting the inflammasome protein ASC reduce inflammation and downstream pathology in multiple disease models.
items.abstract: The inflammasome is an innate immune complex responsible for aberrant interleukin-1β (IL-1β) signaling in numerous chronic inflammatory diseases, including gout and Alzheimer's disease. The inflammasome is composed of several proteins, including the apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a caspase activation and recruitment domain (ASC). We developed vaccines targeting various regions of ASC using a Qβ virus-like particle (VLP) platform to assess the efficacy of anti-ASC antibodies for inhibiting inflammasome activity. Using a mouse model of gout, we assessed seven vaccines targeting mouse ASC for their ability to reduce inflammasome activation and neutrophil responses. Three vaccines targeting different regions of the ASC protein (pyrin domain, linker region, and the caspase activation and recruitment domain) successfully targeted ASC, reduced IL-1β, and reduced neutrophil activation. Combining these three vaccines into one cocktail vaccine yielded similar efficacy in the gout model with a favorable safety profile. The combined ASC vaccine also reduced inflammasome levels and pathologically phosphorylated tau in a transgenic mouse model of tauopathy and did not significantly impair host immune responses to bacterial or viral infections. Thus, Qβ-VLP vaccines against ASC can neutralize pathological inflammasome activity across multiple inflammatory disease models.

items.title: Unraveling Tyrosine Hydroxylase in the Brain of a Crustacean: An Integrative Investigation Using Different Approaches.
items.abstract: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine (DA) synthesis, is conserved across most animal phyla. DA regulates motor activity, sensory processing motivation, neural homeostasis, and protection against oxidative stress. TH and DA have been described in vertebrates and in some invertebrates, including arthropods. This study investigated the anatomical location of TH and DA and characterized the biochemical and molecular structure of TH in the brain of the mangrove crab Ucides cordatus. This species is a useful environmental model for neurodegeneration studies, due to its occurrence in metal-contaminated mangrove ecosystems, and as prey of other species, including humans. Using immunohistochemistry, immunoblotting, and structural modeling, we mapped TH presence and distribution in the crustacean brain and analyzed its molecular and evolutionary characteristics. Our results revealed a TH fragment structurally similar to fragments found in 21 other species and in a complex dopaminergic network in U. cordatus, characterized by diverse neuronal morphologies, widespread projections, and sensitivity to dopaminergic neurotoxins. These findings may support further studies on catecholaminergic neurobiology.

items.title: Impacts of farming practices on pig gut microbiota and their interactions with soil microbial communities in tropical agroecosystems.
items.abstract: Livestock farming systems are associated with differences microbial communities in both animals and soils, yet the ecological mechanisms linking these compartments remain poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of contrasting farming systems (intensive vs. agroecological) on the gut microbiota of Creole pigs and associated soil microbial communities in farms located in Guadeloupe (French West Indies). Fecal and soil samples were analyzed using 16S and 18S Ribosomal Ribonucleic Acid (rRNA) genes metabarcoding to characterize bacterial, archaeal and fungal diversity. Pig gut microbiota was dominated by Bacillota (63.44% and 67.55% for intensive and agroecological raised pigs respectively) and Bacteroidota (24.70% and 18.56% for intensive and agroecological raised pigs respectively), whereas soils were mainly dominated by Acidobacteriota (14.61% and 17.48% for plowed and unplowed soil respectively), Actinomycetota (7.61% and 9.05% for plowed and unplowed soil respectively), and Bacillota (6.62% and 9.87% for plowed and unplowed soil respectively), indicating limited taxonomic overlap. Agroecological management was associated with higher relative abundances of Bacillota and Euryarchaeota in pigs and greater fungal diversity in soils. A total of 234 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were common to all four groups (pig gut-agroecological, pig gut-intensive, plowed soil and unplowed soil), representing the microbial taxa shared between gut and soil environments; however, these taxa were generally abundant in the gut and rare in soils. These results suggest an ecological link between pigs and soil microbial communities that may be mediated by environmental processes. This underscores the interconnectedness of animal and environmental health within a One Health framework.

items.title: Challenges and Opportunities for Kaposi Sarcoma Clinical Trials in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Review
items.abstract: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor that remains a significant global public health challenge, with approximately 70% of cases occurring in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) are highly prevalent. Furthermore, relatively few clinical trials have been conducted in SSA, potentially delaying the development of more effective interventions for this cancer. This review evaluated completed prospective clinical trials for the treatment of HIV-associated Kaposi sarcoma (KS) conducted in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and highlighted the complementary role of investigator-initiated clinical trials in drug development. We searched the internet and medical databases using relevant key terms. We identified 171 indexed HIV-KS clinical trials worldwide and extracted seven that were conducted in SSA between 1984 and July 2022. The first trial took place in Zimbabwe and was published in 2005. The second and third trials were conducted in South Africa and published in 2008 and 2012, respectively. The fourth and sixth trials were done in Kenya, Uganda, South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Brazil, and were published in 2018 and 2020. The fifth was an investigator-initiated trial (IIT) done in Kenya and published in 2018 and 2019. The sixth trial featured the largest sample size and the most diverse study population. The seventh evaluated the effectiveness of locally sourced compression bandages for HIV-KS leg lymphedema in Kenya and was published in 2022. The number of clinical trials for interventions to treat HIV-KS in SSA remains disproportionate to the high burden of disease in the region. Highlighting research gaps may stimulate interest in studies aimed at finding a cure for HIV-KS in sub-Saharan Africa.

items.title: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction: From Mechanisms to Winning Team of Management
items.abstract: Heart failure is a global public health and clinical problem affecting 1-2% of the adult population and course with high mortality despite of significant advances in disease modifying in past few decades. Heart failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) is a progressive clinical state with presence of typical symptoms of heart failure and characterized by high mortality with recurrent hospitalizations. In HFrEF evidence-based management strategies are available based on positive results of large clinical trials outcomes. Recent clinical investigations and consensus statements have generated increased clinical interest to the evidence based treatment strategies. These strategies include renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors, beta-adrenergic blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. In addition, nonpharmacological approaches such as implantable cardiac defibrillators, cardiac resynchronization therapy, moderate physical activity and several other new treatment approaches have been shown to decrease mortality in selected subpopulation of patients with HFrEF. Despite of proven guideline directed medical treatment in HFrEF, significant proportion of patients remain undertreated due to not proven medication and not appropriate combination management, suboptimal dose adjustment, high comorbidity burden. In this review we discuss the proven evidence based efficacy of each pharmacologic and device therapy option in HFrEF as well as novel therapeutic strategies. On the basis of existed evidence the outcome directed effective treatment, improve of outpatient monitoring, escape of vulnerable phases of disease and target of comorbidities should be the aim of management and care on HF patients in everyday practice.

items.title: From Dementia Prevention Literacy to Preventive Agency: A Proposed Theoretical Framework for Translating Knowledge into Action
items.abstract: Dementia prevention education increasingly seeks to translate evidence about modifiable risk factors into meaningful public engagement and preventive action. However, access to information and an understanding of prevention recommendations do not necessarily enable individuals to act on them. This conceptual paper proposes dementia preventive agency as a candidate construct for examining the relationship between prevention knowledge and the capacity to undertake informed, feasible and contextually meaningful action.Building on scholarship concerning dementia prevention literacy, preventive capacity, personal relevance, affective appraisal and knowledge translation, the paper examines whether preventive agency offers explanatory value beyond existing accounts of health literacy, behavioural readiness and self-efficacy. It provisionally conceptualises preventive agency as the situated capacity, exercised alone or with others, to interpret prevention evidence, evaluate its personal significance, exercise informed choice and identify actions that are achievable within one’s circumstances. The paper distinguishes this construct from knowledge, motivation, intention and behaviour, and considers how personal, social and structural contexts enable or constrain its expression.Rather than presenting preventive agency as an established or empirically validated theory, the paper develops six provisional propositions, each paired with the evidence that would weaken it, identifies which of them would discriminate preventive agency from existing constructs rather than merely be consistent with it, and proposes a staged research agenda spanning qualitative exploration, realist evaluation, measurement development and intervention testing. The contribution is a testable conceptual proposal intended to invite scrutiny, refinement and empirical assessment by researchers in dementia prevention, health education and public health. To support boundary-setting and testing, the paper compares preventive agency with its closest frameworks (Table 1), reports a first targeted literature search (Appendix 3), presents a provisional eight-item draft measure (DPA-8), and outlines its validation through exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling, together with a pre-specified pilot protocol (Appendix 4). The problem of translating prevention knowledge into action is not new and is not claimed as a contribution. No empirical data are reported.

items.title: Climate Change and Yellow Fever in South America: Ecological Factors, Emerging Risks and Future Transmission Scenarios
items.abstract: Yellow fever (YF) remains a major public health threat in South America, where transmission is closely linked to climatic conditions, forest ecosystems, sylvatic mosquito vectors, and non-human primates. Climate change, together with deforestation, biodiversity loss, and expanding human activities, is reshaping the ecological interactions that sustain yellow fever virus (YFV) circulation. This narrative review examines how climatic and environmental changes influence YF epidemiology, emerging transmission risks, and potential future scenarios in South America. Increasing temperatures, altered precipitation patterns, humidity changes, and extreme weather events may affect mosquito abundance, survival, vector competence, and geographic distribution. At the same time, forest fragmentation, agricultural expansion, mining, and urbanization modify interactions among vectors, non-human primates, and human populations, potentially increasing spillover opportunities. Recent outbreaks in Brazil, Colombia, and other South American countries underscore the continued vulnerability of populations living near forest ecosystems, particularly where vaccination coverage remains insufficient. Future climate scenarios suggest possible shifts in transmission seasonality, expansion into previously less receptive geographical areas, and increased exposure at forest–urban interfaces. Although sustained urban transmission has not been documented for decades, the widespread presence of Aedes aegypti warrants continued vigilance. Addressing these challenges requires integrated One Health strategies combining climate-informed surveillance, monitoring of non-human primate epizootics, ecological modeling, targeted vaccination, ecosystem conservation, and regional cooperation. Strengthening these approaches is essential to anticipate emerging risks and prevent future YF outbreaks in South America.

items.title: ALSmiR: a curated evidence resource for ALS-associated microRNAs for biomarker discovery
items.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a multifactorial, late-onset neurodegenerative disease with incompletely understood pathogenesis. Limited survival after symptom onset creates an urgent need for biomarkers to support diagnosis, prognosis, and patient stratification. MicroRNAs are among the candidate biomarkers investigated in this disease. Although reviews have synthesized microRNA expression findings, differences in patient populations, biospecimens, and methods complicate comparisons. In the age of data-driven research, we need an updated, searchable resource that links each finding to its context and incorporates growing evidence. Here, we present ALSmiR, a public, manually curated database of polymerase chain reaction-based microRNA expression findings from human biological fluids and their components. ALSmiR currently contains 1,620 expression records from 49 publications comparing patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with healthy controls, covering 816 microRNA names across 13 biospecimen categories. We link publication, cohort, and microRNA-result tables to preserve each finding's clinical and experimental context. We retain significant and non-significant results and provide searchable records and comma-separated values exports for independent analysis. We update ALSmiR annually and verify author submissions against source publications before inclusion. Researchers can use ALSmiR to assess candidate biomarkers, formulate hypotheses, and design independent validation studies. ALSmiR is freely accessible worldwide without registration at https://alsmir.dokhlab.org/.

items.title: Repurposed catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors tolcapone and entacapone preferentially suppress aggregation and seeding of P301 mutant tau in human neuronal models.
items.abstract: Background and purpose Pathogenic aggregation and propagation of seed-competent TAU assemblies drive tauopathies. MAPT P301 mutations accelerate aggregation and enhance seed competence, yet pharmacological strategies selectively targeting these pathogenic species remain limited. We investigated whether the clinically approved catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors tolcapone (TOL) and entacapone (ENT) preferentially modulate mutant TAU aggregation and seeding. Experimental approach TOL and ENT effects on TAU aggregation were evaluated via cell-free assays, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and in silico docking. Functional consequences of compound-modified fibrils were assessed in mutant TAU-expressing SH-SY5Y cells. Translational relevance was examined in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons exposed to pathogenic K18 fibrils, followed by post-seeding compound treatment. Key results Both compounds dose-dependently inhibited TAU aggregation, exhibiting greater potency, stronger SPR binding affinities, and more favourable computed interaction energies for P301S mutant versus wild-type TAU. Fibrils formed with TOL or ENT induced less downstream TAU oligomerization and phosphorylation in SH-SY5Y cells, with TOL showing superior protection. In hiPSC-derived neurons, post-seeding treatment with either compound decreased fibril-induced, sarkosyl-insoluble, TAU aggregation and phosphorylation without overt cytotoxicity. Conclusion and implications TOL and ENT preferentially reduced the aggregation and seeding of pathogenic P301 mutant TAU in the experimental models examined. These findings provide proof-of-concept support for mutation-focused pharmacological approaches and identify catechol scaffolds as starting points for developing more potent and safer TAU-directed compounds. Further studies are required to define the relevant molecular interactions, confirm the neuronal findings across additional hiPSC lines and determine whether effective CNS exposure can be achieved in vivo.

items.title: When Tics and Autism Meet: Phenomenology, Severity, and Treatment Patterns.
items.abstract: Background Tic disorders frequently co-occur with neurodevelopmental conditions, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, the impact of ASD on tic phenomenology, severity, and treatment patterns remains incompletely understood. Objectives To compare clinical characteristics, tic phenomenology, severity, and treatment patterns in individuals with tic disorders with and without comorbid ASD. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 535 participants from Calgary Child and Adult Tic Disorders Clinical Registries. Tic severity was assessed using the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale (YGTSS). Comorbidities, tic phenomenology, and pharmacological treatments were recorded. ASD and non-ASD groups were compared using t-tests and chi-square tests. Results Mean age at tic onset was 6.79 years; 73.3% were male, and 9.2% had ASD. ASD was associated with higher rates of complex motor (arm 20.4% vs 9.9%; hand 24.5% vs 13.9%) and vocal tics (phrases 12.2% vs 3.5%; palilalia 20.4% vs 8.3%; blocking/stuttering 16.3% vs 6.2%) compared with non-ASD participants (all P Conclusions Comorbid ASD in tic disorders is associated with higher rates of complex motor and vocal tics, while severity is similar to non-ASD. Lower tic-related impairment may reflect communication differences. Comorbid symptoms influenced treatment supporting the need for individualized management.

items.title: The Ash Dieback Pathogen Resists the Chemical Defences of Its Host Tree, European Ash, by Depleting Them From the Growth Medium.
items.abstract: Plant pathogenic fungi are major drivers of disease in forest trees, often causing substantial ecological and economic damage. Ash dieback, caused by the ascomycete Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, has resulted in the widespread decline of Fraxinus excelsior populations throughout Europe. As infection is initiated in leaves containing diverse plant defensive metabolites, the ability of H. fraxineus to cope with host chemistry may determine successful host colonisation. We therefore investigated the responses of H. fraxineus to crude ash leaf extracts and individual defensive compounds. In contrast to the non-ash associated fungi tested, H. fraxineus was not inhibited by crude methanolic leaf extracts or most plant defence compounds tested. In addition, H. fraxineus depleted ash compounds extensively from the growth medium. Consistent with these findings, untargeted metabolomics revealed extensive alterations of the ash leaf-based medium by H. fraxineus, with 48% of detected chemical features being significantly reduced following fungal growth. Moreover, the growth of H. fraxineus was promoted by nearly all tested ash metabolites in minimal medium, indicating that these compounds can support fungal growth and may serve as carbon sources. Together, these results suggest that successful colonisation of ash tissues by H. fraxineus depends on its resistance to host defences, facilitated by its ability to deplete defensive compounds from colonised tissue.

items.title: Evolutionary history and taxonomy of the genus Zea.
items.abstract: Premise Taxonomic differentiation of teosinte species (Zea spp.), the closest relatives of maize (Z. mays) is crucial for understanding their distribution, ecology, and evolutionary history. Resolving the taxonomic uncertainties is of scientific interest and has practical implications for biodiversity management, preservation, and utilization. Methods We examined the evolutionary history of Zea based on species representation, improved multilocus phylogenies and estimation of relative times of diversification. Relationships among 379 samples, representing all species of Zea, were inferred from genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) data, morphological, and climatic descriptors. Results Phylogenies from GBS data were congruent, and species and races were identified; multivariate analysis with morphological data and those combining genomic and climatic variables supported the taxonomy and relationships among species. Phylogenetic results showed that Huehuetenango is a sister group to the Mexican annual teosintes, while Zea nicaraguensis is not differentiated from Zea luxurians. The newly discovered populations are distinct from each other and from other Zea species and represent three new entities. Our results reinforce the hypothesis of historical gene introgression events, such as between Zea luxurians and Zea mays subsp. parviglumis. Modern maize originated from Z. mays subsp. parviglumis through a single evolutionary event in northern Guerrero. In the central highlands, maize admixed with what is known as the Chalco race of teosinte, which facilitated its domestication and subsequent adaptation. Conclusions Evidence from multiple independent sources augments previous knowledge of the relationships, origin, and migration of Zea species, supporting a new classification to resolve the taxonomy of this genus.

items.title: Hatch date and early growth characteristics of different subspecies of Schizopygopsis younghusbandi Regan, 1905 in Xizang, China.
items.abstract: Fish otolith microstructure is a fundamental aspect of fish ecology, providing insights into early-life history traits such as daily age, growth rates and hatch dates. To investigate variations in hatch dates and early growth characteristics among different subspecies, Schizopygopsis younghusbandi younghusbandi and Schizopygopsis younghusbandi shannaensis were collected from Xizang, China, during the spring and autumn of 2016 (S. y. younghusbandi) and 2020 (S. y. shannaensis). The formation of the first otolith increment in S. younghusbandi occurred on the second day post-hatching, with subsequent increments increasing at a rate of one per day, as confirmed through the analysis of otoliths from juveniles of known age. The hatch date differed between subspecies: S. y. shannaensis hatched earlier, beginning in January, while S. y. younghusbandi hatched from February onward. The growth rates also varied, with S. y. shannaensis exhibiting a higher rate than S. y. younghusbandi (total length [TL] = 0.096 D + 10.330, R 2 = 0.690 for S. y. younghusbandi, TL = 0.118 D + 12.180, R 2 = 0.886 for S. y. shannaensis). Increment width measurements of lapilli further supported the observation that S. y. shannaensis grows faster. Moreover, individuals collected in autumn demonstrated significantly greater growth than those collected in spring. These findings provide essential information for developing conservation strategies for S. younghusbandi and deepen our understanding of species adaptation to high-altitude riverine environments.

items.title: Astrocytic Ketogenesis Protects Central Nervous System Injury via CPT1A Stabilization and Epigenetic Regulation.
items.abstract: Following central nervous system (CNS) injury, reactive astrocytes proliferate and encapsulate the lesion to facilitate repair. However, the specific metabolic characteristics remain unknown. Here, through integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we uncovered a subset of astrocytes that undergo enhanced lipid and ketone metabolic reprogramming following spinal cord injury (SCI). The ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB) inhibited autophagic degradation of carnitine-palmitoyltransferase-1A (CPT1A) via P300-mediated lysine β-hydroxybutyrylation (Kbhb). Astrocyte-specific deletion of Cpt1a led to impaired wound healing, reduced axonal sparing and worsened locomotor recovery after SCI, effects rescued by exogenous β-OHB. Mechanistically, ketogenesis promotes wound repair and lipid metabolic reprogramming, forming a positive feedback loop via H3K9bhb-dependent epigenetic remodeling in astrocytes after SCI. Furthermore, ketogenic diet (KD) promoted tissue repair across multiple CNS injury models. Clinically, elevated β-OHB levels were associated with better tissue preservation and functional recovery in SCI patients. Collectively, our findings underscore the critical role of astrocytic lipid metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming after CNS injury and identify KD as a promising therapeutic strategy.

items.title: Intraoperative performance errors predict patient outcomes in robot-assisted radical prostatectomy.
items.abstract: Objectives To evaluate the association between objectively assessed intraoperative surgical performance and postoperative functional outcomes following robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP). Patients/subjects and methods Prospectively collected data from 100 patients undergoing bilateral nerve-sparing RARP by seven experienced robotic surgeons were analysed. To control for age-related confounding, a subgroup of 66 subjects was selected from the initial cohort using age-matching. These patients, all of whom were preoperatively potent, were identified from an audited outcomes registry with complete video recordings. In all, 14 trained surgeons trained to score the recordings using validated RARP-specific metrics for procedure steps, errors, critical errors, and nerve-sparing phase errors. Results There were no significant pre- or postoperative differences in demographic or clinical variables between patients with good or poor outcomes. The mean inter-rater reliability of video assessments was high (0.91). There were no significant differences in the number of steps completed or critical errors made. Intraoperative performance in cases resulting in erectile dysfunction at 12 months was characterised by 43% more total errors and 67% more neurovascular bundle (NVB) dissection errors (P Conclusions The objectively assessed intraoperative performance of the surgeon strongly predicted the clinical outcome of the procedure at 1 year. The more errors the surgeon made the more likely the patient was to have erectile dysfunction at 12 months.

items.title: Determinants of Self-Care Practices Among Family Caregivers of Older Adults with Chronic Illness: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.
items.abstract: Background and objectives Caregiver burden significantly impedes self-care, often resulting in poor health and increased vulnerability to chronic illness. Despite these risks, the underlying factors influencing caregivers' self-care remain understudied. This qualitative descriptive study explored the context of caregiver self-care and identified perceived barriers and facilitators to practicing self-care. Research design and methods We conducted four focus groups with 14 caregivers primarily responsible for providing in-home care to older adults (≥ 65 years) with chronic illnesses. Focus groups were audio-recorded and transcribed. A hierarchical coding system was developed and refined using the focus group guide and preliminary transcript review. Coded transcripts were analyzed using an iterative inductive-deductive thematic approach based on established theories. Results Caregivers' multi-dimensional definitions of self-care shaped their perceived barriers and facilitators. Three core determinants of self-care behaviors were identified: capability (caregivers' psychological and physical health, and behavioral regulation); motivation (caregiver identity, emotions, and perceived control); and opportunity (social and environmental influences and resources). Caregivers recognized that self-care deficits negatively affect their clinical, behavioral, and psychosocial outcomes. These results informed the development of a conceptual framework for caregiver self-care. Discussion and implications Findings underscore the importance of integrating caregivers' own perceptions of self-care into support models. Interventions should transition toward personalized approaches that address both intrinsic psychological drivers and extrinsic environmental constraints. The framework derived from this study provides a theory-driven roadmap that informs future interventions, ensuring support systems align with caregivers' unique needs and contexts to foster better self-care and ultimately enhance their health outcomes.

items.title: The ecological signal value of faces: differential effects of threat-related expressions and evolutionarily significant social cues on recognition and source memory.
items.abstract: Extending the dimensional approach to emotion, emerging evidence suggests that facial expressions displaying discrete emotions modulate cognition according to their distinct ecological signal values. However, whether these divergent signals shape source memory processes remains unanswered. Here, we investigated whether angry, fearful, and neutral faces - varying across the evolutionarily significant social cues of sex and group membership (in-group vs. out-group) - differentially influence recognition and source memory performance. Following incidental encoding, participants completed a sequential source-monitoring test requiring confidence-based recognition judgments and forced-choice source decisions. While the emotional stimuli were equated for valence and arousal, a noteworthy portion of our findings indicates that memory is regulated by the communicative value and the threat potential of the expressions. Notably, a recognition advantage emerged for angry expressions, particularly among out-group targets, whereas a more liberal response bias was detected for angry male faces, demonstrating a mnemonic sensitivity to facilitate direct threat anticipation. Contrary to predictions, source memory accuracy was exclusively modulated by group membership, reflecting a robust in-group advantage regardless of the emotional signal or target sex. Collectively, this study illustrates the intricate interplay between emotional expressions and evolutionarily important cues, highlighting how mnemonic mechanisms differentially prioritise the multifarious facial signals to effectively guide adaptive behaviour.

items.title: A sub-Earth-sized TESS planet candidate in the nearby M-dwarf binary GJ 774, most likely orbiting GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274)
items.abstract: Small planets transiting the nearest M dwarfs are the terrestrial planets most accessible to detailed characterisation. We report a sub-Earth-sized transiting planet candidate in the wide (17.6") M-dwarf binary GJ 774 at 12.86 pc, most likely orbiting the M2.5 primary GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274). The signal was a SPOC multi-sector threshold-crossing event (MES = 7.95) and is not a TESS Object of Interest. In eight TESS sectors (2019-2026) a 1.28-h transit recurs every 4.225138 +/- 0.000010 d with a box-mean depth of 365 +/- 32 ppm in A's light. The 2026 data, which entered neither the SPOC search nor our selection, show it at the ephemeris predicted from 2019-2023 data (304 +/- 43 ppm; none of 10^5 phase-scrambled versions of the 2026 data is as deep). The per-target false-alarm probability is < 0.03 at 95%. Odd/even, secondary-eclipse, archival-plate and Gaia radial-velocity tests exclude unrelated blended eclipsing binaries and eclipsing companions on 4.2-d orbits, and hierarchical eclipsing binaries are improbable. The stars are 0.85 TESS pixel apart, so the TRICERATOPS false-positive probability (0.26) is set by a planet on GJ 774 B. B is disfavoured because its own light does not dim enough: PRF-deblended photometry gives 109 +/- 115 ppm in B's light, against 1089 ppm required if B were the host. Conditional on a point source at A or at B, the joint host model gives P(A)=0.59-0.97 (0.97 for the native target-pixel baseline). Over all sectors the PRF photometry is consistent with A, but in the out-of-sample 2026 data 40% of the deficit appears at B's position, an unexplained 2-3 sigma (PSF-model and depth dependent) tension with host A. On A the planet has R_p=0.70 +/- 0.06 R_Earth, S=15.0 +/- 1.8 S_Earth and T_eq=548 +/- 16 K. It is not validated; resolved ground-based photometry of the pair would test host B directly.

items.title: Cyber Soldier project - A threat-led methodology for assessing the Digital Resilience of cybersecurity systems
items.abstract: In order to comply with European regulatory frameworks like the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), we propose the Cyber Soldier approach and tool set, which presents a threat-led approach for evaluating the digital resilience of cybersecurity systems inside enterprises. This approach, in contrast to conventional vulnerability assessments or penetration testing, focuses on simulating the tactics, methods, and procedures (TTPs) of actual attackers in order to assess the efficacy of operational resilience mechanisms and cybersecurity measures in production systems. In order to assess the organization's readiness for complex cyberthreats, the suggested approach combines threat information, red team scenario creation, and detection performance analysis into a single procedure. We show how the proposed framework connects the operational practice of resilience testing with the strategic compliance obligations under DORA. We also provide some preliminary statistics about the use of the Cyber Soldier toolkit in practical settings.

items.title: Machine Learning for Biodiversity Conservation: A Review of Ecological Monitoring, Species Prediction, and Conservation Applications
items.abstract: Biodiversity loss, habitat degradation, climate change, invasive species, and unsustainable resource use have intensified the need for effective and evidence-based conservation strategies. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a valuable approach for processing large and complex ecological datasets, identifying species, predicting species distributions, monitoring ecosystem changes, and supporting conservation decision-making. This review examines the applications, methodological developments, benefits, and limitations of machine learning in biodiversity conservation, with particular emphasis on ecological monitoring, species prediction, and practical conservation interventions. It synthesizes major approaches, including supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning, computer vision, acoustic classification, remote sensing, and ensemble modelling. Evidence from previous research demonstrates that automated camera-trap analysis, bioacoustic monitoring, satellite imagery, and environmental DNA analysis can improve the efficiency and spatial coverage of biodiversity assessments. Species distribution models also support the identification of suitable habitats, climate-sensitive areas, and potential conservation priorities. Furthermore, machine learning can facilitate invasive-species detection, wildlife population assessment, habitat restoration, and protected-area management. However, its effectiveness depends on data quality, representative training datasets, model interpretability, computational resources, and collaboration between ecologists, conservation practitioners, and local communities. Ethical concerns, including sensitive species-location disclosure, surveillance risks, and unequal access to technological infrastructure, also require attention. The review concludes that machine learning can strengthen biodiversity conservation when integrated with ecological expertise, field validation, transparent governance, and long-term monitoring. Future research should prioritize geographically representative datasets, explainable models, uncertainty assessment, and conservation outcomes that can be independently evaluated.

items.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
items.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.

items.title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.

items.title: Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
items.abstract: In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement. We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. The five-axis metrics also distinguish systems with close public benchmark averages and show that high scores need not come with early or efficient gains. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve. Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.

items.title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
items.abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.

items.title: Train An Imaginative Agent
items.abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.

items.title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
items.abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.

items.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
items.abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.

items.title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
items.abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.

items.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
items.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.

items.title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
items.abstract: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.

items.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
items.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.

items.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
items.abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.

items.title: AfriBED: a Speech Recognition Bias Evaluation Dataset for Low Resource African Languages
items.abstract: Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition systems (ASR), current systems exhibit speaker-attribute bias, i.e., their speech recognition performance is biased against certain speakers based on their demographic attributes such as gender, accents, and speaker type. However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. In this paper, we introduce African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset (AfriBED), a novel speech recognition bias evaluation dataset for two low resource African languages, Bemba and Nyanja, to detect and estimate gender and speaker-type bias for ASR systems. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.

items.title: Next Best Action: Causal Constrained Offline RL for Business Action Targeting
items.abstract: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must select among customer interventions (e.g., discounts, promotions, and lifecycle actions), maximize long-term economic value, satisfy complex operational constraints, and remain causally grounded. Existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for meeting these requirements jointly. We address this gap by formulating NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). We then integrate off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the Linear Programming (LP) formulation of the CMDP. The resulting policy selects actions based on customer states to maximize long-term value while explicitly enforcing business guardrails. Furthermore, the LP formulation yields shadow prices that quantify the economic trade-offs of operational constraints (e.g., fairness and user welfare), enhancing policy interpretability. We validate our proposed offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework on an industry case study involving rideshare coupon targeting, where customer states are defined by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) stages. We evaluate performance using model-based off-policy evaluation, with causal dynamics estimated from a temporal holdout. Under the observed coupon budget and RFM state representation, our optimized policy improves customer lifetime value (LTV) by 19% over the estimated behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline. Although the demonstrated action space is binary, the proposed framework is action-agnostic, yielding a general-purpose decision module for targeting systems that manage multiple interventions.

items.title: Mise-en-Video: Fine-Grained 3D Control for Multi-Shot Video Generation
items.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have enabled high-fidelity single-shot synthesis, yet practical storytelling creation requires multi-shot videos with both strong inter-shot consistency and fine-grained controllability. Existing multi-shot video generation approaches achieve strong consistency but still fall short in controllability. In this paper, we propose Mise-en-Video (MeV), a highly controllable multi-shot video generation framework that allows video creators to conduct staging the multi-shot in the 3D space and then generate the corresponding multi-shot video. To achieve this, our framework combines a hierarchical attention mechanism for multi-level narrative consistency with 3D-aware layout guidance for precise, per-shot spatial control. To support training and evaluation, we develop standardized annotation pipelines and construct a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot texts and oriented 3D bounding boxes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MeV consistently outperforms strong baselines in video quality, inter-shot consistency, and subject-level controllability.

items.title: SOMA: Continuous Monitoring and Intervention for System Two Reasoning with System One Models
items.abstract: Reasoning models often run into problems without noticing them, even when symptoms are visible in their own text. In humans, metacognition separates monitoring from control: fast, intuitive signals keep watch while slow, deliberate reasoning unfolds and help decide whether to continue, change course, or stop. System One (S1) decision models, such as Jev, are a natural candidate for this role: they return a calibrated probability for a natural-language question about a text in one fast call, yet they are used only as gates before reasoning. We introduce SOMA (System One Metacognitive Awareness), in which an S1 model continuously monitors a System Two (S2) reasoning model and intervenes when needed. SOMA has three layers: a scenario layer states each objective in natural language with predefined actions, an awareness layer lets S1 judge whether the described behavior appears, and a control layer accumulates these judgments, first reminds S2, and takes over only if the behavior persists. Sharing one S1 model and one controller across tasks, without training, SOMA addresses two different failures on two reasoning models: on overthinking, it cuts reasoning tokens by up to 36\% while improving average accuracy, and on unanswerable questions, it raises abstention from 70.5\% to 87.2\%.

items.title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
items.abstract: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model's consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain.
