items.title: Dhikr and Cognitive Neuroscience
items.abstract: The increasing prevalence of anxiety and psychological distress in the post-pandemic era has intensified interest in spiritual and religious sources of mental tranquility. Although previous studies have discussed the psychological and spiritual benefits of dhikr, the relationship between the Qur’anic concept of tranquility and its cognitive-neuroscientific mechanisms remains insufficiently explored through an integrated interdisciplinary framework. This study examines the relationship between dhikr and ṭuma’nīnah in Q.S. Al-Ra‘d [13]: 28 by integrating Qur’anic linguistic-semantic analysis, spiritual exegesis, and cognitive neuroscience. Using qualitative library research, the study analyzes the linguistic structure of the verse, examines interpretations of selected classical and modern mufassir, and reviews relevant findings from neuroscience and cognitive psychology. The findings show that ṭuma’nīnah is presented as a dynamic and continuous process, linguistically reflected in the verbal structure of taṭma’innu. Exegetically, dhikr involves not merely verbal repetition but the internalization of divine awareness within human consciousness. From a cognitive-neuroscientific perspective, repetitive religious and contemplative practices may support emotional regulation, reduce stress reactivity, and promote physiological relaxation. The novelty of this study lies in proposing an integrative framework connecting the linguistic meaning of ṭuma’nīnah, Qur’anic interpretations of dhikr, and contemporary cognitive-neuroscientific perspectives, contributing to an interdisciplinary understanding of Qur’anic spirituality in addressing contemporary psychological challenges.

items.title: Redirecting Correctional Education Implementation Towards Lowering Recidivism in Nigeria Society
items.abstract: Correctional education programme is purposively for rehabilitation, reformation and reintegration of prison inmates all over the world. This study examined how to redirect correctional education programme implementation towards lowering recidivism in Nigeria Society. Three research questions and objectives guided this study. The study was a qualitative survey carried out in Portharcourt prison. 122 incarcerated inmates in Portharcourt correctional service who have benefited and are benefiting from different Formal and Non-Formal rehabilitation education programmes was the population of the study, all the 122 inmates were sampled based on total enumeration sampling technique. A validated interview schedule was utilized for data collection. Data collected was thematically transcribed. Findings revealed that providers of the correctional education programmes in Portharcourt correctional service do not involve the inmates (beneficiaries) in the selection of choice of programme type; the facilitator utilizes pedagogical approach instead of andragucal approach for facilitation. Also, freed inmates are stigmatized and this contributes to recidivism. Based on the findings, the researchers recommended among others that service provider of correctional programme should always give the inmates the opportunity to choose option of programme to be enrolled into because interest is a motivator for adult enrollment into adult educational programme; facilitators of the programmes should be trained on how to use andragogical approaches to foster learning.

items.title: Effects of cortisol time-scales in a model of emotion regulation
items.abstract: Stress reshapes cortico-limbic dynamics across multiple timescales, with important consequences for healthy and pathological arousal responses. We develop and analyze a Wilson-Cowan model of prefrontal-amygdala circuitry, incorporating excitatory and inhibitory populations involved in emotional regulation. The effects of stress cortisol are represented as history-dependent modulations of two stress-sensitive interactions: recurrent prefrontal excitation and inhibition of basolateral amygdala principal cells. Using numerical simulations and bifurcation analysis, we examine how this self-interacting system organizes transitions between stable activity and infra-slow oscillations, and how this structure changes with cortisol-related temporal memory. To distinguish the effects of memory temporal distribution from those of its timescale, we compare weak and strong Gamma kernels with a discrete-delay limit, representing progressively different ways in which past activity can influence current coupling. Introducing temporal memory reshapes the parameter region supporting oscillations and alters their persistence. Weak and strong Gamma kernels produce remarkably similar global dynamics, whereas the discrete-delay limit generates a substantially richer bifurcation structure, including quasiperiodic activity. Together, these results suggest that the dynamical effects of cortisol depend not only on the characteristic timescale of its action, but also on the shape of the temporal memory through which past neural activity influences the present. Different forms of temporal integration may provide a mechanism by which neural systems implement distinct functional dynamics, while changes in this integration could promote atypical or pathological rhythmic regimes.

items.title: Simulating Alzheimer's amyloid-like pathology on a fly central nervous system connectome
items.abstract: In Alzheimer's disease, the amount of pathology in the brain is an imperfect predictor of how much function is lost. Pathology leads to that loss through neural circuits, but these cannot be observed neuron by neuron in patients. This study therefore simulated the central nervous system of the adult male Drosophila melanogaster: 166,700 integrate-and-fire neurons wired by the MaleCNS connectome. The simulator reproduced a published fly brain model (rate correlation 0.9997). Three kinds of damage reported in amyloid-$β$ flies, a lowered spike threshold, synapse loss and neuron loss, were imposed with assumed magnitudes, and circuit responses were measured in 1,424 simulated flies. The number of neurons lost was a poor guide to the deficit, which depended partly on how many synaptic contacts went with them and whether they included input neurons or one command neuron. With the same 12% of neurons removed, odour-evoked whole-brain activity was 93%, 47% or 31% of the healthy value when damage fell on poorly connected, random or highly connected neurons; these flies lost 20%, 35% and 48% of contacts. When the contacts lost were equalised, the three groups differed less; whether the remaining difference reflects where the damage fell could not be established. In 48 flies, restoring only the contacts that surviving neurons had lost recovered 62% of the whole-brain deficit, and restoring the removed neurons 39%. In flies that had lost neurons delivering the odour, these accounted for about half the deficit due to neuron loss. One neuron could decide an outcome: all 66 flies that lost the giant fibre on the stimulated side, which commands escape, had a giant fibre rate below 100 Hz, against 1 of 254 that kept it. Whole-brain activity revealed damage at milder severity than the learning index, because it changed much relative to its variation between trials.

items.title: Rewiring of adult neural networks - learning from structural plasticity across multiple scales
items.abstract: Synaptic connections are continuously formed and eliminated even in adult neuronal networks. This process - called structural plasticity - allows networks to change their topology to learn and adapt to their environment or compensate for lesions. Yet, in contrast to synaptic plasticity, structural plasticity is less well studied and understood. We here present the current state of knowledge as well as open problems in the field along three guiding questions: (1) What regulates structural plasticity in biological neural networks? (2) What are the functional consequences and advantages of structural plasticity in adult neural networks? (3) How can our understanding of structural plasticity be translated into clinical and technological applications? We argue that understanding structural plasticity is a problem involving multiple temporal and spatial scales. Solving this problem thus requires collaborative efforts of experimentalists, theoreticians as well as computational modelers, and has the potential for comprehensive neuroscientific insights that can guide the development of medical applications, artificial neural networks as well as neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Rethinking World Models for Biosignals
items.abstract: World models promise to learn how systems evolve and respond to actions, enabling simulation, planning and decision-making. Bringing this promise to biosignals requires more than accurate prediction of physiological recordings. We examine existing biosignal world models through two requirements for intervention use: a genuine action and evidence of its causal effect. We identify three fundamental bottlenecks rooted in physiology: Temporal Latency, the variable delay between an action and its observable effect; System Openness, the influence of drivers beyond the modelled intervention; and Endogenous Dynamics, the system's ongoing evolution without that intervention. Drawing on published evidence, we outline corresponding research directions and propose an Intervention-Effect Validation Checklist to guide evaluation. The aim is to help the biosignal community realise the core promise of world models by learning the latent mechanisms that govern physiological evolution and responses to interventions.

items.title: The Psychology of False Confessions
items.abstract: False confessions represent one of the most significant challenges to the fairness and reliability of criminal justice systems, often leading to wrongful convictions and undermining public confidence in legal institutions. While confessions are traditionally regarded as compelling evidence of guilt, research has demonstrated that innocent individuals may admit to crimes they did not commit under the influence of various psychological, cognitive, emotional and situational factors. This paper examines the psychological mechanisms underlying false self-incrimination, with particular emphasis on the interaction between cognitive vulnerabilities, emotional distress, and interrogation practices. The analysis explores the principal categories of false confessions—voluntary, coerced-compliant and coerced-internalized—and discusses the individual characteristics that increase susceptibility, including youth, intellectual disabilities, mental disorders, heightened suggestibility, memory distortions and elevated stress levels. Particular attention is given to the impact of psychologically coercive interrogation techniques, prolonged questioning, authority pressure, fatigue and social isolation on decision-making processes. The paper further evaluates empirical findings from forensic psychology and criminology, highlighting the role of cognitive biases, compliance and emotional regulation in shaping confession behavior. From a legal perspective, the study emphasizes the importance of procedural safeguards designed to minimize the risk of false confessions, including mandatory electronic recording of interrogations, access to legal counsel, evidence-based interviewing methods and specialized protections for vulnerable suspects. By integrating psychological and legal perspectives, this paper contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of false confessions and underscores the need for investigative practices that prioritize both the effective administration of justice and the protection of fundamental human rights.

items.title: Enforcing Thermodynamic Consistency in Parameter Optimization and Bayesian Inference of Biochemical Reaction Networks
items.abstract: Subcellular signaling pathways regulating, e.g., cell division or synaptic plasticity, are often modeled as dynamical networks of reactions satisfying the law of mass action. To remain physically grounded, these models must satisfy different physical conservation laws, such as conservation of energy. This gives rise to thermodynamic constraints formalized by the Wegscheider conditions, which ensure that the system is in detailed balance at thermodynamic equilibrium. Explicitly imposing Wegscheider conditions requires identifying cycles in the reaction network. This can become computationally cumbersome, especially in large, complex systems. Furthermore, even when these constraints are explicitly available, enforcing them requires choosing a reparameterization of the network, which may introduce asymmetries among the parameters and affect numerical conditioning. Moreover, this approach often causes inverse uncertainty quantification methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to struggle. Instead of imposing Wegscheider conditions directly in the parameter space, we propose an approach for promoting physical consistency by penalizing parameters that violate detailed balance. We first illustrate the approach on a simple reaction network containing a single cycle. We show that parameter values inferred without thermodynamic constraints can reproduce the experimental data seemingly accurately, while substantially violating the Wegscheider condition. In contrast, the proposed approach preserves the agreement with the observed dynamics while yielding posterior samples that approximately satisfy the thermodynamic constraint. We further apply the approach to a model of PKA-calcineurin signaling in synaptic long-term depression, demonstrating its applicability to a more complex biochemical reaction network.

items.title: Biodiversity conservation and its associations with economic performance, inequality, and peace
items.abstract: Abstract Biodiversity conservation is increasingly recognized as a product of coupled social–ecological systems shaped not only by ecological processes, but also by economic capacity, social inequality, and geopolitical stability. Here, we examined whether national conservation performance is systematically associated with economic prosperity, income inequality, peace, and the importance of natural resources in the national economy across 142 countries. Conservation performance was represented using the Nature Conservation Index (NCI), a composite metric integrating biodiversity threats, land management, governance capacity, and future environmental trends. We analysed relationships between NCI, Gross National Income per capita, the Gini coefficient, the National Peace Index, and the total nature resources rents using a generalized additive model that accounted for nonlinear relationships and income stratification. Together, these societal variables explained deviance of 52.2% for the NCI model. Economic prosperity was positively associated with NCI, although the relationship was nonlinear across income groups, suggesting that conservation capacity does not increase uniformly with development. Counter to commonly assumed relationships between inequality and biodiversity loss, income inequality showed a positive multivariate association with NCI scores. This result suggests that high national conservation performance can coexist with unequal social conditions, potentially reflecting centralized or exclusionary conservation systems that elevate institutional conservation metrics without necessarily improving equitable biodiversity outcomes. We also found that more peaceful countries consistently exhibited higher conservation performance, supporting the view that geopolitical stability provides enabling conditions for sustained conservation governance and institutional continuity. We further suggest that national conservation indices may partly capture governance capacity, reporting infrastructure, and political commitment rather than ecological condition alone, while telecoupled trade systems may allow wealthier nations to externalize environmental pressures beyond their borders. Although the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, our findings highlight the need to interpret global conservation indicators cautiously and to incorporate social equity and externalized environmental impacts more explicitly into international biodiversity assessment frameworks.

items.title: Leadership, burnout, and organizational mental health: a neuroscience-informed perspective
items.abstract: This article argues that the persistent burden of burnout reflects a fundamental conceptual problem—burnout continues to be framed primarily as an individual condition rather than as an occupational phenomenon shaped by interacting structural, organizational, and leadership conditions. Burnout has emerged as a major occupational health challenge. In a 2024 survey across eight predominantly high and upper-middle-income countries, 48% of respondents reported currently grappling with burnout. Separately, depression and anxiety cost the global economy approximately one trillion dollars annually in lost productivity. Drawing on evidence from neuroimaging, stress biology, cognitive neuroscience, and organizational research, this article examines plausible pathways through which leadership behavior may influence conditions that contribute to or protect against burnout, including social threat–reward processing, cognitive flexibility, emotional intelligence, psychological safety, emotional contagion, and stress-related neurobiological responses. Among physicians, burnout has been associated with depression and anxiety, while evidence regarding substance abuse is less consistent. These proposed mechanisms are proximal and potentially modifiable, but operate within broader structural conditions that constrain or enable their effects. Human-centered work design and neuroleadership-informed leadership practices are proposed as complements to broader structural interventions, with implications for health systems, workforce sustainability, and policy design.

items.title: Christian Education and Child Development in Contemporary Society: Process, Challenges and Prospect
items.abstract: This paper examines Christian education's vital role in fostering children's moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social development within contemporary society. Amid shifting cultural values, rapid technological change, and increasing pluralism, Christian education provides a formative framework that grounds children in biblical principles, cultivates godly character, and equips them with life skills for holistic growth. While acknowledging significant challenges such as secular influences, family instability, limited resources, and the widening gap between faith and practice, the paper argues that the prospects for Christian education remain robust. By exploring its foundational processes, addressing its current challenges, and highlighting emerging opportunities, this study underscores Christian education's enduring potential as a transformative force for nurturing spiritually mature, socially responsible, and intellectually capable children in today's world.

items.title: Conservation of Biodiversity in the Hot Arid Rangelands of India
items.abstract: Interest, awareness and discussions about biodiversity conservation in India have increasingly expanded to include rangelands on both national and international platforms. Rangeland ecosystems are characterized by a vital interplay between plant species that serve as forage and grazing animals that act as consumers. The hot arid rangelands in India provide a habitat for a distinctive array of flora and fauna that have evolved to thrive in harsh climatic conditions. This paper explores the biodiversity and conservation issues of hot arid rangelands and highlights the role of traditional conservation practices in addressing these challenges.

items.title: The neuroscience of transformers
items.abstract: Abstract Neuroscience has long informed the development of artificial neural networks, but the success of modern architectures invites, in turn, the converse: can modern networks teach us lessons about brain function? Here, we examine the structure of the cortical column and propose that the transformer provides a natural computational analogy for multiple elements of cortical microcircuit organization. Rather than claiming a literal implementation of transformer equations in cortex, we develop a hypothetical mapping between transformer operations and laminar cortical features, using the analogy as an orienting framework for analysis and discussion. This mapping allows us to examine in greater depth how contextual selection, content routing, recurrent integration, and interlaminar transformations may be distributed across cortical circuitry. In doing so, we generate a broad set of predictions and experimentally testable hypotheses concerning laminar specialization, contextual modulation, dendritic integration, oscillatory coordination, and the effective connectivity of cortical columns. This proposal is intended as a structured hypothesis rather than a definitive account of cortical computation. Placing transformer operations and cortical architectonics into a common descriptive framework sharpens questions, reveals new functional correspondences, and opens a productive route for reciprocal exchange between systems neuroscience and modern AI. More broadly, this perspective suggests that comparing brains and architectures at the level of computational organization can yield genuine insight into both.

items.title: Physical education teacher education for intercultural citizenship in a traumatized society
items.abstract: In divided and conflict-affected societies, higher education institutions offer opportunities for sustained intergroup encounter. Yet proximity alone does not produce meaningful interaction, trust, or cooperation. This challenge is particularly acute in Israel, where Arab and Jewish students enter higher education after years of segregated schooling, amid tensions and intensified fear, mistrust, and collective trauma following October 7, 2023, and the subsequent war. This perspective article argues that Physical Education Teacher Education (PETE) offers an underexplored space for fostering intercultural citizenship. It synthesizes relevant theoretical perspectives and evidence from studies by the authors and others to develop a framework for PETE in divided and traumatized societies. Integrating intergroup contact theory, intercultural citizenship, Sport for Development and Peace, and trauma-sensitive pedagogy, the framework positions PETE as a space for structured contact, embodied cooperation, civic engagement, and resilience. The framework is illustrated through the “Roaming Course,” an experiential, student-led PETE model combining on-campus learning, encounters in diverse communities, shared physical activity, and guided reflection. Drawing on studies involving Arab and Jewish PETE students in Israel, the article shows how structured, discipline-based contact may narrow the gap between willingness to engage and actual intergroup interaction while strengthening students’ capacity to cope with social tension and collective trauma. It demonstrates the value of embedding intercultural citizenship within core curricula rather than relying on extracurricular interventions. It concludes that PETE can prepare future educators to act as agents of social connection, inclusion, and resilience in divided societies.
